items.title: Murdered woman's family make appeal 30 years on
paragraphs: The family of a woman whose murder remains unsolved 30 years after she was killed has urged anyone with information to come forward.
Vera Holland, 47, was last seen alive on 14 November 1996 after she left her home in St Barnabas Road in Reading, Berkshire, to buy a takeaway from KFC in Shinfield Road.

She failed to return home and was reported missing. Her body was found two days later on a fly-tip close to the Thames Water pumping station on the A327 between Arborfield and Shinfield, about three miles (4.8km) away. She had been strangled.
Speaking on behalf of Holland's family, her daughter Dawn Bennett said her family "feels the loss and heartbreak of losing her every day".
She said the mother-of-three was "devoted" to her family and a "very proud grandmother of seven".
Bennett continued: "She was robbed of the chance to watch her grandchildren grow, and those born after her death never got to experience her boundless love and affection.
"Someone out there knows exactly what happened to our mum. I implore you to come forward and contact the police with any piece of information, no matter how small.

"Thirty years is an agonisingly long time to wait for justice, especially while the person responsible has been allowed to carry on living their life freely and we feel the loss and heartbreak of losing her every day."
Thames Valley Police (TVP) investigators believe Holland never reached the KFC because she was not captured on its CCTV.
She was wearing a pink coat, green tartan shirt, black jumper and black shoes. None of the items have ever been recovered.
"Someone, somewhere, knows what happened to Vera," said Peter Beirne, from TVP's Major Crime Review Team.
"There may be someone who thought a piece of information was insignificant at the time, someone who was frightened to come forward, or someone whose loyalties have changed over the years," he added.

items.title: Extreme weather leaves gardeners hedging their bets
paragraphs: Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather.
West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought.
The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely.
Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there.
Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year.
"That's probably going to continue," he said.
"We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things.
"That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers."

items.title: UK-EU breakthrough will allow airport-style checks at Eurotunnel to avoid border ‘chaos’
paragraphs: Airport-style passport and fingerprinting controls are to be introduced at Eurotunnel in an attempt to prevent “short-term and long-term chaos” in Folkestone and Calais.

In a breakthrough for travellers, the European Commission has agreed to a new system in which an “eagle eye” camera system, already used in Rome and Paris airports to supervise fingerprinting and facial imaging, will be used at the border between the UK and France.
Yann Leriche, the chief executive of Getlink, the Eurotunnel owner, said it had tried to replicate the “airport experience” but wanted to go much further.

Instead of getting out of the car and getting biometrics taken at a terminal building, holidaymakers and business travellers will now be greeted with special drive-through terminals in Folkestone and Calais.

Both sides are now equipped with 120 kiosks under the case of an eagle-eye camera that will be monitored by police, similar to e-gates at airports where police are not physically present at each gate.

In the coming weeks, Leriche will meet UK and French authorities presenting a 40-page proposal to allow Eurotunnel to become a “laboratory” for an “intelligent border” using emerging tech and lessons learned from the US and Singapore.

The entry and exit system (EES) requires all third-country citizens including British passport holders to submit fingerprints and facial images as they enter and exit the Schengen area, but has been delayed for years.
EES was supposed to be active across the EU by 9 September, but nine of the 27 EU member states, including France, have yet to be deploy it fully because of continued technical issues.
It has always been a logistical nightmare for Eurotunnel and a potential cause of miles-long tailbacks at the approach to the terminal.

Originally, Getlink had planned to use a tablet to hand to the passengers in their cars to allow them to self-fingerprint and capture a facial image. It also looked at a system involving passengers parking up and going into the terminal to get fingerprinting.
But both models would have required the physical presence of police officers for first-time fingerprinting.

Leriche said: “We told the authorities: it is going to be a mess. Many people are going to the wrong place and you can’t have police jumping from one place to the next to solve the issues. It would also means customers would have a bad experience, particularly at peak time.
“This is not something people in airports experience, but nobody approached this before, thinking we could have an airport experience at the border here. But we said: why not?”

He said that after “many, many discussions” with the European Commission and the French authorities, finally they were “authorised” to trial “eagle-eye cameras” at each kiosk. “The French authorities are also on board because for them it is more efficient, too, so we are all aligned on the trial,” he said.
The trial will last two years, but Eurotunnel hopes the experiment will become permanent.

Each car will be able to pull up to an individual kiosk, with two stands per vehicle to read passports and take fingerprints and facial images. “It will prevent the chaos in the long term and the short term and if the experiment works, as hopefully it will, then it will become permanent,” said Leriche.
He said the company had been inspired by visits to the US/Mexico border controls, where drivers and passengers remain in their cars.

The requirement of having a police officer present each time a first-time passenger, or “primo” as they are known, submits their fingerprints was designed as a safeguard against subterfuge. Criminals, for example, could use a fellow passenger for example with a “clean skin” fingerprint.

Leriche said he had no idea when the system will be introduced by France. “It has been delayed and delayed and delayed, but our kiosks are there, they are can function but the connection with the French system is still not working. It is a question was are asking all the time.”
This week it emerged that the EU had filed a lawsuit against IBM and two other companies involved in the implementation of EES.

items.title: Why so much love between Ireland and Garth Brooks?
paragraphs: Country music superstar Garth Brooks will perform a multi-city tour of Ireland in 2027
Fans of Garth Brooks will be brushing off their Stetsons and polishing their cowboy boots after the country music superstar announced he will be performing in multiple cities across Ireland in 2027.
The tour includes Belfast, Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork and will be the first time he has played in Northern Ireland since his King's Hall gig in November 1998.

The singer has said in the past that Ireland is his favourite place in the world to sing, and the love appears to be mutual as his first two Belfast concerts sold out, with an extra date already added.
So why has an American country music star remained so popular with Irish fans for so many years?
Cathy O'Reilly previously saw Garth Brooks live at two of his Dublin concerts in 2022
Cathy O'Reilly, who is originally from County Monaghan but lives in Belfast, managed to get her tickets for the very first show of Garth Brooks' tour on 21 May 2027 at Boucher Road Playing Fields.
She has already seen Brooks perform live before - twice during his run of concerts in Dublin in 2022 and her love of his music was passed on from her parents and uncles.
"It's growing up listening to him it brings me back to my childhood. My uncle gave me his cd, he didn't even buy me one - just gave me his because I loved him so much."
She believes the Irish link to the US and the fact that fans on the island give the best welcome to performers, are the reasons for Garth Brooks' popularity in Ireland.
"He [Garth Brooks] gives us energy and we're giving it back ten-fold nearly, and we're just so welcoming so he really enjoys coming here."
Garth Brooks last performed in Ireland in 2022
Peter Aiken, from Aiken Promotions, told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the new Belfast gig is "red hot".
"There could be a fourth show in Belfast," he said.
Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history and is the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold.
In 2014 about 400,000 fans booked tickets to five concerts he had planned for Dublin's Croke Park but Dublin City Council only granted permission for three of them.
Brooks said he would only perform all five concerts or none at all and so the shows were cancelled.
Stephen Butler performs as a Garth Brooks tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls and described his job as "easy" due to the love of Garth Brooks' fans
Stephen Butler from Newtownabbey performs as a Garth Brooks' tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls.
His love for the musician also goes back to his childhood.
"My mother was a fan when I was younger, she was always playing his music and buying his albums so I loved the songs.
"I knew, with me loving Garth and there being such a following in Ireland, I knew it was the right thing to do."
He went to the Dublin concert in 2022 and while he hasn't yet got tickets for the Ireland dates next year, he hopes to get tickets to at least one of them closer to the time.
Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music"
"I was able to get four or five tickets about a week or two before the Croke Park shows, I'll definitely go - I have to go.
"His band is amazing, he's amazing, and his songs - he's got an endless amount of anthems."
Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music".
"I'm not saying I'm as good as Garth Brooks, but I definitely have his enthusiasm.
"I talk about him and how much I love him throughout the songs and I just identify with them as much as I can.
"My job is easy, I just have to go on there and get everybody singing along with me."
Garth Brooks performing at the King's Hall in 1998
Butler says he thinks the reason Garth Brooks remains so enduringly popular in Ireland is because the people here identify so strongly with his songs.
"Everybody loves Friends In Low Places, people of Ireland love it, they love Callin' Baton Rouge.

"I speak to a lot of people after I play the shows and a lot of people identify with some of the words in the songs, they tell me about a relative that's passed and they seem to have some kind of identification with the songs Tomorrow Never Comes or Unanswered Prayers - it talks about love and about how Garth feels.
"And in amongst Thunder Rolls and the big hits that Garth has, he sings big rocky country rock and ballads, so it's exciting and it's sad - it's an emotional roller coaster," he said.
"And he's such a down-to-earth, genuine, caring person, he seems to be a good soul and I think people people identify with his personality.
"It's a big working-class country and they love someone that's genuine and that talks from the heart."

items.title: From Fjord to U2: your complete entertainment guide to the week ahead
paragraphs: Fjord Out now Romanian auteur Cristian Mungiu’s latest stars Sebastian Stan and Renate Reinsve in a Norway-set drama about a Romanian couple whose five children are taken from them by the state. Based on real events, it looks at how an intersection of immigrant status, religious beliefs and prejudice may have contributed to the separation.

How to Rob a Bank Out now Not to be confused with the Netflix true-crime doc of the same name, this action comedy sees a gang of bank robbers, in modern parlance, “posting through it”, ie documenting their heists on social media, thereby handing the police a few free clues. Nicholas Hoult leads a cast including Zoë Kravitz, Pete Davidson and John C Reilly.

Prima Facie Out now Writer Suzie Miller adapts her own stage play, with Cynthia Erivo taking on the role originated by Jodie Comer of a barrister who specialises in defending those accused of sex crimes, but whose perspective shifts after she herself is sexually assaulted and has to give evidence. Susanna White directs.

Being Heumann Out now Disability rights activist Judith Heumann, known as the “Mother of the Disability Rights Movement”, is portrayed by Ruth Madeley in this biopic, which dramatises Heumann’s fight for civil rights protection for people with disabilities. Catherine Bray

Beabadoobee 14 to 18 November; tour starts Glasgow In the space of four albums of sweet and sour alt-rock, Londoner Bea Kristi has scored two UK chart-toppers, a US Top 10, and now an arena tour. The vast venues make sense: recent album Pylon is full of blossoming choruses and relatable angst. Michael Cragg

London jazz festival Various venues, to 22 November The second week of the spectacular London jazz festival includes vocalists Lizz Wright and Melody Gardot (15 & 16 Nov), avant-funk explorers GoGo Penguin (16 & 17 Nov), postbop originals Artemis (17 Nov), Andy Sheppard (18 Nov) and Jasper Høiby (19 Nov). John Fordham

The Marriage of Figaro Bradford Arts Centre, 17 & 18 November; touring to 25 November Bradford opera festival gives Mozart’s revolutionary hit a Yorkshire twist: a new English-language adaptation by Ian McMillan transports this class comedy to 1970s Bradford, complete with nods to Bollywood and an ensemble of western and Indian classical musicians. Flora Willson

Hayden Thorpe 14 to 19 November; tour starts Kendal After his band, baroque four-piece Wild Beasts, split in 2018, Hayden Thorpe and his florid vocal stylings immediately set about on his solo journey. With two years having passed since his third album, 2024’s Ness, these shows should see him road-test some new material. MC

Louise Giovanelli White Cube Mason’s Yard, London, 20 November to 16 January One of the UK’s most exciting young painters returns with new works dealing with her favourite themes: curtains, hair, female screen idols and the cinematic kiss. It’s dramatic, dreamy, ultra-theatrical and quasi-religious art.

David Nash The Burton at Bideford, 14 November to 17 January He is best known for shaping living trees into immersive sculptural installations, but this Devon show looks at how drawing has always been central to shaping David Nash’s approach to depicting and working with the natural world.

Ryan Gander Towner Gallery, Eastbourne, 14 November to 11 April For his first UK institutional show in almost 20 years, playful conceptualist Ryan Gander turns up the humour dial with a series of installations featuring animatronic mice, repurposed toys and paintings of balloons.

Angela Harding Yorkshire Sculpture Park, near Wakefield, 14 November to 28 February Linocuts, oil paintings and decorated wooden birds by this hugely respected illustrator, returning to Yorkshire Sculpture Park 10 years after her last show with more nature-loving ecological imagery. Eddy Frankel

Rosie Holt Maidenhead, 14 November; Birmingham, 19 November; touring to 5 March Holt and her MP alter ego (originally Tory, now Labour) return to poke fun at the political classes in a madcap current affairs pastiche underpinned by a more heartfelt meditation on the sexism faced by women in the public eye. Rachel Aroesti

Matthew Bourne’s Cinderella Plymouth Theatre Royal, 16 to 21 November; touring to 8 May A revival of Bourne’s Cinderella, which turns the fairytale into a wartime romance set in London during the blitz. Dancing with the drama of Prokofiev’s fantastic score, it’s a love story that also nods to the darkness of real events. Lyndsey Winship

Nine Night Kiln theatre, London, to 2 January Amit Sharma revives Natasha Gordon’s sparkling hit, about a Jamaican family gathering in their suburban London home for the traditional nine nights of grieving after the death of beloved matriarch Gloria. Miriam Gillinson

Cranford Orange Tree theatre, London, to 16 January The Orange Tree has a reputation for brilliant festive shows that feel both cosy and contemporary. This year, Josh Roche stages Elizabeth Gaskell’s sumptuous novel, with Tamsin Grieg as the intriguing woman at the centre of 1840s Cranford. MG

The Altruists Netflix, 19 November From Artificial to You Can See Everything, tech’s most infamous billionaires are all over our screens at present. This drama relates the spectacular rise and fall of crypto boss Sam Bankman-Fried (Say Nothing’s Anthony Boyle). Julia Garner co-stars as his girlfriend and business partner, Caroline Ellison.

Bill’s Included BBC One & iPlayer, 20 November, 9.30pm The predicaments of landlords don’t usually tug at the heartstrings, but an exception may well be made for Rob Brydon’s Bill, a lonely divorcee who tries to befriend the students he rents his spare rooms to in this cross-generational houseshare sitcom from comedy duo the Pin.

Honey BBC One & iPlayer, 14 November, 9pm Early 1980s East Berlin is the irresistibly retro setting for this zany and stylish new cold war spy thriller from Emma Moran (Extraordinary), in which a rookie MI6 agent joins forces with a CIA operative to take down a Stasi officer. Ann Skelly and Rory Kinnear star.

When a Witness Recants HBO Max, 18 November Made in collaboration with Ta-Nehisi Coates, this devastating documentary by Dawn Porter hears from the three Baltimore men who served 36 years in prison for a murder they didn’t commit – as well as the schoolboy who was forced to provide false testimony against them. RA

Grand Theft Auto VI PS5/Xbox; out 19 November Well, it’s the big one. Thirteen years of memes in the making, Rockstar Games’s Florida-inspired crime opus is upon us. It stars a criminal couple on the run, Jason and Lucia, and as well as taking them on stick-ups, car thefts and all the usual cop-baiting shenanigans, you can also take them on cute little dates, which is certainly new for GTA. Only a game this vast could ever hope to live up to the hype.

Spirit Crossing PC, Switch, Switch 2; out now In a world above the clouds, players work together to make a home, coming together to build towns, protect them (and each other) from storms, and help guide lost spirits. A welcoming, optimistic hangout of a game. Keza MacDonald

U2 – Carnaval de Luz Out now On their first album of new material in nine years, U2 sound more invigorated than they have since popping music on people’s phones without permission back in 2014. Ragged single Silencio rattles along like a much younger band, while Street of Dreams is classic widescreen Bono.

Snoh Aalegra – Legendary Love Out now Sweden-born, LA-based Snoh Aalegra drapes her silk-soft voice over 13 new songs, headlined by beautiful lead single I Love You. Full of vintage Prince-isms in the production and a luxurious chorus, it’s very nearly matched in quality by the slowburn ballad Just Friends.

Royal Blood – Dead Company Out now Worthing rockers Royal Blood, AKA Mike Kerr and Ben Thatcher, return after a short hiatus with this fifth album. Mixed by Alan Moulder (Depeche Mode, Foo Fighters), songs such as the blistering title track and Swallow the Bomb’s sweary chorus seem ripe for next summer’s festivals.

Say Now – Say What You See Out now Since launching as Needanamebro in 2022, UK girlband Say Nowhave been searching for a sound, flitting between 90s R&B (Brick By Brick) and Raye-penned breakup anthems (Supermarket). On this six-track EP – executive produced by PinkPantheress – the trio comfortably ride a suite of punchy dance-pop bops. MC

This Is Our Story With Seth Pinnock Podcast London-based youth charity Symphony Co’s new audio series hosted by founder Seth Pinnock gets into the deep questions of purpose and creativity with celebrity guests, including the actor Billy Porter.

Antony Cooke Substack Home chef Antony Cooke’s newsletters are full of recipes that blend readily available ingredients with a touch of restaurant glamour. Follow along to make everything from a Mexican-inspired squash soup to a showstopping fish pie.

Kazakhstan’s Chess Gambit BBC World Service, 19 November, 9.32am Keen to develop their homegrown chess talent, the Kazakh government introduced state-led initiatives to encourage young people to take up the game. Journalist Zoe Strimpel investigates how chess has since become central to Kazakhstan’s nation building. Ammar Kalia

items.title: This week Sony revived its classic Walkman headphones
paragraphs: This week on Dezeen, Japanese electronics company Sony launched a remake of its original Walkman headphones, which have colourful foam pads and lean into 1980s nostalgia.

The headphones, called MDR-3R, resemble the model that debuted with the first portable Walkman cassette player in 1979. However, the new edition has a USB-C connector that works with most modern devices.

Other design news included Swedish designer Gustaf Westman’s unveiling of his full collection for media company Disney, including a bookstand shaped like Donald Duck and a mirror that resembles Pluto.

“Mickey’s ears and white gloves, Minnie’s bow, Goofy’s playful silhouette – they’re instantly recognisable shapes, and that made them really fun to work with,” Westman told Dezeen about working with the familiar characters.
American architect Steven Holl has designed a colourful watch for Swiss watch brand Cauny informed by a compliment architect Álvaro Siza once gave him, telling Holl he used colour “like Matisse”.
The colourful watch, which has a three-dimensional dial with red, green, yellow and blue colour blocks, was designed to be a dialogue between the two architects.
A housing development in Andorra designed by French studio Ateliers Jean Nouvel and Spanish studio Ribas & Ribas Arquitectos has been damaged in a fire.

Called La Querola, the project is shortlisted in the housing category of this year’s Dezeen Awards and recently won the awards’ public vote. The cause of the fire is unknown and no official estimate of the extent of the damage has been released so far.
In Shanghai, access to the staircase of the Grand Opera House by international studio Snøhetta has been restricted to ticket holders.
Access to the spiral staircase, which leads up to the roof and has become a popular spot for photos, now costs £5.60 per person. Snøhetta told Dezeen that “visitor management is necessary”.
In car news, Swedish brand Polestar has unveiled its Formula 2030 concept car that the brand says “screams performance”.
The low-slung sports car has signature Dual Blade headlights and was intended to project power, with a long bonnet, wraparound windscreen, short overhangs, muscular haunches and 22-inch wheels.
In a roundup, we explored five examples of Mesoamerican modern architecture that combine principles from ancient architecture with modern techniques.
Curator and writer Su Wu chose five homes, which she says “reflect the complex aesthetic cultures of Mesoamerica”, from her book on the subject.
Popular projects on Dezeen this week include a former agricultural barn in Cornwall, a viewpoint informed by Viking rings and a playful Portuguese retreat.
Our podcast this week looked at the Cybertruck, asking: was it a flop or a design success?
This week on Dezeen is our regular roundup of the week’s top news stories. Subscribe to our newsletters to be sure you don’t miss anything.

items.title: Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins wins race for Alaska governor, replaces a Republican
paragraphs: Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a Democrat, has won the race for governor of Alaska and will replace the outgoing Republican. Here he's seen at a polling station at the University of Alaska Anchorage on Election Day. Eric Stone/Alaska Public Media hide caption

Democrat Jonathan Kreiss-Tomkins, a former state representative from the small island community of Sitka, won the race for Alaska governor, according to a race call by the Associated Press. At 37, he'll be the youngest governor in state history.
Kreiss-Tomkins will replace outgoing Gov. Mike Dunleavy, a term-limited Republican who has been governor since 2018. The state's last Democratic governor was Tony Knowles, who left office in 2002.
Kreiss-Tomkins, known by his initials JKT, made his "high-energy, bipartisan, problem-solving approach" a centerpiece of his campaign.

He's said he plans to build an administration of Democrats, Republicans and independents and described himself at a debate as a "man of the middle." He was endorsed by three former governors — a Democrat, a Republican and an independent — along with Republican Sen. Lisa Murkowski.
Alaskans have had enough of zero-sum partisan politics, he said in an interview just before voting at a precinct in Anchorage on Election Day.
"I strongly believe people just want things to work, and want people to work together," Kreiss-Tomkins said.

The AP race call came after over a week of counting votes, including those coming in by mail and from remote parts of the state. In the ranked-choice system the state uses, he faced three Republican candidates, including one backed by President Trump. Winning requires getting a majority of the votes.
Voters were also facing a question on the ballot about whether to scrap that unique, ranked-choice system. That proposal failed, according to another AP race call, keeping the system in place.
With Kreiss-Tomkins' win and others in the midterms, Democrats will hold 30 governors' offices across the country, up from 24 now.
Kreiss-Tomkins will take office in a state where voters have loudly complained that things aren't working as they should.

Rising costs and relatively flat state funding have forced schools to close and class sizes to rise. Already-high costs for food, fuel and housing have risen sharply, and a looming shortage of easily accessible natural gas near the state's population centers is threatening to push prices higher. And Alaskans have been migrating out of the state for more than a decade.
The Republicans in the race were Trump-backed business owner Bernadette Wilson, former Anchorage Mayor Dave Bronson and former Alaska Attorney General Treg Taylor.
Kreiss-Tomkins is set to take office at noon Dec. 7.
Eric Stone covers state government for Alaska Public Media.

items.title: University hounded out of Hungary by Orbán reaches out to new government
paragraphs: A university that Viktor Orbán tried to chase out of Hungary is open to expanding its presence in Budapest, in a mark of confidence in the country’s democratic future.

Carsten Q Schneider, the interim president and rector of Central European University (CEU), said it was interested in increasing its programmes in Budapest, as long as this did not damage the student experience.

So far the CEU has not held formal talks with Hungary’s new government, which has promised to restore academic freedom, “but our hand is reaching out, their hand is reaching out – it is just that they have many things to do”, the academic told the Guardian.

The CEU relocated its main activities to Vienna from Budapest in 2019, after pressure from the previous government led by Orbán. But the outlook changed when Péter Magyar won a landslide victory in April pledging to root out corruption and reform the state.

The CEU, founded by Hungarian-American financier and philanthropist George Soros in 1991 to entrench democratic change in the region, was forced to cease awarding degrees in Budapest in response to a law widely seen as targeting the institution.

The EU’s highest court struck down Hungary’s “Lex CEU” in 2020, finding that it violated the EU charter of fundamental rights, but the verdict came too late for the university. The CEU retains 312 staff in Budapest, mostly administrative, but the majority, 476, and all its teaching, are in Vienna.

Schneider said upgrading the status of the CEU, which is privately funded, in Budapest would be “a symbol for academic freedom [and] of resilience” but depended on goodwill and funding independent of the Hungarian government. He said a decision on its future in Hungary would be taken by the CEU’s 13-member board, whose members include Soros and his son, Alexander Soros.
“We don’t want special treatment,” Schneider said. ‘“We are a great asset, so let’s work out something.”

But the CEU, which he said was “thriving tremendously” in Vienna, does not plan a wholesale return to Budapest. Any change would have to ensure the quality of the student experience, for instance, assuring that students would be able to combine courses, say in economics and history, without having to travel the 200km-plus distance between the two cities.
Focused on social sciences, law and humanities, the CEU has more than 1,400 students from 103 countries, mostly doing master’s and PhD programmes.

According to Schneider, for the first time in the CEU’s 25-year history, students from the US now make up the largest cohort of master’s students (10%). The CEU has seen an increase in US applicants since Donald Trump returned to the White House and launched a sweeping campaign against elite universities, including slashing federal funding and seeking to exert control over internal policies.

The CEU rector has had informal talks with US academics on how to maintain academic freedom under pressure from rightwing populists. He described his message as: “Don’t be naive for a second. These people have a plan, so it’s not by accident that they attack universities. They want to have cultural hegemony.” He added, however, that Trump and allied movements, such as Germany’s Alternative für Deutschland, have identified “real problems”, such as in the US how universities have entrenched “a reproduction of elites”

When coming under political pressure, he said universities needed “to look for allies”, among other academic institutions, students, alumni and parents. Institutions also had to stand up for disciplines under attack, such as gender studies, Schneider added.
He recalled the outpouring of support for CEU – when tens of thousands of people protested in Budapest in defence of the university – as “one of the most humbling experiences I have had”.
Schneider, a German political scientist who specialises in the study of democracies and regime transition, said Magyar had successfully used Orbán’s political machine against him.

“Nobody has a better idea than [Magyar] how to defeat the most potent and the most skilled illiberal populist [Orbán]. So he knows something.” He added: “The people and skills that you need to bring a non-democratic regime down are not the same and sometimes the opposite of what it takes to establish a democracy. So the question now is whether he [Magyar] has the skills to basically reinvent liberal democracy for the 21st century.”

Schneider said Hungary could be the world’s first “post-illiberal democracy” – a model for democratic restoration, just as Orbán inspired rightwing populists around the world. But he also raised doubts about this thesis, saying there were questions about how Magyar and his Tisza party might develop in the context of Hungary’s “very difficult economic situation”.

The test would be, he suggested, when Magyar faces losing support and, eventually, defeat at the ballot box. “So what happens when he loses support and then cracks in his movement appear? Will he be the visionary leader who manages … to establish a three, four, five-party system, where people compete? That is to be seen.”

items.title: Trump, Putin and Xi plan historic joint meeting in China next week, White House says
paragraphs: Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The unprecedented meeting between the leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.
"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.
It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Moscow and Beijing are yet to comment.
No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior American official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21-member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the President of the United States, the President of the People's Republic of China, and the President of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said the president's trip, which will also include attending an Association of Southeast Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".
Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.
Earlier this month, Russian state news agency Tass reported that Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov had said there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

items.title: US-bound flights out of Australia grounded as telecommunications outage affects American travel
paragraphs: Some US bound flights from Sydney Airport were grounded or delayed on Saturday after to American authorities halted departures and delayed landings at all US airports.
Flights from Melbourne Airport were also affected, with travel for passengers expected to depart for Los Angeles shortly after 10am being delayed by more than two hours.
Sydney Airport confirmed the US ban on flight arrivals was lifted shortly before 1pm, although it was not known how this would impact delays.
Earlier, the airport confirmed some US bound flights had been grounded.
“We are aware of the nationwide ground stop issued by the US Federal Aviation Administration and are monitoring the situation closely,” the spokesperson said.
“Passengers travelling to or via the United States should check with their airline for the latest information regarding their flight.”

The US Federal ⁠Aviation Administration announced the nationwide pause in response to “a temporary telecommunications outage”. It has since lifted the grounding order, as it continued to investigate the cause of the outage.
Passengers on two US bound flights from Melbourne Airport, which were due to depart at 12.00pm and 12.45pm, were also told to expect delays due to the situation in the US.
These include a Qantas flight to Dallas, and an United Airlines flight to San Francisco.
Flights to the US were also delayed at Brisbane Airport, where passengers on one US bound flight began boarding at around 1pm.

items.title: Stuart Bonds made ‘racist’ and ‘divisive’ comments. But One Nation is showing no sign of dumping the NSW candidate
paragraphs: In a Facebook video from a Sydney anti-immigration rally on Sunday, as a man dressed like a medieval knight watches on, One Nation leader upper house candidate Stuart Bonds launches into a speech against “mass” migration.
“Make no mistake, we are being demographically replaced inside our own nation,” he says.
“If we don’t support Australian mothers having Australian children, we [are] going to pay for other cultures’ children to be brought up in our lands.”

In an apparent allusion to the “great replacement theory”, a far-right conspiracy theory that white westerners are being actively “replaced” by non-white immigrants, he continued: “That’s the socialist plan, is to destroy and bring down and tear down the fabric of your civilisation.”

The comments sparked a wave of criticism, but the party has shown no signs of taking Bonds off the ticket for the 2027 New South Wales state election. One Nation did, however, dump one candidate this week: the Victorian branch disendorsed a lower-house candidate over an old social media post describing Hitler as the GOAT, an acronym for the greatest of all time.

The rally was not a one-off. On a podcast released on Monday with the rally’s organiser, the Australian Lobby Group, Bonds appeared to double down on the remarks. He did not challenge host Scott Challen’s assertion that Labor governments were building “ethnic voting blocks with Middle Eastern and subcontinent people … to stack the numbers to entrench power for themselves”, instead responding: “Mate, and that’s why we’re going to get rid of all of the multicultural grants, right?”

On Wednesday, in an interview with ABC Upper Hunter, Bonds responded to questions about his comments by citing Australian Bureau of Statistics data that shows the proportion of Australians born overseas has trended upward since the end of the second world war, from 10% in 1945 to 32% in 2025. He did not mention that the proportion of Australians born overseas was at its highest – 32.4% – in 1891, the first year of available data.
Bonds said with the Australian birthrate beneath the 2.1 required to replace the population, “I would just like to know what people assume is going to happen.”
“Where are these people going to come from?” he said.

NSW Labor pounced on the rally comments immediately, with the state’s premier, Chris Minns, calling them “frankly outrageous and racist”. The government passed motions in both houses censuring Bonds, not yet a member.
The Coalition followed four days later. On Wednesday afternoon, the opposition leader, Kellie Sloane, said Bonds’ language was “clearly divisive”.
But she did not rule out a confidence and supply arrangement with One Nation after the March state election.
“We will not form a coalition with One Nation, [but] we’ll work with anyone post-election if we’re in a minority government,” she told reporters.

The Australian Financial Review has reported many of her MPs privately expect the party to go into a Coalition with One Nation. And with the Coalition consistently polling behind One Nation, that makes Bonds not a fringe candidate, but a potentially influential figure.
The ABC’s former election analyst, Antony Green, said the remarks played straight into Labor’s hands.
“This will certainly be something the Labor party uses in all those multi-ethnic seats in Sydney,” he said – seats like those on the rural fringes of Sydney, which One Nation said it plans to target.

Indeed the deputy premier, Prue Car, who has Indian heritage and whose electorate of Londonderry is one of the seats in question, gave an impassioned critique of Bonds’ comments in question time on Tuesday.
“Who’s he [Bonds] talking about when he talks about this?” she said. “I tell you who he’s talking about – he’s talking about families like mine, and families that I represent.”

Kos Samaras, a former Labor strategist who is now a director of polling group Redbridge, said that while the comments likely won’t play well in Sydney seats – including alienating moderate Liberal voters worried about the party going into Coalition with One Nation – “you might be able to get away with it in certain parts of NSW”.
And Bonds, a former coalminer, has made his base in the Hunter.
Samaras said One Nation could “clean the deck” in the regions, including Labor-held seats in the Hunter, and “pretty much anything else the coalition hasn’t got bolted down to the ground”.

The NSW One Nation leader, Mike Newman, who in September said he “made a mistake” when he told a Sydney rally he wanted to stop abortions, did not respond directly when asked if he agreed with Bonds’ comments or if he would rein in his first-placed upper house candidate.
“What I will say is that what Stuart Bonds is a patriotic Aussie. He’s a coalminer. He has very, very strong views,” he said on Tuesday.

Newman, who previously rejected claims that One Nation was racist, said on Tuesday: “What we want to do is … protect Australian values, and that is the fundamental thing that Stuart Bonds is pushing for. It’s about assimilation.”
The NSW treasurer, Daniel Mookhey, whose parents immigrated to Australia from India in the 1970s, told the ABC that Bonds’ comments were not grounded in reality.
“I think he’s saying that there is a deliberate conspiracy to use migrants to replace the way he puts it, native-born Australians for political reasons,” Mookhey said.
The quota for election to the upper house is 4.5%, making Bonds all but guaranteed to be elected, with One Nation polling in the high 20s and low 30s in recent months.

Green expects the party to pick up four or five seats in the upper house; so far it has only named three candidates: Newman, Bonds and Jeff Bacon, a firearms manufacturer who is second on the upper house ticket.
But unlike Victoria, NSW has optional preferential voting, which means when that state goes to the polls in March, lower house preferences flows aren’t guaranteed.
But Bonds has downplayed whether he may have jeopardised a future preference deal with the Coalition.
“If the Coalition have a problem with facts, the same as the Labor party, then maybe it will,” he told the ABC.
“But I’m not here to impress the Coalition.”
