items.title: Microsoft ‘deeply sorry’ for global disruption that could have billion-dollar impact on Australia
paragraphs: The Microsoft outage could be a disaster for the Australian economy that forces some small businesses to close, with costs expected to run into the billions of dollars, experts have warned.

The US software company has said it is “deeply sorry” for a widespread outage that caused disruption to millions of users, organisations and businesses across the globe – and that it has “addressed the underlying issue”.
The company said the outage was a “technical issue” not related to cyber-attacks or AI agents, and that it continued to gradually restore services.
Experts have said the outage exposes “Australia’s reliance on foreign technology” and that people unable to be paid, send an invoice, or access government services “are entitled to be worried”.

The outage of Microsoft’s services, which began on Friday morning, lasted roughly 18 hours before services started to recover. Microsoft said it was bringing back services gradually to ensure a stable restoration.
Ashwin Pal, a partner at the risk advisory firm RSM Australia, said his clients had activated business continuity and disaster recovery plans, but many businesses didn’t have a fallback.
“A protracted event like this can easily be the straw that breaks the camel’s back for smaller entities,” Pal said.
Pal said Microsoft had obviously struggled to recover, which raised bigger questions.
“I’m a technologist and I’m actually flabbergasted as to how something like this could have happened … they pushed out a change which should have been tested,” Pal said.

The Australian Computer Society has renewed calls for the federal government to urgently review which critical IT systems rely on a single provider, and where backup options could keep the economy running.
The society’s chief executive, Prins Ralston, said the outage had “exposed Australia’s reliance on foreign technology”, particularly on small businesses.
“Australians who couldn’t get paid, couldn’t send an invoice, or couldn’t reach a government service this morning are entitled to be worried,” Ralston said.
Australian hospitals and health clinics were affected by the outage, although the Australian Medical Association (AMA) on Friday said had been no impacts for patient care.

“We’ve had some facilities return to using paper for scripts because authentication to get into lots of prescribing software requires multifactor verification, which requires you to be able to access your Microsoft-supported email,” said the AMA’s president, Dr Michael Bonning.
Courts in South Australia and Victoria reported that the outage had affeced its email system. Many schools across the country were also affected.
Service NSW, the one-stop shop agency for residents, drivers, and business owners to access government services, encouraged customers to delay their visits to its service centres.
Federal government departments have also been maffectedy the outage, including national security agencies.

The head the domestic spy agency Asio, Mike Burgess, on Friday said the organisation’s systems “operate on multiple levels”, adding that they had been affected “on one level, yes, but not completely”.
The outage has affected businesses and organisations across the world that use Microsoft products.
In the UK, healthcare systems were disrupted and several British police forces urged people not to try to report crimes online and to phone them in instead.

US government offices across the country have been affected by the outage, including congressional offices that heavily rely on Outlook email. The US House’s chief administrative officer that handles IT for the chamber sent out a “campus-wide alert” to staffers on Thursday about the outage, Politico reported.

In Japan, the shipping company Sagawa Express said it was unable to accept online reservations for some of its services at airports and train stations while Taisho, a leading pharmaceutical company, said it was having to handle orders by phone.
When stock market trading opened on Wall Street, shares in Microsoft dipped slightly, down 1.1% at $516.86.
Microsoft has suggested the outage may have been caused by problems with the settings applied to servers responsible for keeping Microsoft 365 up and running.
Microsoft’s executive vice-president of Copilot, Charles Lamanna, said: “We regret that today’s outages caused disruptions for our customers, and we are working to address the issue.”

items.title: When to put up a real Christmas tree - according to an expert
paragraphs: The appropriate time to put up your Christmas tree is a question almost as divisive as whether Yorkshire pudding has a place on the Christmas dinner plate. Some might feel the best time is just after Bonfire Night, others may think Christmas Eve is more apt, and most will probably plump for somewhere in between.
Tesco started selling Christmas trees at half-price this week and said more than 90% of its trees had sold out by the end of November last year.
Lidl and some other retailers are also launching their ranges next week, while others including Dobbies Garden Centres are waiting until the last week of November.
But with Christmas Day still six weeks away, is it unwise to rush into buying a real tree so early? And do you risk spending your Christmas week cleaning up piles of pine needles?
Probably, says Mick Walker, from Bolton Christmas Trees, which grows trees in the Scottish Highlands before sending them to homes across the UK.
"It might last until the beginning of Christmas, but it won't last the full holiday," he warns. "Unless its a potted one, it's going to be sagging by Christmas Day - big time."
He calls Tesco's half-price deal "insane", adding that it's "sucking them into buying something now that isn't going to do the job".
So when would he suggest is the best time? "If it was me, I'd put it up a week before Christmas eve, [and it will] last straight through until New Year."

The most popular Christmas trees available in the UK are the Nordmann fir variety, which are non-drop, meaning they don't drop their needles. Norway Spruce is another common variety and have a strong pine scent, but generally should be kept outdoors or put up just before Christmas.
Pine trees, Walker says, have the longest lifespan, but he concedes they lack that classic Christmas look.
Or, of course, you could opt for a tried-and-tested artificial tree, which is what Katie McDonald from Belfast put up in her house last week.

"When I was a kid my mum always waited to the last minute to let us kids put the tree up. We would be the last house on our street and the last of all our friends to get the tree up," she tells the BBC.
"So I made myself a wee childlike promise that when I had my own house I'd be one of the first to put my tree up."
She says she will replace her artificial tree with a real one in a few weeks, so it is in prime condition come Christmas Day.

items.title: Even Grand Theft Auto's original creators haven't been able to play GTA 6
paragraphs: GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D games
After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks, the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.
The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.
And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.
"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.
Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?
Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.
Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft Auto
The original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.
Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.
Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table.
"At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"
Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".
He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".
The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D
The team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer.
But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book".
"At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.
Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it".
"For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow.
"And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"

Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt.
"We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."

Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.
Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald.
"It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."

Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.

Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA.
"It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says.
"Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."
The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's map
When GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.
The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming.
"I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.

MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.
She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.
As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life".
"It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."
"It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, left
GTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.
Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.
This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.

The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game.
"Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald.
"It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time.
"It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."
Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?
"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says.
"But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."
Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful".
"It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."

items.title: Brand, Walliams and MAFS: Is this a reckoning for the entertainment industry?
paragraphs: This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.
On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.
Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.
By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.
Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.
These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.
In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.
All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.
"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.
In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.
Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.
It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him. The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".
When looking at what’s driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement.
It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed.
In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one.
Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued.
"There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman.
It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing.

When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar.

Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked. Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused".
One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking.
"I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me.
But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up.
Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs.
She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained.

"There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriously”.
For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult.

Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention."
Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up.
And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate.
Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change – although not always.
Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted.
Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past.
But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judge’s remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths.
When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."
"I think attitudes have changed,” said Freeman. “It doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.”
Events of the past few weeks highlight how figures who rose to prominence in the nineties and noughties did so in an era with different standards.
Lad culture and celebrity status shielded Brand and others from scrutiny.
Now, behaviour once dismissed as eccentricity or womanising is increasingly being reassessed and called out. Times are catching up with some men of that era.
However, it would be an error to assume this sort of behaviour is confined to the past.
"This is not just about nineties/noughties culture," Wark told me. "It can't be dismissed as a hangover of the past, this is about right now and the industry changes that must happen.
"There will be more cases to come, sexual abuse, coercive control, verbal and physical abuse. It is not OK, and it never was OK."
This week, comedian Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women were "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.
And in the past few days, I've had tip-offs about other celebrities allegedly abusing their power. No doubt other journalists have too.
None of those is reportable, yet. As Freeman said: "There are other names out there, but you and I couldn't name them as we'd be sued".

But one "cheering thing", she said, was that the sort of jokes and innuendos from the nineties and noughties, or even the optics of seeing a much older man with a younger girl would no longer be "glossed over".
"It wouldn't be laughed at, and it wouldn't be 'nudge nudge'," Freeman said. "That kind of open, in your face, weirdness won't happen any more".
"On the downside, that may make it harder to identify predators, if it means these things are kept more in the shadows."
Then there’s the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out.
Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named.

"There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me.
This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use.
Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday.
When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.
It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code.
There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims.
"People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark.

"Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate".
What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change.
Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment.
If you have more information about this story, you can reach Noor by email at noor.nanji@bbc.co.uk

items.title: Bluetongue virus confirmed on County Down farm
paragraphs: Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to DAERA.
"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety – milk and meat are safe to consume."
Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.
"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.
"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."
The disease was first detected here near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.
A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.
Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.
The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.

items.title: Widespread frost and freezing fog forecast as cold health alerts continue
paragraphs: Arctic air will maintain its grip on the UK to start the weekend, as cold health alerts remain in place for a large swathe of England.
Saturday will dawn with another sharp and widespread frost with the coldest conditions expected in England and Wales.
Patches of freezing fog could also be a hazard, reducing visibility and bringing a risk of very slippery surfaces in southern and eastern England.
Then it is all change by Sunday with most areas having a frost-free start, but heavy bursts of rain and brisk winds will sweep across the country later.
Freezing fog and rime ice may mean some slippery conditions on untreated roads and pavements in the south on Saturday morning
Saturday will start with temperatures widely below freezing in parts of England and Wales.
Lows in towns and cities are expected to fall to -2 or -3C, but in the countryside they could be as low as -5C.
In southern and south-east England there could also be some patchy freezing fog which forms in air that is below freezing.
Super-cooled water droplets remain suspended in the air and it can be particularly dangerous as they can freeze on impact turning untreated pavements into instant ice rinks.
Yellow cold health alerts from the UK Health Security Agency (UKHSA) are in force for the West Midlands and north-west England until 12:00 Saturday, external.
More of a breeze further north will mean most places will be a few degrees above freezing.
The frostiest conditions on Saturday morning are likely to be in the southern half of the British Isles
After the fog and frost clears, Saturday will largely become a bright and dry day.
By the afternoon, temperatures will rise across the UK - ranging from 7C in parts of the Highlands to a milder 12C in south-west England.
England and Wales are forecast to see long spells of sunshine, away from the odd shower early on in the far north-west.
Northern Ireland will have some bright spells in the morning, with thickening cloud in the afternoon and rain by evening.
A few showers are expected in parts of Scotland where is will also be a breezy day, and will feel colder due to the wind chill.
Expected rainfall totals this weekend will be highest in Scotland and Northern Ireland
The chilly but mainly dry spell of late will be replaced by something more unsettled on Sunday as low pressure sweeps in from the Atlantic.
Areas of showery rain will drift from west to east across much of the UK.
The heaviest of the rain is likely in Scotland and Northern Ireland, as well as southern and western parts of England and Wales.
This is generally good news for places still suffering from drought or severe drought, although parts of eastern England may avoid most of the rainfall.
You can keep up to date with your local forecast by checking BBC Weather online and on the app.

items.title: Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?
paragraphs: In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.
More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.
Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'
Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.
Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.
Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".
"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.

Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.
When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people

Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says., external
Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."
King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.
"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."
Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo

African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.
But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.

In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.

It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.
"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.
"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."
Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response

Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.

The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.
And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".
But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.

No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.
Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.

These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.
The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".
Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events
The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.
"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.
And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.
"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.
Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives

Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."

Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."
But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.
Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.
"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."
That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.
"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.
"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

items.title: Amazon has a plan to index the world’s online shopping data
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

Amazon has plans to build a vault of data on every product sold anywhere on the internet, even products Amazon doesn’t sell, and make the information available through its own site, according to Reuters. The project, called the “World Product Graph,” is meant to make it less likely that shoppers leave Amazon to do their product research on Reddit or Google, and make it more likely shoppers end up at Amazon even if they’re searching for a product sold elsewhere. The same goes for AI agents — if Amazon has the largest stockpile of shopping data, AI agents may rely on its index of products over others, so even people shopping with bots will end up on its pages.

Links to outside retailers’ products have already started popping up on Amazon through the “shop direct” feature it launched last year. The company also has its own AI shopping assistant, Alexa for Shopping, previously called Rufus. The World Product Graph project would also be aimed at fixing issues with the AI by providing it more data. According to Reuters, an internal Amazon document on the project says “Many Rufus answers are factually wrong or incomplete” and running users’ Amazon searches with the AI is expensive. Adding more data is reportedly supposed to make the system more accurate and able to use cheaper models.

Whether this actually ships is still up in the air. The internal document reportedly says the project “depends on discovering how brands organize their products on their own websites,” which could involve Amazon crawling other retailers’ sites. Reuters says it’s unclear “if or when this plan may be implemented,” but said the document on it included an October 1st, 2027 release date.

Amazon said in a statement to Reuters that “Draft, outdated documents often paint an incomplete picture and the existence of a brainstorming document such as this one doesn’t necessarily reflect our current plans.”

items.title: How the Jensen Huang scandal created a headache for business-friendly Singapore
paragraphs: Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy
ByTessa Wong and Osmond ChiaReporting fromSingapore

A major scandal involving Nvidia founder Jensen Huang and a suspected Chinese spy based in Singapore has cast a spotlight on the city-state's success as a global chip hub - and a location for alleged illicit trade.

On Thursday, Huang stepped down from the US chip giant after admitting he had an affair. He was reportedly involved with a woman named Alice Huang, who ran Singaporean data centre company Megaspeed, a major buyer of Nvidia's chips.
For decades, Singapore has painstakingly cultivated a reputation as an open, business-friendly economy offering easy access to both the US and Chinese markets.
With the AI boom, it has become a major hub for the trade of high-end semiconductor chips in recent years.
Singapore was the second-largest billing centre globally last year for Nvidia, accounting for nearly a fifth of what the US chip giant earns.
But notably, less than 1% of its earnings were for chips that actually entered Singapore, as the island acts as a hub for many Asian companies to place orders and send them elsewhere.

Since 2022, when the US restricted advanced American semiconductors from being exported to China or acquired by Chinese companies, US officials have been concerned that other countries such as Singapore could be used by Chinese companies to gain access to the chips.

It became the biggest buyer of Nvidia's chips in South East Asia and is suspected of giving backdoor access to these chips to Chinese companies via its data centres in Malaysia, Indonesia and Thailand.
While Singapore does not prohibit the transfer of advanced AI chips to companies abroad, such moves can breach US export controls.
Singapore has said that while it does not enforce "unilateral export controls imposed by other countries" it expects all companies in its jurisdiction to respect such regulations.
The city-state has had some success in policing this.

It has charged four companies and five individuals - including Chinese nationals - for various offences including fraud, following US concerns that Chinese AI company DeepSeek had been buying Nvidia chips from third parties in Singapore, among other places.
They also tried to probe Megaspeed, but were faced with a number of difficulties.

In a statement released on Thursday, the government said that since February 2025, they had been looking into whether Megaspeed and other firms had made false declarations about data servers which were purchased and exported through Singapore.
The companies stated the equipment would end up in neighbouring Malaysia, but Singapore authorities suspect the equipment's final destinations were elsewhere.

Singapore said it sought assistance from US authorities several times to get more information from one of the investigated companies - Supermicro, a US-based company which the BBC understands was supplying computer servers to Megaspeed.
But "despite these repeated requests, Singapore has to date received limited information or assistance", it said in its statement. The BBC has sought comment from the US State Department.
Singapore authorities said they had also investigated Alice Huang - not for espionage, but for any possible role in Megaspeed's suspected fraud.
In the end, they found "insufficient evidence" of crime and let her leave Singapore in February this year, after holding her passport for several months.
Since launching their probe nearly two years ago, Singapore has yet to bring any charges against Megaspeed or any of the companies and individuals linked to the case.
Singapore and US investigations into Megaspeed are still ongoing.

In 2024, US officials had paid a visit to a Malaysian data centre owned by Megaspeed and saw Nvidia technology still in their boxes, raising concerns that Megaspeed was shipping high-end chips out elsewhere, according to a report by the New York Times.
Last year, Megaspeed appeared to have imported 50,000 more chips than Nvidia could account for, according to a Bloomberg report. Nvidia later adjusted its own figures after visiting more warehouses.
Megaspeed has maintained it has always acted lawfully and that previous inspections by authorities found no evidence of illegal activity.
On Thursday, the company said it "welcomes appropriate government scrutiny" and that it is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government".
China has also long refuted accusations that its companies and institutions are illegally obtaining high-end US chips.
Jensen Huang resigned from Nvidia on Thursday following a board meeting
How Megaspeed and Alice Huang came to Singapore highlights other vulnerabilities stemming from the city-state's openness.

In recent years, the city-state has become a prime destination for Chinese companies, with tech firms such as TikTok and Manus making it their global headquarters. Besides Singapore's ease of doing business, it has a population that is mostly ethnically Chinese and largely views China positively.

For a Chinese firm, Singapore offers a base near the mainland and a "neutral address" that global customers and investors accept, said Winston Ma, adjunct professor at New York University's School of Law.
But critics say this has given rise to "Singapore-washing", where Chinese companies use the city-state's clean image to obscure their origins, reduce suspicions and even cover up dubious activities.
Washington-based security analysis group C4ADS told the BBC they had assessed Alice Huang's setup of Megaspeed to be such a case.
BBC checks of corporate records in China, Hong Kong and Singapore found that in 2019, Huang sold a gaming company and its subsidiaries to Chinese gaming firm 7Road.
In March 2023, a 7Road subsidiary in Singapore named Huang as its executive director. The next day it changed its name - to Megaspeed.
Huang was in charge for eight months before she transferred the company to a Singaporean man.

During this period, Megaspeed went through "a critical period of corporate restructuring and regional expansion", and her corporate relationships raised questions about whether "Megaspeed's Singaporean identity is genuine or effectively Chinese-controlled", according to C4ADS.

Even after she transferred Megaspeed, C4ADS assessed that she was still "practically in control" of the company, based on her links to Megaspeed via another company as well as LinkedIn posts where she continued to identify herself as Megaspeed's "chairwoman" at conferences.
Megaspeed has not answered BBC queries regarding the company's and Alice Huang's links to China and the Chinese government.
Alice Huang, seen here in Taipei with Jensen Huang last year, ran Megaspeed for several months in 2023
All this reinforces the dilemma faced by Singapore.

"For the longest time, Singapore has managed to enjoy the best of both worlds with excellent relations with US and China," Nanyang Technological University politics and international studies lecturer Dylan Loh said.

Singapore has long positioned itself as a neutral party between the two superpowers. Its prime minister Lawrence Wong has insisted that his country is neither pro-China nor pro-America, but "pro-Singapore".
But Loh says this balancing act "has now fast become very difficult to manage and sometimes quite fraught too" with the US-China dispute over chips.
With the Megaspeed case, the tightrope Singapore has walked is set to get even narrower, according to analysts.

Beijing may ask why Singapore is investigating issues pertaining to US restrictions and whether they are siding with the US' interests, says Chong Ja Ian, a Singaporean political scientist and non-resident scholar with Carnegie China.
Washington, in turn, might read Singapore's latest statement as "pushing blame" on the US, which could lead to backlash from the White House, he said.
"Singapore has made a policy position not to take sides. But by not choosing a side, they run the risk of being seen as complicit" in either side's agenda, he said.

But Benjamin Ho, an assistant professor and China expert at Singapore's S Rajaratnam School of International Studies, noted that this was "not the first or last time Singapore will be caught between the US and China".
"This is the price that an open economy has to grapple with - you get caught in the middle when things turn sour."
Additional reporting by Jack Lau of the BBC's Global China Unit.

items.title: Iranian satirist Saeed Shakiba gets five years for Khamenei impersonation
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Persian article.

Saeed Shakiba, an Iranian blogger and satirist who was arrested after posting a satirical video impersonating late Supreme Leader Ali Khamenei’s voice, has been sentenced to five years in prison by a Tehran Revolutionary Court.

The Human Rights Activists News Agency (HRANA) reported on Friday that Branch 28 of the Tehran Revolutionary Court issued the sentence on the alleged charge of “assembly and collusion against national security.” Shakiba is being held at Greater Tehran Penitentiary.
The Hengaw Organization for Human Rights also confirmed the report, saying that Shakiba’s hearing took place last week and that the verdict was delivered to him in prison.

Saeed Shakiba was arrested in mid-October after posting a satirical video on social media in which he imitated the voice of Ali Khamenei, the Iranian Supreme Leader who was killed during the joint U.S.-Israeli military operation against the regime.

Following the video's publication, Mizan News Agency, which is affiliated with Iran’s judiciary, announced that a case had been opened against a blogger, describing the published content as “insulting and abusive.”

On October 25, the agency also reported that an indictment had been issued in the case. A statement from the judiciary cited several alleged charges during the proceedings, including insulting officials, propaganda against the state, and supporting Israel.
According to HRANA, however, Shakiba’s five-year prison sentence was issued on the alleged charge of “assembly and collusion against national security.”

The satirist’s conviction comes after the U.S. State Department documented severe restrictions on freedom of expression and the prosecution of critics of the Islamic Republic in its 2023 annual human rights report on Iran.
The report said Iranian authorities use criminal laws to intimidate and prosecute people who criticize the government, the Islamic Republic’s leader, or official policies.

The State Department also noted that Iran’s security and judicial institutions have, in some cases, used citizens’ remarks and social media posts as grounds for bringing national security charges against them.

The report further cited the arrest and punishment of government critics, restrictions on media activity, and censorship of online content among the violations of freedom of expression in the Islamic Republic.

items.title: What we know about the FAA nationwide ground stop
paragraphs: The Federal Aviation Administration took an extraordinary step Friday afternoon by issuing a nationwide ground stop. No planes are taking off at any airport and millions of passengers are stranded.

The U.S. air travel system is slowly getting back off the ground. The Federal Aviation Administration has lifted the rare nationwide ground stop it issued earlier today, citing telecommunications failure. That grounded thousands of planes at airports across the country, stranding millions of passengers. NPR's transportation correspondent Joel Rose is here. We've been talking all afternoon and evening trying to sort this out. Joel, now we have a little bit of a resolution, but not really. What's the latest?

JOEL ROSE, BYLINE: Yeah. We just heard from the transportation secretary, Sean Duffy, that, as you said, the airspace has reopened. The ground stop is lifted. But it's going to take some time to get this hourslong - to get through the backlog of canceled and delayed flights. And it's going to take even longer to figure out, apparently, what happened here.

During the news conference, Duffy said that investigators are still trying to understand exactly what the problem was. Duffy blamed the - Duffy cited intermittent communications, intermittent radar and blamed this on outdated air traffic control equipment that was overloaded with data. We have old switches, old routers, he said. It's an old system that went down. It got overloaded. Here's more of what Duffy said.
UNIDENTIFIED PERSON: We're getting very little information. Our pilot's been great and has been giving us updates every 15 minutes, which has been really helpful and reassuring.
DETROW: I think we had the wrong tape there, Joel. But...
ROSE: That's the wrong cut. Well, you got...
ROSE: I'll tell you more about Secretary Duffy.

ROSE: So he spent a lot of this press conference blaming old gear that failed. But when reporters pushed and asked for clarity on exactly what went wrong today, he wasn't able to give them a whole lot of specifics. He pivoted again and again to pushing for more money to rebuild the nation's air traffic control system, which has been a big priority for this administration but was - we just don't - we still have only Duffy's word that this was the old gear that failed. We don't have a lot of detail on what it was.

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin was at this press conference too. He said, there's no indication that this was a cyber attack, but he could not rule that out entirely - also started the press conference by saying that this outage is not related to the Microsoft outage that knocked out Outlook and some other services yesterday.

DETROW: Yeah, I feel like I had a lot of questions watching that briefing, as did many other people. And meanwhile, there's people all over the country trying to get home. Our reporter at Washington National Airport, Ava Berger, says she is hearing announcements that the hold's has been lifted, but the announcements are saying - urging people to please be patient. About half the board there is red with canceled flights. But she said people are now starting to optimistically slowly go back to their gates to see if their plane's ever going to leave. I mean, Joel, what is the situation like on the ground at other airports around the country?

ROSE: This is a mess, and it's going to be a mess for days. I mean, we've canceled - airlines have canceled thousands of flights. Thousands more are delayed. Planes are out of position. Crews are out of position. This is, you know, imagine if you had a giant blizzard at every airport in the country all at once.
ROSE: You know, it's like the whole system is scrambled, and it's going to take days, optimistically...
ROSE: ...Before we are back to normal in the U.S. aviation system.
DETROW: We've got about 10 seconds left. Remind us how rare something like this is.

ROSE: Very unusual. This is the second nationwide groundstop since September 11. The most recent was in 2023, and that one only lasted less than 2 hours. So this now appears to be the longest nationwide groundstop since September 11 of 2001.

items.title: Hungary seizes $19.5m in cash found buried in forests amid graft inquiry
paragraphs: Hungary’s anti-corruption agency said on Friday it had seized cash worth $19.5m (£14.8m) buried in forests and hidden elsewhere while investigating an ex-minister of nationalist former leader Viktor Orbán’s cabinet.

Miklós Seszták, Hungary’s minister of national development between 2014 and 2018, is accused of taking bribes in a scheme involving the state transport company, purchasing secondhand buses at inflated prices.

The prime minister, Péter Magyar, won a landslide election victory in April, ending Orbán’s 16 years in power after promising to investigate alleged corruption and abuse of office during his rival’s rule.
Seszták, two other Orbán-era ministers and the former premier’s brother have been taken into custody in different cases as graft inquiries have gathered pace in recent weeks.

The National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH), an anti-graft body with sweeping powers established as part of Magyar’s accountability drive, said it searched several locations on Thursday and Friday as part of the criminal proceedings against Seszták.

“During the search, investigators found large amounts of cash: buried in forests, hidden in agricultural and warehouse buildings as well as residential properties, and stored in high-value safes in secluded locations,” the statement said.
“The total amount of cash found during the two-day search was 5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and US $1,257,100,” it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m.
NVVH said its staff deposited the cash into the Hungarian State Treasury’s account.
“Upon receipt, 12 Treasury employees spent 8 hours counting the money using 5 counting machines,” the finance minister, András Kármán, said on Facebook.
Magyar hailed the seizure as a potential turning point.
“This officially marks the end of the Fidesz-KDNP mafia!” he said in reference to Orbán’s former governing coalition.
The former leader did not react to the latest development. Orbán had previously denounced the probes targeting his inner circle as “political persecution” aimed at imprisoning him.

items.title: Trump–Xi talks to test progress on trade, SI and strategic stability
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

U.S. President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping are preparing to meet in Shenzhen next week, testing whether their personal diplomacy can deliver progress on trade and super intelligence (commonly referred to as artificial intelligence or AI) risk management.

Preparations continued on November 11, when Secretary of State Marco Rubio spoke with Chinese Foreign Minister Wang Yi about Trump’s visit to the November 18–19 Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit and Xi’s planned attendance at December’s G20 summit in Florida.

The State Department said the call, requested by China, covered the importance of substantive leader-level conversations on peace and denuclearization, including at a potential meeting with Russian President Vladimir Putin.
China described the call as positive and constructive. Its account emphasized policy continuity and managing differences but did not mention denuclearization or a trilateral summit.
The Shenzhen encounter would be Trump and Xi’s third meeting this year, following reciprocal visits in May and September.
U.S. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent, who said he would accompany Trump, outlined plans on November 10 for the bilateral dialogue on super intelligence.

In prepared remarks to the National Committee on U.S.-China Relations, he described exchanges on evaluating advanced models before release, preserving human control, and creating a direct channel for reporting serious incidents.

Those plans follow September’s agreement to establish a technology dialogue and an incident communication channel. His remarks did not say whether that channel was operational, leaving implementation as a concrete measure of progress.
China this week extended the suspension of an additional 24% tariff on U.S. goods for two months from November 10, while retaining an additional 10% tariff.
It also continued suspensions of restrictions affecting American entities, subject to licensing and review requirements.

Washington is pressing for implementation of trade commitments agreed upon last year. In a November 6 call with Chinese Vice Premier He Lifeng, Bessent and U.S. Trade Representative Jamieson Greer discussed economic ties. Greer emphasized agricultural purchases, rare earths, and other critical minerals, according to his office.
Beijing has linked expanded farm purchases to implementation of reciprocal tariff reductions covering $30 billion of goods in each direction.

Yun Sun, director of the Stimson Center’s China Program, told VOA that changes in U.S. Congress ushered in by the midterm elections would not automatically produce a fundamental shift in Beijing’s approach.
“I do not think China’s assessment of the United States or its policy will undergo major changes,” she told VOA.
Congress can complicate administration policy through hearings, investigations and oversight, she said, but Trump’s preferences and White House decisions would remain influential.
“Beijing will certainly face more uncertainty, but that uncertainty is not unlimited,” Sun said.
Taiwan, trade, Chinese investment and human rights could all become sources of congressional pressure.
A possible Trump–Xi–Putin meeting could broaden the agenda, but the Rubio–Wang call did not confirm such a meeting.
Trump has said potential discussions could cover denuclearization and ending the Iran war.

Sun questioned whether Beijing could offer consequential concessions on Iran, saying a substantial reduction in Chinese oil purchases was unlikely. Uncertainty over Washington’s next steps also made it premature to assess the conflict’s impact on China policy. Regardless, she says there will be little impact on current U.S.-China ties.

items.title: FAA ground stop shuts down flights nationwide
paragraphs: A communications problem is reportedly affecting Air Route Traffic control centers.
A communications problem is reportedly affecting Air Route Traffic control centers.
is a senior editor following news across tech, culture, policy, and entertainment. He joined The Verge in 2021 after several years covering news at Engadget.

Takeoffs from airports throughout the US paused on Friday after the FAA issued a national ground stop “due to extraordinary circumstances and for reasons of safety.” US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy tweeted:

The FAA issued a nationwide ground stop for all U.S. airports following a communication issue impacting all Air Route Traffic Control Centers. FAA technicians are investigating the issue. We will provide immediate updates as we have them.

Jon Ostrower of The Air Current reports that the FAA has said it’s “due to several impacts to ATC Frequencies and/or Radar capabilities.” According to CNN, the last time there was a nationwide ground stop was in 2024 when a pilot notification system went down, and the last one prior to that was after the attacks on September 11th, 2001.

items.title: Amnesty International calls on Aussie government to recognize ‘gender apartheid’ in Afghanistan
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Dari article.

Amnesty International Australia has called on the Australian government to support international recognition of "gender apartheid" and back efforts to hold the Taliban accountable for what it describes as systematic violations of the rights of Afghan women and girls.

In an open letter, the rights group urged Canberra “to support recognition of gender apartheid under international law and follow through on accountability for the Taliban's crimes against women and girls.”

The appeal is part of Amnesty Australia's campaign, "16 Days of Activism Against Gender Violence and Persecution in Afghanistan," launched alongside the global 16 Days of Activism Against Gender-Based Violence initiative observed annually from November 25 to December 10.

Since returning to power in 2021, the Taliban have barred women from secondary and higher education, restricted most employment opportunities, and imposed limits on freedom of movement. Human rights organizations and Afghan women's groups increasingly describe these policies as "gender apartheid," arguing they amount to a system of institutionalized gender-based oppression. While gender apartheid is not currently recognized as a distinct crime under international law, advocates are pushing for its formal recognition.
Amnesty also encouraged the public to sign the open letter and amplify the voices of Afghan women and girls through advocacy and social media campaigns.

Recent findings by U.N. Women have highlighted the worsening situation for women in Afghanistan. The agency reported in August that the Taliban have issued more than 100 decrees affecting women and girls since 2021, restricting access to education, employment, justice, freedom of movement, and public life.

The United Nations Assistance Mission in Afghanistan (UNAMA) has also documented enforcement of the restrictions. In an October report, the mission expressed concern over arrests and detentions of women in Kabul and Herat for alleged violations of dress-code regulations, saying the measures undermine women's rights to freedom of movement, expression, and personal autonomy.

Amnesty International Australia said the campaign seeks to ensure Afghan women and girls are not forgotten amid competing global crises and to maintain international pressure for accountability and the restoration of their rights.

items.title: All-female Kurdish force in Syria to join Interior Ministry
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

The Women’s Protection Units (YPJ) has announced that Syria’s Ministry of Interior has agreed to integrate two special battalions of the all-female Kurdish force. The announcement comes after months of negotiations between Syrian government officials and Kurdish leaders over the future of the force, following an agreement to integrate northeast Syria into state institutions.

Ruksen Mohamed, a spokesperson for the Kurdish group, said Thursday that the interim Syrian government has agreed to integrate 800 YPJ fighters into two special battalions under the Ministry of Interior. The Syrian government has yet to confirm the announcement.

The YPJ was a major component of the Syrian Democratic Forces (SDF), once a U.S. partner in the fight against the Islamic State terror group in Syria. The SDF formally announced its dissolution in August 2026, after government forces took control of the region it had administered in northeast Syria.
The Kurdish group said it had also submitted the names of nearly 1,500 other personnel but had received no response from Syrian authorities regarding their status.
VOA contacted the Syrian government for comment but had not received a response.

Since negotiations over the integration of Kurdish-led forces and institutions into the Syrian state officially began more than a year ago, the status of Kurdish female fighters has been a major point of contention. The Islamist-led Syrian government has opposed integrating Kurdish female fighters into the country's military but has shown some flexibility toward incorporating them into police forces and other local security structures.
Political observers say a lack of transparency surrounding the integration process has further complicated negotiations between the two sides.

“When the specific method for integrating these forces has not been officially announced, it implies that negotiations are still underway and have not yet concluded,” said Abdulhalim Sulaiman, a political observer based in Qamishli, Syria.

“I believe there are ongoing discussions over the specifics and details, determining exactly how the YPJ will be incorporated into Syria’s security structure, particularly within the Kurdish regions,” he told VOA.

Gulistan Gulo, a spokesperson for the Star Congress, an umbrella organization for women’s groups in northeast Syria, said any attempt to marginalize the YPJ or strip it of its military identity would likely face opposition within the Kurdish community, where the female fighters are widely respected for their sacrifices in the fight against terrorism.

“We do not agree with the interim government’s position that the YPJ cannot be accepted as a military force within the army,” she told VOA. “The YPJ belongs to the Ministry of Defense and the army, given its years of military experience.”

items.title: Microsoft outage 'stark reminder' of how much we rely on tech
paragraphs: A critical Microsoft outage lasting more than 22 hours has raised questions about how heavily vital services rely on a handful of major tech firms.
The disruption, which affected Microsoft 365 services such as Outlook, was caused by routine automated checks that took some servers offline, overloading the remaining ones with traffic.
The recovery took nearly a full day while engineers gradually restored services, highlighting how embedded the tech giant's services are in modern society.

Flora Hamilton, executive director of the Small Business Charter, said the outage was a "stark reminder" of how much firms "rely on digital systems" - like Microsoft Outlook - "to keep their operations running".
"For many small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs), access to email is fundamental to everything from communicating with customers and suppliers to generating income," she said.
The disruption was not just confined to businesses, but also affected organisations and public institutions around the world.
Around 430 million people globally use Microsoft 365, and issues were reported across more than 70 countries.

The fallout from the outage had a wide-ranging effect, knocking out email systems for the US House of Representatives and Australian intelligence agencies, as well as disrupting court systems in Singapore and airline support desks in India.
Microsoft has since apologised for the issue, which it said was due to a technical failure rather than a cyber-attack.
There was no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered, Microsoft added in a statement late on Friday (GMT).
Walter Pasquarelli, an AI strategist, told the BBC that for governments, businesses and critical infrastructure, the outage had "put their vulnerabilities and dependence in plain sight".
"Looking ahead, as AI assistants are plugged into our email, calendars and files, a failure like this may spread even further," he said.

Gergely Orosz, a former leading software engineer at several major tech companies, said while these kinds of outages weren't unheard of, what was unusual was the time it took for Microsoft to recover from it.
A spokesperson for the US tech company said "given the scale of demand" it restored services gradually.
"While this took longer, it helped ensure a stable restoration," a spokesperson said.
Orosz said the resulting upset showed "our reliance on a few large US corporations".
He said a solution for the future could be to split services per region to reduce the impact, something which already happens with Amazon's cloud computing service, AWS.
For now, Microsoft said it was reviewing what went wrong, with the findings expected to inform steps to prevent a similar disruption from happening again.

items.title: Microsoft 'deeply sorry' for global outage after almost 24 hours of disruption
paragraphs: Microsoft has said it is "deeply sorry" for the service outage to its products, including Outlook and Teams, which has caused disruption around the world.

Services were broadly recovering by Friday afternoon, nearly 24 hours after issues began. Microsoft said it was making "encouraging progress", but added it does not know when services will fully recover.
The outage hit more than 70 countries, disrupting everything from business operations to government services and personal users. More than 430 million people use the affected products worldwide.
Microsoft said it was a technical issue introduced during a "network capacity upgrade" and not related to cyber or artificial intelligence agents.
Experts said the event was a "stark reminder" of how heavily businesses and vital services rely on a small group of big tech providers.
Users began reporting they were having trouble accessing Microsoft 365 products on Thursday.

By Friday, the far-reaching issue was affecting institutions from the Japanese government and the Philippines Supreme Court to the Australian spy agency, and trains, hospitals and courts in North America.
In the UK, some parts of the NHS, including GPs and hospitals, were affected, as were some schools and police forces.
UK cyber minister Liz Lloyd said the incident had "limited" impact on critical frontline services such as 999 calls, and there had been no disruption to the transport network.
In Canada, however, the national rail network said passengers may not be able to receive email updates about their trips, and hospitals across the country also had issues with emails.
In the US, staff members from the House of Representatives told Politico it had set back an entire day of legislative work as everything was on Microsoft's Outlook.
Singapore's government acknowledged some of its systems had been impacted, and in India, the outage disrupted work for many on Friday.
In Turkey, advisers and officials attending the COP31 climate summit in Antalya were left frustrated by being unable to access Outlook.
The issues also affected smaller businesses and individuals.

Microsoft first acknowledged users in the Americas were unable to access Exchange Online mailboxes at 17:54 GMT on Thursday, and shortly after warned the disruption was possibly affecting Microsoft 365 globally.
While it launched an investigation and engineers began working to restore services, by 04:36 on Friday Microsoft was reporting only a "partial recovery" in some parts of the world.
By 13:32, the tech giant said there were "broader improvements" in North America, "sustained improvements" across much of Europe and "encouraging recovery signals" in the Asia Pacific region.
Microsoft said it restored services gradually due to the scale of the problem and to help ensure services remain stable once they are up and running again.
"We are deeply sorry for the disruption this incident has caused our customers and partners," a Microsoft spokesperson said.
"We know the trust they place in our services and take that responsibility extremely seriously."
Microsoft said it has no "ETA" for when services will be fully recovered.
A full post-incident report will be released once Microsoft has completed a review.
Experts said while workers may have been happy to not have email access for the day, the incident showed the dependence many organisations have on these cloud-based services.
"The global Microsoft outage is a stark reminder of how heavily we rely on a handful of big tech providers," said Rob Demain, chief executive of cybersecurity firm e2e-assure.
Matt Saunders, field chief technology officer at tech consultancy Adaptavist, said it would be challenging to mitigate against a similar problem.
"Classic IT disaster planning strategies suggest using a second service for resilience, but in practice, it's almost impossible for a business to function without tools such as Microsoft," he said.
"In the wake of this outage, organisations must have a plan in place for how to work without such tools, for when incidents like this occur."

items.title: Microsoft outage disrupts work and gives some a chance to unplug
paragraphs: Millions of individuals, organizations and businesses were left without access to Microsoft's Outlook email on Thursday. Some people celebrated a day without email, while others work around obstacles.

items.title: ChatGPT Wallet lets OpenAI’s Dots agents make purchases for you
paragraphs: is a news writer covering all things consumer tech. Stevie started out at Laptop Mag writing news and reviews on hardware, gaming, and AI.

After launching its Dots AI agents platform earlier this year, OpenAI is launching a wallet for the agents. ChatGPT Wallet is rolling out starting today for ChatGPT Pro subscribers in the US aged 18 and older using a US billing address and “eligible US-issued American Express, Chase, Mastercard and Visa cards.”

After adding a card to the wallet, your Dots agents can use it to buy things in response to your prompts, but they’ll check in with you each time before checking out. OpenAI’s support page says every purchase with ChatGPT Wallet requires a security check with biometric verification like Face ID or a fingerprint scan.

After you review the AI agent’s purchase and sign off on it, OpenAI says that, similar to using tap to pay, Apple Pay, or Google Wallet, it substitutes your credit card details with a payment token, so your actual card info isn’t shared with your Dots agent or the business you’re buying from. Eventually, OpenAI says it expects “users to be able to delegate purchases entirely to their agent by setting clear parameters—such as spending limits, purchase categories, or time periods—and pre-approve those purchases.”

ChatGPT Wallet might not work everywhere. Some retailers have restrictions on AI agents or block them altogether. Earlier this year, Amazon blocked Meta’s Muse agents. OpenAI says that in order for agents to use ChatGPT Wallet, “websites need to ensure agents are not inadvertently blocked, and payment and risk systems need to recognize legitimate purchases made by agents.”

items.title: CMF’s milk carton-shaped Bluetooth speaker is down to a new low price
paragraphs: is a tech journalist and commerce writer based out of Portland, Oregon. He’s contributed to sites like Digital Trends, Business Insider, and WIRED.

Bluetooth speakers are often boring boxes in plain colors, but not this one! As part of Nothing’s ongoing early Black Friday promo, you can grab its unique, milk carton-shaped CMF Speaker S from Amazon and Nothing for just $39. That’s a solid $20 discount and the lowest price we’ve seen on Nothing’s newfangled wireless speaker, which hit the market about a month ago.

The CMF Speaker S is the smaller of the two recently-released models — the larger Series M is also on sale at Amazon for $79 ($30 off) — and sports a 45mm driver with two passive radiators to help with low-end frequencies. It can run for up to 18 hours on a single charge and carries an IP68 rating for water and dust resistance. Despite its carefree aesthetic, it also supports stereo pairing with a second Seris S speaker, Bluetooth 6, fast pairing via multiple methods (including NFC and Google Fast Pair), and audio over USB-C.

In addition to their great sound and compact footprint, both the Speaker S and Speaker M feature removable faceplates and multifunction front knobs. Not only can you swap them out to customize the colors, but CMF plans to share STL files so anyone with a 3D printer can create their own attachments and looks.

items.title: SpaceX to attempt double catch of huge Starship rocket
paragraphs: The 124m-tall rocket is scheduled to blast off from the Starbase launchpad in Texas at 1645 local time (2245 GMT) with a 75-minute-long launch window.
After six and a half minutes, the first planned catch will be attempted when the bottom part of the rocket - the Super Heavy booster - returns to the launch tower.

The top part of the rocket, called the Ship, will continue its journey to space and deploy 26 satellites. These will form part of the Starlink constellation that provides high speed internet from space.
The Ship is then due to complete 14 orbits around the Earth before returning for the second catch attempt about 22 and a half hours after taking off.
Until now, SpaceX has managed to catch the Super Heavy Booster on three earlier test flights.
But the upper stage of the rocket, which only reached orbit for the first time in September, has never been grabbed by the chopsticks. Instead it's splashed down in the ocean.
SpaceX said it would only decide to try to catch the Ship after carefully assessing the vehicle while it's in space.
If any problems are detected there are various points during the flight when the rocket stage can be brought down in the ocean.
After SpaceX went public earlier this year, its shareholders will be carefully monitoring this flight, as will the US Space Agency.
The progress of Starship has direct implications for Nasa's attempt to land humans on the Moon in 2028 - a highly ambitious timeline.
SpaceX has been given a Nasa contract to configure the Ship into a lander that will eventually take astronauts down to the lunar surface.

But it's not the only company working with the US Space Agency. Blue Origin, owned by rival tech billionaire Jeff Bezos, also has a contract to use its New Glenn rocket and lander for the Moon touch down.
Both companies will also play a key role in Artemis III, which is currently planned for summer 2027- another challenging schedule.
This mission will see four astronauts in Nasa's Orion spacecraft attempt to dock with both SpaceX and Blue Origin's landers.
Starship will need to make a lot of progress in the coming months to meet these commitments - the pace of the rocket's development has been far slower than SpaceX had intended.
But Blue Origin also has much work to do. The company suffered a major setback earlier this year when its rocket exploded, totally destroying its launchpad in Florida.
Blue Origin had said they would be back in action by the end of this year, but a return to flight has now been delayed to early in 2027.

Nasa is under pressure to meet its timelines. Its administrator Jared Isaacman has said America is in a race with China to get to the Moon. China plans to land its Taikonauts on the lunar surface by 2030.
