items.title: A lipsmacking journey from kisses galore to tears of despair – How Do We Find Love? review
paragraphs: To quote 1980s soft rockers Foreigner, I want to know what love is. And I want the Sainsbury Centre to show me. This big winter series tackles love in all its guises – and for now comprises two shows, one about smooching called The Last Human Kiss, another about desire and heartbreak called Ecstasy and the Aftermath.

The problem is, love is probably the biggest topic in human history, let alone art history. Think of the endless novels and poems and films; think of how many songs have been written, how many paintings painted. Love is an endlessly vast topic and this show barely scratches its surface.

The first exhibition begins, like so much love, with a single kiss – a gaunt couple locking lips on a 15th-century Italian vase. They don’t look too thrilled about it but, hey, that’s the reality of love. Sometimes it’s not great. The show then takes you on a salivary journey through every possible kind of kiss: political, maternal, interracial, divine, familial.

Allegories of righteousness and peace give each other an awkward peck in a William Blake watercolour, the infant Christ and St John the Baptist hold each other close in an Anthony van Dyck painting. Then a priest kisses a nun in a Benetton ad, the USSR’s President Brezhnev kisses East German leader Honecker, Cupid kisses Psyche. And that’s before you even get to the bulk of the show with its snogs by Edvard Munch, Wolfgang Tillmans and – obviously – Rodin, whose carved marble canoodle dominates the middle of the exhibition. It’s enough to give you chapped lips.

What they want you to see is the vast complexity of kissing, to understand its different histories and implications. So they show it through a postcolonial lens, a religious lens, a political lens, and so on. But kisses are not some underexplored, subconscious thing – they’re universal. We think about our kisses, we remember them, treasure them, long for them. The whole thing just feels obvious, like someone telling you the plot of a movie you’ve already seen.

There are works that deal with love more widely – including a Tracey Emin neon that says “The Heart has Its Reasons”, as if anyone on Earth needs to see another Tracey Emin neon. But they feature no actual kissing. The concept isn’t bad, and neither’s the execution, but in the end there are only so many images of people necking you can hack before you get mental jaw ache. It’s a whole exhibition of people locked in embraces, a whole show of painterly PDAs, and it wears thin.

The second exhibition, Ecstasy and the Aftermath, tackles the joy of new love, the despair of heartache, and everything in between. That’s where it really falls apart. There are some good works: a Somaya Critchlow nude, a set of deeply romantic and poetic Judy Chicago prints, a Jane Hayes Greenwood painting of leaking, breast-like plant forms, the Marina Abramović and Ulay video of him on the verge of unleashing an arrow into her heart. But the theme is so broad it sends you spinning.

There are works about motherly love, romantic love, desire, the gaze, heartache, grief. There are photos of people dancing in queer nightclubs, because community is a form of love. There’s a Paloma Proudfoot ceramic of gossiping mates, because really liking your pals is love, too. There’s so much to explore, each of those themes could have been a whole exhibition in its own right, but it’s all just been squeezed into one room.

The only way this could have worked is if they’d narrowed the focus. Or if they’d deleted all the wall texts, got rid of the faltering conceptual themes and restrictions and just whacked together a bunch of artworks about desire, adoration, romance, heartache and snogging and let you make your own way through it.
But if you want to know what love is, these two shows do actually provide a pretty good answer. Sometimes it’s beautiful, sometimes it’s joyful, but more often than not, it’s a bit of a mess.

items.title: NHS, schools and police forces hit by Microsoft outage
paragraphs: Key services across the UK, including the NHS, GPs and schools, have been affected by a global Microsoft outage.
Pharmacies and businesses have also been hit after email and messaging services went down.
NHS England said patients should still attend appointments unless told otherwise, while several large police forces are urging the public to call if they want to report a crime.
Microsoft said services were now gradually being restored globally after a problem caused by a higher-than-usual stress on its servers, but users could still experience disruption.
The government said it was working closely with the firm to assess any impact on its services, while local authorities warned that some council services were being affected.
The full extent of the impact of the outage - which is affecting Outlook, Teams and Copilot - and the time it will take to restore the systems remains unclear hours after users first reported issues.
Some 430 million people use the online tools worldwide.
The chief executive of the NHS Alliance, which represents the healthcare system in England, Wales and Northern Ireland, said the outage was affecting some services including emails.
NHS trusts in England were enacting measures to minimise disruption to critical services, a spokesperson said.
Patients have been told to continue to use 999 in an emergency and otherwise contact 111 by phone or online, or their local pharmacy.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains. Practices in Hampshire and Shropshire have told patients to phone them or come into the surgery if they have an urgent need.

A National Pharmacy Association spokesperson said the outage was affecting pharmacies' ability to communicate with GP practices and some patients, so "waits may be longer than normal and there may be delays to some prescriptions".
The overall impact on health services remains unclear. Much of the NHS calendar is linked to diaries using the Microsoft system, but workflow practices differ between hospitals and trusts.
There are anecdotal reports of c-sections being cancelled and hospitals only accepting urgent referrals - though the impact on elective treatments has yet to be confirmed.
The GMB union's national secretary Rachel Harrison said the outage was having a "serious impact" on ambulance and NHS trusts.

"Those who work in 111 and 999 services are unable to refer patient details in the normal way which is creating a massive backlog and has the potential for chaos," she said, though "emergency and life-threatening call outs appear to be unaffected".

Meanwhile, police forces in England and Wales - including the Metropolitan Police, Greater Manchester Police and Police Scotland - have said online forms may be affected. They are urging people to call them about any time-critical by non-emergency matters.
Downing Street said it was looking to get a "full picture" of the the extent of the outage's effect on government services.
In England, the Local Government Association warned that some services may be disrupted but plans were in place to ensure people "continue to receive the support they need".
Because the outage affects key organisational and communication platforms that are integrated, many other workplaces have been affected.
That has included schools, where teachers, office staff and parents have all had to navigate being unable to access key resources on calendars, emails and internal cloud servers.

One head teacher at a primary school near Newcastle said safeguarding systems had also been affected, meaning staff were having to report concerns in person instead of logging them, while another in Cheshire said his had been forced to delay sending out termly school reports.
Universities have also suffered disruption to online systems, including tools used to submit assignments.
Some, like the University of Portsmouth and University of Aberdeen, have extended deadlines or waived late submission penalties.
Royal Mail said some of its online services were unavailable and email notifications about deliveries may be impacted, but post was still being collected and delivered as normal
MPs have been unable to access their parliamentary accounts. A spokesperson said alternative arrangements were in place
The Scottish government has activated its "resilience operations" as it assesses the impact of the outage
MSPs also confirmed that Holyrood's emails systems were down, meaning they were unable to communicate with constituents or access urgent casework
Some businesses are reverting to using paper or moving to different communication platforms like WhatsApp.
Microsoft and cyber-security experts have ruled out a cyber-attack being the cause of the outage.
The tech firm said a large number of its servers had become "unexpectedly unavailable", meaning traffic was sent to the servers that remained online, putting them under strain.
"Just like on a motorway, when you block one lane, you have to put all of the excess traffic through just, say, one or two lanes," Jake Moore, a cyber-security adviser at ESET, explained.
"Everything goes and backs up. It slows down, and that's what we're seeing here."
He told BBC Radio 4's Today programme that this incident should "hammer home" the need for contingency communication networks that are "independent of others".
"Unfortunately, we just put so much emphasis on just a few providers - so when one big one like this goes down, the knock-on effects are just huge."
His sentiment was echoed by Nicky Choo, who said his cyber-security firm Mimecast used Microsoft tools but had built-in alternatives to prevent disruption.
Some workplaces are reverting to using paper or moving to alternate communication platforms like WhatsApp to keep their businesses ticking over.
But others have been left struggling without the Microsoft tools.
Caroline Wade, who runs her own PR agency in Kent, told the BBC that the outage had caused her "huge disruption" as she was unable to send pitches and invoices.
Meanwhile, 29-year-old Georgia Young, from Staffordshire, was due to complete a house purchase today with her partner but said it had now been delayed.
"We've waited eight months to get to this point, it seem like it's out of reach again," she said.

Dave Walker said the outage was threatening his fledgling bakery and wine bar's online pre-Christmas sales, while Stirlingshire resident Lewis Bowles said he was unable to access his tickets for a Sunday rugby match.

items.title: Courts, spies and MPs: How the Microsoft outage has been felt around the world
paragraphs: In the US, staff with the House of Representatives told Politico, external their work had been halted by the outage.

"We all use Outlook, that's our life, everything is there, our calendar is there, our boss's calendar, so it has been a challenge … with no access to our Bible," one House staff member said. "There goes a day of legislative work."
Tech giants OpenAI and Anthropic have both reported problems.
OpenAI, which makes ChatGPT, said it was investigating an issue affecting its connections to Microsoft's services, which caused some tools not to work as expected.
Courts from Los Angeles to Texas also warned that communications might be delayed.
Electric truck maker Workhorse Group, which was expected to report third-quarter results on 12 November, rescheduled to 16 November, citing business disruptions caused by the outage.
Meanwhile, officials in some US cities encouraged citizens to call local offices and agencies where needed instead of using email.
The City of Austin in Texas account posted on X early on Friday: "Due to an ongoing Microsoft Outlook outage, City of Austin employees cannot receive or send emails at this time.
"City phone lines remain operational, and 911 Emergency services are not impacted."
In Canada, a healthcare network running several hospitals in Toronto had declared a "code grey", indicating an infrastructure failure.
The company, Unity Health Toronto, said its teams were having trouble sending or receiving email but that patient care was not affected.
Other hospitals, including Canada's largest children's hospital SickKids, also reported its staff having issues accessing phone calls and emails.
Via Rail, Canada's national train network, said in a post on X that its passengers may not be able to receive emails about their trips due to the outage.
Disruptions have also been reported by Canadian municipalities, including the City of Ottawa and the City of Vancouver. Both urged residents in a notice to call in for any urgent issues.
In Japan, some companies reportedly turned to fax machines to maintain communications.

"Can't send emails because of a Microsoft outage, so we're switching to fax for the regular updates we usually send as PDFs. Analog is strong," one unnamed X user was quoted as saying by the Japan Times, external.
The Japanese government said its shared IT platform had been disrupted.
"We understand that Microsoft is working to restore services, and we will continue to monitor the company's response," Deputy Chief Cabinet Secretary Masanao Ozaki told reporters.
Singapore also confirmed the outage had affected some government systems, but stressed "emergency services remain fully operational".
Singapore's courts also said they were "experiencing issues with incoming and outgoing emails", urging people to contact them by telephone for urgent matters.
In the Philippines, the Supreme Court warned that "responses to emails and other transactions may be delayed".
In India, the outage was disrupting work for many on Friday, with emails not landing and Teams calls not going through smoothly.

People working in the equity markets told BBC News they had panicked when they realised they could not access daily research reports before their morning meeting where they make their big decisions of the day.

"Outlook wasn't working. We fortunately have an alternative so it was not a problem. But we conduct most of our calls, especially with big clients, on Teams - that has been a challenge," a senior executive with a big Indian brokerage said on condition of anonymity.
Firms in China use software that has been made locally - WPS Office is a favourite - but the Microsoft outage caused frustration there too.
Outlook is one of the few reliable channels for many offices and businesses in the country who work with colleagues across the world.

China operates one of the world's most sophisticated systems of internet censorship, known as the Great Firewall, which restricts access to many Western websites including Google, Facebook and Instagram along with many international news organisations including the BBC.
European stock market operator Euronext advised listed companies on Friday morning to use the phone to communicate corporate information because of the Outlook email disruption, Reuters reported.
In the UK, GPs, police and pharmacies are among services affected.

Some GP surgeries have urged patients not to submit messages via their website while the problem remains, while several large police forces are urging members of the public to call if they want to make a report.
Politicians are also affected. At Westminster, MPs were reporting their access via parliamentary accounts to Microsoft products was down.

A parliamentary spokesperson said: "We are aware of the global issue affecting Microsoft email services, which is impacting users of the parliamentary network. We are working with Microsoft to resolve the matter as quickly as possible.
"Alternative communication arrangements are in place, allowing today's business to continue."

items.title: You know that butter bot from Rick and Morty? You can buy that now
paragraphs: Struggling to find a Christmas or Black Friday prezzie for the person who owns every novelty mug on Earth? Why not gift a palm-sized robot programmed to endure a relentless existential crisis on your desk?! Ladies and gentlemen – here is the Butter Bot.

Following a successful 2024 Kickstarter and two years of intensive engineering, creative tech studio CircuitMess is finally shipping its officially licensed Rick and Morty Butter Bot. And yes, theoretically, it will be able to pass you the butter. Better yet, it rolls around on rubber caterpillar tracks delivering deadpan commentary about the futility of its own existence. Yes please!
However, even though this grumpy little companion looks like the product of some of the best 3D printers out there, it will set you back $349. Yeah, it's for the ultra-fans only.

Inspired by a two-second gag from the intro of an Rick and Morty episode, Butter Bot started life as a cult Kickstarter project backed by 2,715 eager fans ($441,349 pledged). CircuitMess spent two years, and three electronics revisions plus custom steel moulds, turning that animated gag into a real, palm-sized AI desk robot.

And yes, of course this includes AI. Under the hood, it packs an onboard AI camera, dual microphones, edge sensors, and a remote controller featuring a live first-person video feed. Because its voice, face, and object recognition run on-device, it should recognise its owner, identify random desk clutter, read out phone notifications, tell jokes, control your TV, and – crucially – ferry sticks of butter across the table (though how the hell this is done is currently a mystery to me).

Left alone, it roams your workspace, avoids table edges, and loudly questions its own purpose. Pick it up and it panics; shake it and it disapproves; press the controller’s 'Poke' button and you’ll visibly irritate it.

Tinkerers can also snap on six modular add-ons, including an air-quality sensor, motion-sensing intruder alarm, and LED light show. O you can reprogram its open-source brain from scratch using C++ or CircuitBlocks (I'll leave that to the people in the know).
Available worldwide now at circuitmess.com for $349, it’s a wonderfully over-engineered piece of pop-culture hardware that can turn existential dread into festive cheer. If you can afford it!

Beren cut his teeth as Staff Writer on digital art magazine ImagineFX, and has since worked on and edited several creative titles, including Paint & Draw and Computer Arts. As Ecom Editor on Creative Bloq, when he's not reviewing the latest audiophile headphones or evaluating the best designed ergonomic office chairs, he’s testing laptops, TVs and monitors, all so he can find the best tech deals for Creative Bloq’s digital professional audience.

items.title: Blink-182 to make Download debut as 2027 festival headliners
paragraphs: Blink-182, Evanescence & Bring Me The Horizon have been announced as headliners of next year's Download Festival.
The trio are among more than 100 rock and metal acts set to play the event at Donington Park, Leicestershire from 9 to 13 June.
Other acts on the bill include The Prodigy, 5 Seconds of Summer and a special performance by heavy metal legends Mötley Crüe.
US pop-punk band Blink-182 will be making their Download debut, while Evanescence will become the festival's second female-fronted headliner.
The American rock band were founded by singer Amy Lee in the mid-1990s and had a UK number one with their best-known single Bring Me to Life in 2003.
It's the second year in a row a female-led band has headlined the festival, after Linkin Park topped the bill in 2025.
The nu-metal group have reformed with Emily Armstrong as their lead singer, after the death of former frontman Chester Bennington, who took his own life in 2017.
The choice of Emily upset some fans, who pointed to her alleged ties to the Church of Scientology and past support for convicted rapist Danny Masterson - someone she distanced herself from.
Next year's Download will be a first for Blink-182, who emerged from the California skate punk scene in the 1990s.
They've had two UK top 10 singles and had their first number one album in 2016, 21 years after their first record.
Their drummer Travis Barker is married to Kourtney Kardashian and survived a plane crash in the US that killed four people in 2008.
British rockers Bring Me The Horizon are more familiar to Download regulars, headlining for the second time in five years.
The four-piece band, formed in Sheffield, announced earlier this year they're celebrating 20 years of the debut album Count Your Blessings by re-recording it.
That 2006 record was in the deathcore genre, known for its heavy and aggressive sound, but the band have since moved towards metalcore, pop and electronic rock.
Some fans questioned if the original lyrics, which frontman Oli Sykes admitted could be interpreted as misogynistic, were still appropriate.
But the 39-year-old lead vocalist told the BBC Radio 1 Rock Show that going back to their roots was "a lot of fun" as they "got to remake the album how we wanted it to sound back then".
Download bills itself as a festival "spanning the full spectrum of rock, metal, punk, emo, hardcore, alternative and classic rock".
It called this year's line-up "bigger, better and bolder than ever" and said it features "something for everyone, from huge artists to electric newcomers".
But not everyone who commented on the festival's Instagram post was as convinced.
Writing about Blink-182, one person said "the fact they've been posted as some mega headliner at a metal festival blows my mind".
"Literally not one headliner that's proper metal," they added.
Fan Madison Travers, who's hoping to go to her ninth Download in a row, says she's "really happy with the line-up" - but thinks there's more to the festival.
"I don't think it matters about the line-up specifically," the 27-year-old tells Newsbeat.
"I think the community there and just the energy all weekend is what we look forward to."
Other acts announced include Turnstile, Faith No More, Body Count ft. Ice-T and Malevolence - with the festival saying more will be revealed.
Some pre-sales are currently available but tickets go on general sale at 10:00 GMT on Sunday.
In recent years Download has also featured pop acts and surprise guests, with the Vengaboys an unlikely addition to 2024's line-up.
And Dogstar - the band formed by actor Keanu Reeves - performed in 2026.

items.title: The dark side of reselling apps: ‘If you include your pants, I’ll pay more’
paragraphs: In June, Hannah* listed her seven-year-old daughter’s pink swimming costume for sale on Vinted, hoping other parents surfing the reselling site would snap up the £1 offer. Her inbox pinged.
“So a little girl wore this yh [yeah]?” wrote a user with a male handle.
After sending back a barbed “What do you think?”, Hannah swiftly blocked the user and reported the incident to Vinted. She described the exchange as “disgusting” and “disturbing”.

Her experience is just one of the many innocuous listings of children and young people’s secondhand clothes on reselling apps that are attracting sexualised comments through their direct messaging function.

The Children’s Society has said some young users of resale sites are increasingly being asked for indecent photos in exchange for money or gifts. Some photos of young users posted on the platforms have been AI deepfaked into nudes without their consent.

In response, ministers are considering banning under-16s from platforms such as Depop, eBay and Facebook Marketplace, according to the Sunday Times, over mounting fears that their private messaging functions are the latest frontline in child exploitation. Vinted, which has a minimum age of 18, would have to join the other sites in gating access with strict age verification features.

The culture secretary, Lisa Nandy, said on Sunday that the government was “looking seriously” at expanding the under-16s social media ban to include online marketplaces. It is understood the regulations were sent for cabinet signoff this week, with Nandy expected to present them to parliament in December.

Young women have posted on TikTok and Reddit about their concerning interactions with buyers. Those exchanges include asking the seller if the item will come with used underwear if they buy it, or unsolicited sexual comments about their appearance.

Lucy* started reselling her pre-loved clothes on Depop when she was 15 and has been subject to many unsettling experiences. Once, she listed an item of clothing for about £10 and a user requested to raise the price. “The person had changed it to £30 and said: ‘If you include your pants I’ll pay more’,” she said. “That made me feel like, oh my God, awful.”
She then discovered that images of her taken when she was under the age of 18, posted to advertise her clothes, had been scraped from Depop and were circulating on Reddit.

“These pictures are actually still being resurfaced on these Reddit pages, which is quite frustrating,” she said. “It would be me at 17 trying to sell a bikini, and these men have screenshotted these images … It’s not just me, it’s hundreds of other girls.”

About two years ago, Lucy came across another social media platform, Discord, where she found users had stolen her old Vinted and Depop photos and manipulated them using AI to make deepfakes of her “fully nude”. She said: “It’s deplorable that people think it’s acceptable to take people’s images and make them into AI porn – I felt really, really upset.”

Vinted says minors can only access the site under the supervision of adult account holders, while Depop says users must be aged 13 or over to set up an account, and over 18 to use PayPal and the Depop payment systems. However, the UK communications watchdog, Ofcom, has found that 15% of eight to 14-year-olds use Vinted each month, while another report has suggested that some children are able to bypass checks and access age-restricted online services.

Some child safety campaigners have expressed fears a sweeping social media ban could exclude children from the internet entirely. Karen Garland, the head of policy at the Marie Collins Foundation, a charity that supports victims of technology-assisted child sexual exploitation, said: “We need to make spaces for children and young people that are safer by design. And so, in some ways, extending a ban into other spaces may not be the best route overall.”

Despite her experience, Lucy is conflicted about the ban. “It’s a real shame because there are probably very young girls that maybe are from different backgrounds … that maybe really need that money.”

However, she acknowledged that there could be “extremely dangerous” consequences to selling clothes on Vinted. She said that as she was now 25 and has continued to find sexualised images of herself online,, the risk did not end at 18.

A Vinted spokesperson said: “We have zero tolerance for harmful or explicit content and use a combination of dedicated moderation teams and detection tools to spot and remove activity that breaks our rules. When we identify inappropriate behaviour, we take action, up to a permanent ban or reporting to the relevant authorities.”

An eBay spokesperson said: “We have clear policies and safeguards to protect our community, including encouraging people to keep conversations on eBay, avoid sharing personal contact details and report any suspicious or inappropriate behaviour. Where we or our customers identify policy violations, we take appropriate action.”

Depop said: “Using someone’s images without their permission is a violation of our terms of service, which explicitly prohibits users from using or sharing another user’s content without their consent, whether on Depop or elsewhere. We take the safety of our community extremely seriously and we have robust policies, controls and processes in place to protect our users.”

items.title: How a sex scandal at Nvidia is putting pressure on the White House
paragraphs: How close is Donald Trump to Jensen Huang?

The Nvidia boss was one of the few business leaders with direct access to the US president. He had met Trump repeatedly, travelled with him to Britain and, in May, joined him on Air Force One for his trip to China.

Jensen Huang wasn't just another tech billionaire seeking the president's ear. He had become an important voice in one of the biggest arguments inside the administration: how much of America's most advanced technology should be allowed to reach China.

Nvidia makes the chips that power the AI revolution. Washington has restricted exports of its most advanced processors to China since 2022, believing they could help Beijing develop its military and technological capabilities.

But enforcing those restrictions is difficult. Chips can be bought legally by customers in countries such as Singapore and Malaysia and then diverted to China. Chinese companies can also rent access to computing power through data centres outside the country.

Jensen Huang has long argued that the restrictions are counterproductive. They shut Nvidia out of a huge market and encourage Chinese companies to develop their own alternatives. Trump appeared sympathetic to this view, allowing Nvidia to resume sales of certain chips to China last year in return for a share of the revenue, although its most advanced Blackwell chips remain off limits.
But that relationship now looks rather more complicated.

The allegations surrounding Jensen Huang's reported affair with Alice Huang, of no relation but a former executive at Singapore-based company Megaspeed, have raised the possibility that a foreign intelligence operation was targeting not just a powerful businessman, but someone with unusually close access to the American president.

US intelligence reportedly suspects Alice Huang of having links to Chinese intelligence. Beijing has rejected the allegations. Nvidia's board says it has no reason to believe company secrets or national security were compromised. But the affair has opened up a much bigger question: what did the administration in Washington know, and what did it do about it?
That question leads directly to Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick.

His department was responsible for controlling exports of sensitive American technology. It was also being pressed to act on concerns about Megaspeed, an Nvidia customer suspected of helping divert advanced chips to China.

On Thursday, Megaspeed chief executive, Tan Yong Pong, also known as James Tan, said the company "takes its compliance obligations under US export control laws extremely seriously" and is "committed to working constructively and transparently with the US government". He said the company had co-operated with US Commerce Department inspections.
A highly classified memo was shared with Lutnick about the concerns surrounding Alice Huang and Megaspeed. He resisted taking action against the company, a decision that is now under scrutiny.
Other senior officials wanted a tougher response. Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent was among those who reportedly questioned why Megaspeed had not been placed on the Commerce Department's blacklist.

There were also questions about why an investigation into the Singapore-based company was stopped after Nvidia intervened. The New York Times reported that Nvidia's general counsel contacted Commerce Department investigators probing suspected chip smuggling by Megaspeed invoking a senior Trump appointee. The department allegedly then froze its investigation and handed the case to the Justice Department.

This apparently highlighted a significant disagreement about the direction of Trump's China policy. Huang wanted access to the Chinese market. Other officials were supposedly worried about the national security consequences. Lutnick was caught in the middle.

Members of Congress from both parties want answers. Democrats have launched an investigation into how the Commerce Department vetted Chinese companies approved to buy AI chips. Republicans are also questioning the administration's approach.
And Jensen Huang's departure has not eased the pressure.

Republican representative John Moolenaar, who chairs the House Select Committee on China, said it was in the national interest for Nvidia and other American AI firms to succeed, but that companies "should never jeopardise our nation's security" by giving Chinese firms access to their most advanced chips.

Senator Elizabeth Warren, the top Democrat on the Senate Banking Committee, said Huang's resignation did not absolve him of responsibility, and urged Lutnick to explain why export control loopholes remain open.
Meanwhile Jensen Huang's team told Republican lawmakers on Wednesday that he plans to cooperate with their request to testify behind closed doors.
The White House has not responded to the BBC's request for comment.
It has, however, told the New York Post that Trump has complete confidence in Lutnick, describing him as "the most transformative commerce secretary in modern history".
That is a fairly emphatic show of support, particularly amid reports that officials are weighing whether Lutnick should be forced out.

There are some obvious questions. If Lutnick had indeed been warned about the risks, why did his department fail to act? And if other senior officials were indeed pressing for action, why did it take so long?
The BBC has contacted the Commerce Department for comment. But there is an even bigger question for Trump.

The president cultivated a close relationship with Huang. He was directly involved in decisions about chip sales to China. And, according to reporting in the New York Times, he was briefed on the intelligence concerns.
This is becoming difficult to dismiss as the misjudgement of one businessman or one government department.

Jensen Huang's personal life may have triggered the crisis, but the questions now reach into the White House itself. How much influence did he have? What did the president know? And who was ultimately responsible for protecting America's most sensitive technology?

items.title: More women make allegations against Russell Brand
paragraphs: Warning - this story contains graphic content
More women have come forward to make allegations about disgraced entertainer Russell Brand, in interviews with the Times and a new Netflix documentary.
Brand was jailed earlier this week after being found guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault at a trial in London.
Allegations against him first emerged after an investigation by the Times, the Sunday Times and Channel 4's Dispatches in 2023.

The Times has now reported, external accusations of what it called sexual misconduct and predatory behaviour by a further six women, which the newspaper said could not be reported until the criminal case had ended. He has denied non-consensual sexual activity.
The Times report was published on Thursday evening, and a Netflix documentary, titled Russell Brand: Open Secret, was made available on Friday morning.
The programme included an interview with a woman referred to as Emily, not her real name, who said she was in a relationship with Brand when she was in her twenties.
On one occasion, she said she "literally begged" Brand to stop after he refused to wear a condom during sex.

Emily, who was portrayed by an actress in the documentary, said: "I said to him, 'No, Russell, please, let's just use protection.' I kept saying 'No'. I said, 'Stop Russell, stop, please don't, please.'
"I begged him. I literally begged him. I tried to kick him off, I tried to draw my knees back, to kick him in his belly, but he was too strong for me."
But he "just pinned my hands back behind my head" before forcing himself upon her, she alleged.
"When it happens you just feel like, is this... is this rape? Because I'm with this guy [in a relationship]," she said, according to the documentary.
"I know I said 'No', but you question yourself and you think, did I do something wrong?"
She "left his as quickly as I could" and told one friend what had happened, but "back then women felt shamed", she said.
"You didn't talk about it. I just felt completely violated and unseen and unheard. I was saying 'No'. I kept saying, 'No, stop, please, stop, stop, no'."
Another ex-girlfriend, Jordan Martin, claimed in the documentary that Brand sexually assaulted her and smashed her phone in a hotel after she had spoken to an ex to arrange to collect her belongings.
"He snatched my phone out of my hand and broke it apart into pieces," she said.
Brand then followed her into a different room, she said. "He didn't say anything. He put his hand down the front of my jeans and he inserted a finger and then he walked away."
She added: "I look at myself back then and I feel sorry for myself. And not in a bad or pitying way, I just feel like it wasn't very fair."
Martin also said Brand was jealous and controlling, and had made her "brush her teeth until gums bled".

"He wanted me to taste anonymous," Martin said. "And so he was asking me to brush my teeth, but it just was never enough. And so he's standing over me and I'm brushing and I'm brushing, and then I'm seeing my teeth bleeding."

The Times and Sunday Times reported that at least five sexual partners said Brand had forced them to brush their teeth, including the fifth complainant in the trial, whom he was convicted of raping in 2009.
Among the new claims reported by the paper is one from a woman referred to as Alex, who claimed she had asked Brand to stop having sex after noticing he wasn't using a condom.
"I said, 'No, stop', and I started to sort of try and move. And... that wasn't happening," she said.
When he continued, she decided "I'm not going to fight", she said, because "who knows what he could do?"
Alex said Brand apologised in person and by text message after the alleged incident.
"I justified it in my head by saying to myself, at least he admitted it," she told the Times.
A woman called Vicky also claimed she had asked him to stop twice after they started having sex without any build up.
"My body wasn't ready for this and it was painful", she remembered.
"An uneasy wave hits me and I'm scared. And I say, 'It's painful' and he doesn't stop. And then it gets worse and it's really painful. And I say 'Stop' and he doesn't stop."
She added that it had felt like he "just wasn't present".
She claimed he said afterwards: "Tonight was consensual. Nobody did anything they didn't want to do."
Another woman named Zoe said Brand was "annoyed" after she turned up to his hotel late.
"He basically sort of just grabbed me and manhandled me around a little bit and he put his hand on my throat," she told the Times.
"And then he shoved his other hand down my trousers and penetrated me with his finger.
"I didn't resist. I just sort of let it happen."
On Monday, Brand was sentenced to 10 years and six months in prison following his trial. He is expected to serve seven years.
He denied the charges and was acquitted on two further rape charges and one count of attempted indecent assault.
Police have said Brand is being investigated over rape allegations made by two more women.
The Metropolitan Police have said they are also "assessing" information from several people who contacted them during the trial "to provide information or report a potential criminal allegation".
Brand has been placed inside HMP Wandsworth. BBC News has asked his legal representatives for a response to the latest allegations.
If you are affected by any of the issues in this story, help and support is available at BBC Action Line.

items.title: Summer heatwave put bin crews lives at risk, says council worker
paragraphs: Goddard, the council's streetscene service manager, said: "We had maybe five or six operational challenges that all came at the same time in a perfect storm this summer.
"Unfortunately, the heatwave was one of them and it was a contributing factor. We do have to prioritise staff safety above all else.
"My number one job every day is to make sure that everybody goes home safely and we take that really seriously within streetscene. That was only one of several contributing factors.
"That level of change is naturally going to cause a few bumps in the road, particularly with staff being asked to do a little bit more. There were some staffing issues during that period too."
Councillors praised Flintshire residents for largely embracing three-weekly residual waste collections and ensuring that the authority remained on-target to hit its statutory recycling rate.
"Three-weekly was very controversial at the time it came in," said Saltney councillor Richard Lloyd.
"It's quite clear to see now that the three-weekly black bin collection has been a good new factor. Recycling has improved at the kerbside."
Councillors said in the authority's meeting the change to three-weekly bin collections meant the council should still hit target despite the disruption.
The council also cut the amount of waste it sent to landfill or Parc Adfer by 6,467.49 tonnes between 2024 and 2026, and that improvement continued this year despite problems this summer.

items.title: US university students tell surveillance cameras to Flock off
paragraphs: Angela Nguyen, a senior at Stanford University, has been on a mission to make sure her school doesn’t use automated license plate readers, like those made by Flock Safety, for mass surveillance. The 21-year-old computer science major helped collect hundreds of signatures earlier this year from students, faculty, alumni and residents to demand that Stanford drop its current Flock contract and codify safeguards for similar tech tools the school may use in the future. The fear, Nguyen says, is that these cameras, which show where a vehicle was at a certain point in time, can be exploited to victimize vulnerable people.

Stanford cut ties with Flock this summer, and it’s not alone. The privacy reckoning over the company’s surveillance cameras is gaining momentum at schools nationwide. Since April, at least ten university campuses across seven states, have scrapped contracts with Flock. That includes Cornell University, Penn State University, Elgin Community College, Emory University, Binghamton University, Kent State University and the University of Wisconsin’s Madison, Milwaukee and Oshkosh branches. Last week, the University of Buffalo announced an indefinite pause on its plans for a 60-day pilot program.

Elgin Community College tried, unsuccessfully, to cancel its Flock contract before it expired in April. School officials said they resorted to placing black plastic trash bags over the cameras “out of an abundance of caution” until the company removed the cameras after the agreement lapsed.

A few schools – Appalachian State University and the University of North Carolina’s (UNC) Charlotte and Chapel Hill campuses – have kept Flock contracts but restricted national access to the cameras’ records. UNC Charlotte made the change after local news outlet WBTV found that the Houston police department had searched the school’s Flock camera network more than any other agency between March and May 2026: a total of 183,000 times.

Schools that haven’t yet restricted what agencies can access Flock or dropped contracts are feeling the pressure. At the University of Florida and Florida State University, activists have turned to protests, online campaigns and petitions to express their discontent. The state of Florida recently banned Flock cameras and other license plate readers from its highways, but those laws don’t extend to private property or local rights-of-way.

The uproar on campuses reflects a broader uprising. This year, dozens of cities have deactivated, canceled or rejected Flock contracts. Vigilantes have damaged and destroyed the devices to the delight of their social media followers.

Flock Safety said in an emailed statement that its cameras help solve crimes and increase public safety by giving campus police credible leads. The company highlighted cases in which local law enforcement said Flock cameras helped track down a shooter at Brown University, arrest a person who shot a gun in the parking lot of a high school in Colorado and find a suspect in an investigation about more than $100,000 in stolen equipment from an on-campus construction site at UNC Charlotte.

“We understand that schools and universities must evaluate public safety technology, and we respect each institution’s authority to make those decisions, but taking away these tools could impact the safety of students,” the company said in an emailed statement.

Flock also denies that its cameras fuel mass surveillance and that it partners with federal immigration authorities, although news reports have documented indirect ways that local police have used the network to help US Immigration and Customs Enforcement. This summer, Flock also introduced updated policies around auditing, as well as data retention and sharing.
Student protesters are confronting many of the same challenges organizers in cities that have dropped Flock have faced: most commonly, a pivot to license plate readers from other vendors.

Stanford is already installing replacement automatic license plate recognition (ALPRs) from the Canadian company, Genetec. Nguyen, the Stanford student, still counts the move away from Flock as a win but says there’s still work to be done, as student organizers’ goal is “to prevent any possibility of mass surveillance on campus”. She’s speaking with the university’s transportation department to push for transparency around who can access the data captured by the cameras.

On the opposite coast, in New York state, Binghamton University has announced a switch to Axon, an even larger police tech company, after dropping Flock. Claims of police abuse have not dogged Axon’s cameras in the same way as Flock’s, although many activists still have data privacy concerns.

Hatim Husainy, a junior at Binghamton who canvassed in dining halls to get more supporters for a petition to drop Flock, said removing the company was a “huge win” but added that students’ goals are to push the university to end the use of any ALPRs.

At UW-Madison, Bradley Keenan, who protested Flock on campus, has said the devices are “a signal from the police and university that everybody is under suspicion”. But the sophomore didn’t celebrate when he learned that his university had dropped its contract with the company because UW-Madison indicated that it would be immediately looking for alternatives.
Keenan said organizers have since updated their demands to push the university not to pursue a contract with any ALPR company.

Stanford did not respond to a request for comment but has said that Genetec, a Canadian company, will continue to store data on its internal servers for 30 days and that the new system is “designed for use within a single institution”. UW-Madison did not respond to a request for comment. A spokesperson for Binghamton University, Ryan Yarosh, said in an emailed statement that school officials have met with concerned faculty and students, and respects their “right to express their concerns”.
High schoolers are getting in on Flock activism, too.

In northern Colorado, high school senior Gabe Sayer and a friend started a petition to ban Flock cameras in the city of Loveland, and took particular issue with devices placed outside three high schools, including his own. Gabe said he first learned about Flock last year in his government class when discussing constitutional rights. His research led him to believe that the network is a dragnet that violates the fourth amendment. Sayer has been tabling outside a local grocery store to get signatures on the petition and meeting city councillors to share his views on Flock cameras.

In Georgia, two seniors at Alpharetta high school created a petition to remove Flock cameras from their campus. Aditya Manchanda and Henry Jones, who are part of their school’s Young Democratic Socialists of America chapter, made a video on TikTok about ALPRs and their petition attracted local news coverage.
“Schools should be a safe place, and we don’t feel safe,” Aditya said. “We feel our privacy being violated with the presence of these cameras.”

After gathering signatures, the duo emailed the school’s principal. “I know he wasn’t too pleased because we got media attention, and that’s not a great look,” Aditya said. The principal referred the boys to Fulton county school board members. Their emails have so far gone unanswered, so they’re planning to show up to an upcoming board meeting to relay their concerns.

items.title: Colette Kress becomes Nvidia's interim CEO after Jensen Huang resigns
paragraphs: Nvidia's CEO Jensen Huang is out, and the company's chief financial officer Colette Kress is taking over as interim CEO. She'll have to guide the company through an exceptionally challenging time.

items.title: Nvidia's interim CEO inherits risky AI bets and a legal mess
paragraphs: Embed <iframe src="https://www.npr.org/player/embed/nx-s1-6038868/nx-s1-10003569" width="100%" height="290" frameborder="0" scrolling="no" title="NPR embedded audio player">
Jensen Huang delivers a keynote at Nvidia's GTC event in Berlin on Oct. 21, 2026. Markus Schreiber/AP hide caption

A suspected intelligence scandal, reports of multiple extramarital affairs and the abrupt departure of one of Silicon Valley's most influential CEOs. It's been a dizzying week for Nvidia and the AI industry.

Jensen Huang helped bankroll the AI boom. Now, after 33 years at the helm of the leading company in AI, he's out, leaving questions about the future of an industry that has relied heavily on his company's financial backing. Longtime finance chief Colette Kress has stepped in as interim CEO.
"Nvidia has put itself basically in a position of being a bank, backstopping everything," Gary Marcus, a cognitive scientist and longtime AI researcher, told Morning Edition.

He was describing circular financing: Nvidia invests in AI companies that then use the money to buy Nvidia's chips. OpenAI, Anthropic and CoreWeave have relied on that funding, he said, even as many AI businesses struggle to turn a profit.
"Jensen was kind of a swashbuckler, willing to make bets of arbitrary size," Marcus said.
Unlike Huang, whose background is in engineering, Kress comes from finance and appears more cautious about making large financial bets, potentially changing how Nvidia backs the wider AI industry.
Kress will also have to contend with potential federal and congressional investigations into Nvidia's dealings involving China, leaving her to "clean up that mess," Marcus said.
He said lawmakers need answers about what information Huang may have shared with Alice Huang and why Commerce Secretary Howard Lutnick had not intervened earlier.
"Why didn't Lutnick shut some of this down when he was asked to?" Marcus said.
Listen to the full interview by clicking the blue button above.
The radio interview was edited by Simone Popperl and the web copy was edited by Suzanne Nuyen.
