items.title: Does Nvidia need a new logo as well as a new CEO?
paragraphs: Today, the Nvidia logo is recognised not only by dedicated gamers and creatives interested in the best graphics cards for video editing. The company's stock performance has turned it into a household name, while the demand for computer components amid the AI boom has ensured that a new headline is never far away.

Alas, it turns out that the DLSS 5 controversy is the least of its problems. Former CEO Jensen Huang has now resigned after embroiling Nvidia in a honeytrap scandal worthy of a spy novel. CFO Colette Kress has stepped up as interim CEO and an executive search has begun.
But the debacle has also resurfaced another question. Why does one of the world's most valuable companies still have such a terrible logo design? And could this be the moment for a refresh?
See our guides to the best laptops for graphic design and the best monitors for graphics artists if you need new tools for your own work.

Over on Reddit, designers are debating the "least aesthetically pleasing, most poorly designed corporate logo" still in use today, and the Nvidia logo is the example that was used to get the ball rolling. Other contenders put forward on the thread include the X logo and, of course, the infamous Kia logo.

I can see where the OP is coming from. Nvidia was the world's most valuable company until the Jensen Huang honeytrap controversy hammered its share price and put Apple back in the lead on the Nasdaq. The identities of those two companies couldn't look or feel more different. The Apple logo is sleek and minimalist. It feels modern and premium. The Nvidia logo is... weird.

"So many things I hate about this design: The Aztec-looking spiral eye, the half inverted color, the lime green, black, and white color pallette, the '80s sci-fi font. None of it coheres well," the OP writes on Reddit.

Of course, Apple and Nvidia are very different beasts. Apple is mainly consumer facing and Nvidia's business is mainly corporate. On the consumer side, Nvidia's GPUs are packaged and sold by other brands rather than by Nvidia directly. But the company is becoming much more of a household name as its tentacles spread.

Nvidia components are being promoted more visibly in GeForce RTX laptops, and the company's being collaborating on workflow developments with creative software developers like Adobe, Blackmagic (DaVinci Resolve) and the Blender Foundation.
There is a compelling case for a change. Nvidia's visual identity was born in a very different age of technology back in 1993. Its last logo redesign was twenty years ago in 2006.

Time alone is never a reason for a rebrand, even for a tech company. IBM's had the same logo since 1972. But with Nvidia, the age shows. The wonky eye, brat green colour palette and retro-futuristic type feel rooted in the late 1990s and early 2000s, when aggressive, futuristic aesthetics dominated PC hardware branding.
Compared with the cleaner, more restrained identities of companies like Apple, Microsoft, OpenAI and even AMD, Nvidia's main rival in the GPU space, the branding feels tied to gaming origins.

There's also a somewhat dark occult reference going on. In the company's name, the 'NV' comes from the shorthand that was used to identify the 'next version' in file names, while the 'invidia' part means 'envy' in Latin.

That feeling will be familiar to anyone who has a colleague with an RTX 5090, but it's a strange choice for a brand. The word is often associated with malice and the 'evil eye' and was sometimes used as the Roman name for the ancient Greek deity, Nemesis, the personification of divine retribution. Yikes.

Today, the firm's influence and ambitions extend far beyond GeForce. It sells AI infrastructure, networking technology, autonomous vehicle platforms and enterprise computing systems. A more refined visual identity could reflect its status as a global AI platform rather than a 'mere' component manufacturer.

That said, for all of its weirdness, Nvidia's mysterious green eye is one of the most distinctive marks in tech. A rebrand could risk of abandoning something that has aged better than critics might admit.

While the eye doesn't feel especially contemporary, it is unique. At a time when many companies are converging towards minimalist sans-serif wordmarks and simplified geometric symbols, the identity stands out precisely because it has character, and distinctiveness is arguably more valuable than modernity.

The strongest argument would probably be for a careful evolution. The company could modernise the typography and tweak the eye. It might be able to find a more appealing shade of green. A relatively subtle refresh could preserve decades of recognition while signalling that Nvidia has entered a new chapter.

But it remains to be seen how much the last two weeks have changed things. It looked like Jensen Huang was going to hang on until yesterday's resignation announcement. The company might also decide that the controversy requires a clear visual break from the past.
There's plenty of branding inspiration about this week that Nvidia might want to check out, from the solid Caixa rebrand in Brazil to the intriguing new Takara Tomy logo .
Let me know below if you agree that Nvidia has the worst corporate logo in tech, or if you feel that there's a stronger candidate.

Joe is a regular freelance journalist and editor at Creative Bloq. He writes news, features and buying guides and keeps track of the best equipment and software for creatives, from video editing programs to monitors and accessories. A veteran news writer and photographer, he now works as a project manager at the London and Buenos Aires-based design, production and branding agency Hermana Creatives. There he manages a team of designers, photographers and video editors who specialise in producing visual content and design assets for the hospitality sector. He also dances Argentine tango.

items.title: National Trust takes back land for nature restoration
paragraphs: Northfield has been acquired by the trust for the first time since the 1960s, following an agreement with the owners.

The site has a rich natural and cultural heritage as well as a chalk stream, with the trust describing the area as "a distinctive fen-edge landscape where low-lying fenland meets the higher chalk ridge".
There is evidence of human activity on the site stretching back thousands of years including the Roman period.
The National Trust said it hoped that, over time, species such as harvest mice, water voles and turtle doves would benefit.

Northfield is the first project within the trust's new masterplan for the area, which forms part of a wider Wicken Fen Vision and long-term initiative to "create a more connected and resilient landscape for wildlife and people stretching from Wicken Fen to the edge of Cambridge".

Ormond-Bones added: "Northfield has the potential to deliver meaningful benefit to both people and wildlife and we want local people to play a vital role in helping shape what that future will look like."
The charity said it was keen to understand what mattered most to local people and how the site would become a place people felt connected to, valued and enjoyed for generations to come.
Community drop-in sessions about the vision, external will be held between Saturday 21 November and Friday 27 November.
Feedback will be used to help inform the next stage of planning before proposals are developed during 2027.

items.title: Firms help migrants pose as artists and tech experts for 'Global Talent' visas, BBC finds
paragraphs: Things would be made to look like our undercover reporter had been an artist for some time, said Peter (pictured)
ByBilly Kenberpolitics investigations correspondent and Phil Kemppolitics reporter
Companies are offering to help migrants pose as talented artists and tech experts to make fraudulent UK visa applications under a fast-track immigration scheme, the BBC has found.
The UK government's Global Talent visa was launched in 2020 to attract the "brightest and best" scientists and researchers from around the world. It is also open to creative artists.
Following our investigation, the Home Office is now revoking visas issued to two Nigerian men who claimed to be fine art photographers, because it believes they were obtained by deception.

Applicants for Global Talent visas are not interviewed. People granted them need to prove they are exceptionally talented or promising in their field. They can then bring their families to the UK and there is a potentially quick path to permanent residency - in three or five years.
We have discovered that wealthy migrants looking to cheat the system are being offered fake art portfolios which they can pass off as their own work for a large fee.

A consultant from one company in London told our undercover reporter - who was posing as a potential client - that his firm could supply artwork produced in China, as well as arrange exhibitions, media coverage and letters of recommendation.
No clients taking the "fully inclusive" package - costing more than £100,000 - had ever been refused a Global Talent visa, he said.
In the case of the two Nigerian men, our investigation was alerted to apparently faked newspaper articles reviewing their artistic work.
A well-known Nigerian art critic told us her name had been attached to online reviews praising the work of the two seemingly obscure artists.
"There is a real problem whereupon fake articles are being implanted onto newspaper websites using bylines of reputable culture journalists," said Molara Wood.
Art critic Molara Wood told us her byline was added to online articles she had not written

Another woman we spoke to, who tried to get a talent visa via the tech route from India, told us a company she had used fabricated evidence for her application - including a made-up mentoring award and material falsely suggesting she had been a speaker at an event. Her application was rejected.
The Home Office described the findings of our investigation as "extremely serious" and said the company offering the £100,000 package to our reporter was already under investigation.
A spokesperson said they "will not tolerate anyone cheating the UK immigration system".
They added that the Global Talent route was already under review and "the home secretary will take whatever action is needed to stop it being abused".

The man who told us artwork could be created in China for clients said he was from a company called iCareer Consultancy UK, based in Canary Wharf. That is also where its sister company, ADArt Global Ltd, which is registered with the government regulator to offer immigration advice, is based.
Social media posts by iCareer employees pitch Global Talent visas as a route for wealthy Chinese nationals to come to the UK, without the need to speak English.
Our Global Talent visa service has "guaranteed approval", Peter told followers on social media
During a phone call and subsequent meeting with our undercover reporter, who spoke in Mandarin, the iCareer consultant told us:
At least four of his clients had obtained a Global Talent visa this year - and he suggested he currently had 10 people in the process of applying
The company could supply an employee to pose as a client and network at gallery openings - to help build evidence for a visa application
For an extra £28,000 the reporter could win a Chinese art award sponsored by Forbes magazine, also to help bolster an application

iCareer denied selling visa services and claimed the consultant had left its employment before he spoke to the undercover reporter - despite continuing to be listed on the company's website and providing us with a contract with the company's name and contact email address.

We began investigating iCareer after receiving a tip-off about its activities in the aftermath of our first investigation into fraudulent asylum claims, when we exposed how law firms and advisers were helping migrants pretend to be gay to obtain asylum.
The company, founded in 2018, is based in a co-working office and advertises itself as providing job search and careers coaching.
A consultant, who gave his name as Peter, had posted multiple times on the Chinese social media platform Xiaohonshu.

In one post from February this year, he boasted: "It doesn't actually matter whether you're an artist… Our Global Talent visa service in the arts is fully inclusive, with guaranteed approval… We say we can do it even if you aren't an artist, because we include the artworks as well."
An ADArt brochure is filled with photos of art galleries

In another video, Peter - whose real name is Shilong Guan - said he recommended the Global Talent visa in the arts because every other route to UK settlement had an "extremely high English language requirement".
Included in his posts on another social media platform, under the username "iCareerPeter", were redacted names of people whose applications had been approved, he said.

While we could not clarify Peter's claims, a senior immigration lawyer, Harjap Singh Bhangal, who reviewed all our findings, said helping people pose as artists in this way amounted to a "sophisticated fraud".
The whole purpose "is to attempt to defraud the Home Office and convince them, and an endorser, that I'm a genuine person, a genuine artist," he explained.

Although introduced by the Conservatives, Global Talent visas have been enthusiastically championed by the current Labour government - even as it toughens rules elsewhere to try to reduce net migration.
About 6,600 were granted in 2025, with applications in the arts and culture category nearly doubling between 2023 and 2025.

Applications must be approved by the relevant body, which for arts and culture applications is Arts Council England. It endorsed just under half of the nearly 3,500 applications it received last year.
The only way around this is if applicants have won a major award. In the film and TV sector, for example, the award must be an Oscar, Bafta or Golden Globe in one of the main categories.
Arts Council England told us it took allegations of fraud seriously and investigated where evidence was "suggested to have been misleading or fraudulent".
We would be provided with up to 15 pieces of evidence, stated the contract we were sent
Peter told our undercover reporter it was not a problem if she had no background in art and could not speak English. He could help her get a visa for artists who show "exceptional promise", he said.
"We would handle the production of all your artworks," he explained, adding it was cheaper to commission artists in China than in the UK.
Our reporter would get up to 15 works and have to pay about 10,000 yuan (£1,120) postage to get the works from Beijing to London.
Fine art options included oil paintings, illustration, sculpture, installation, digital art and photography, he explained.

To help her application, Peter said iCareer would arrange exhibitions and media coverage critiquing the reporter's work. Some information would be backdated to make it look like she had been an artist for some time.
During the call, and a subsequent face-to-face meeting, Peter also outlined how he could help our reporter win a prestigious award for Chinese artists - sponsored by American media company, Forbes.
Our contract also stated we would get help winning a Forbes-sponsored award

Being a winner in the Forbes China Future Artists Awards would help her visa application, he said, but the additional fee would be about 250,000 yuan (£28,000). Money would be refunded if she did not win.
The BBC approached Forbes for comment and it confirmed to us that the awards are genuine and that ADArt, iCareer Consultancy's sister company, is a sponsor.
It said the judging process is based on the "high standards of Forbes globally" and handled by the Forbes China editorial team, with assistance from professional judges.
Also as part of the visa deception, our reporter would have to do some "work experience… online or in person", said Peter. The reporter asked how she could do this, given she could not speak English.
This was no problem, he responded - one of his colleagues could do it, and also pose as her at gallery openings, to network on her behalf.
Officials administering the visas "don't look at photographs" said Peter.
The whole process would take at least two years, he explained, meaning her application would not be ready until the end of 2028 or early 2029.
The price for the "fully inclusive" visa service would be 880,000 yuan (about £98,000) paid in three stages - with an additional 20% VAT due if our reporter chose to pay in sterling.
The BBC was sent "a contract to break the law", according to immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal
During the call, Peter sent over a contract setting out how iCareer would provide "necessary endorsement materials" for a visa application.
The reporter asked if there was any possibility the application wouldn't pass.
"There's no such possibility," Peter replied. "We keep working for you until we get the result."
He added that the reporter would be refunded if her application failed because of material provided by iCareer.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal said Peter had sent us "a contract to break the law".
When we called Peter to confront him about the claims he had made to our undercover reporter, he denied he was willing to help people pretend to be artists or have artwork made.
"We are not doing anything wrong or illegal, all of our artists are real artists," he told us.

iCareer, via lawyers, subsequently said that Peter's employment had ended in early October, shortly before he spoke to the undercover reporter - adding that the company strongly denied "offering any visa services whatsoever".
"The meeting described by the BBC was not authorised by iCareer," it said. "We do not endorse the representations or purported services attributed to him."
The company added it had been unaware that Peter and another employee had made social media posts promoting these services and would investigate.

It said that ADArt, which has the same owner as iCareer and was described by Peter to the undercover reporter as another division within the iCareer group, "signs artists and helps them curate exhibitions and develop professional relationships".
Peter continued to be listed as an employee on iCareer's website, and on his own LinkedIn profile, until the company was contacted by the BBC, which iCareer described as an oversight.

Our undercover meeting with him took place in the same Canary Wharf building where iCareer and ADArt are based, a co-working space. He also provided us with an iCareer brochure and sent a contract with a corporate iCareer email contact address.
Immigration lawyer Harjap Singh Bhangal says he has no doubt that some fraudulent claims will get through.

We have learned that the two Nigerian men purporting to be fine art photographers - whose visas have now been revoked because of our investigation - successfully obtained talent visas on the basis of faked evidence.

Their deception first came to light when art critic Molara Wood discovered articles reviewing their work in the Nigerian Tribune - which were under her byline despite the fact she had not written them.
The articles were taken down after she alerted the paper's editors.
The Tribune told us it had identified a "staff member who had posted the articles on our website without authorisation".
It said the employee admitted that "an individual outside the organisation had supplied the articles" but that he had denied being paid for it.
Wood said the criticism attributed to her was of poor quality, as were the artworks.
"It is writing that I would not want associated with me," says Wood. "The images were not worthy of comment."
Part of the article, including artwork purporting to be by Silva Ndifon, that Molara Wood did not write
Other critics have also had the same thing happen to them, she says.
Artists applying for the Global Talent visa have to provide at least two examples of recent press coverage reviewing or profiling their work.
The two men who were supposedly reviewed by Wood - Silva Ndifon and Adanu Emmanuel Okoko - are now thought to be living in the UK.

While one of them does boast an online portfolio, it does not feature the kind of fine-art photography described in the article that Wood did not write. The other appears to have little to connect him to photography, or any other kind of art, beyond the article Wood found.
Neither responded to the BBC's requests for comment. After the Home Office was contacted by the BBC, it is now understood their visas are in the process of being revoked.
If you would like to contact our team about this story you can email on: politicsinvestigations@bbc.co.uk, external

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 1
paragraphs: One million people come to see Pope Leo at night in Argentina. The Pope talks to many young people. He asks them to be kind. He tells them not to worry only about money, online popularity, or good looks.

Many happy people wave their phones and bring their babies for a blessing. The pope is visiting three countries in South America to talk about God and help poor people. He also asks the country’s leader to help people who do not have much money.
Many young people are very happy to see the pope and listen to his words.
Difficult words: popularity (when many people like someone), wave (to move your hand when you are saying hello to someone), blessing (a time when people ask for God’s help).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 2
paragraphs: Pope Leo spoke to a crowd of one million people during a night event in Buenos Aires, Argentina. He told young people not to focus only on money, physical appearance, or getting likes on social media.

This gathering was part of his 12-day trip through South America, which also includes visits to Uruguay and Peru. Large crowds came to see the pope, including 2.5 million people at a historic Mass earlier in the week.

Pope Leo is visiting Argentina to support Catholic followers and help poor communities. During his trip, he also asked Argentina’s president not to hurt poor people with government spending cuts. Many residents and students thanked the pope for caring about people in need.

Difficult words: physical appearance (the external, visible features of a person), gathering (when many people meet together for a specific event), cut (reduction made to financial spending, resources, or services).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.

items.title: Pope Leo visits South America – level 3
paragraphs: Pope Leo drew a crowd of one million people at a nighttime vigil in Buenos Aires on Tuesday during his 12-day South American tour.

The pontiff addressed the gathered youth, urged them not to be consumed by the pursuit of wealth, physical appearance, or social media popularity, and warned against humiliating others online. This event followed an outdoor Mass in Cordoba earlier that day, which attracted 650,000 attendees, and a record-breaking gathering of 2.5 million people in Buenos Aires on Monday.

As the first pope to visit Catholic-majority Argentina since 1987, Leo seeks to revitalize the Church’s presence in the region against growing evangelical competition. Throughout his visit, the US-born pope has also voiced strong criticism of Argentine President Javier Milei’s strict austerity policies. He argued that government spending cuts disproportionately harm the country’s poorest citizens.

Difficult words: pontiff (the Pope, who acts as the chief bishop and leader of the Roman Catholic Church), pursuit (chasing or striving to achieve something), austerity (severity in government spending cutbacks and financial discipline).

items.title: Pablo Castillo partners with Decibel on 3D-printed chair with under-seat storage
paragraphs: A bookshelf slots in below the cantilevered seat of Kino, a 3D-printed chair developed by Barcelona-based designer Pablo Castillo.
Castillo designed Kino for Decibel, an American company that specialises in 3D-printed furniture and installations. It is shortlisted for seating design of the year in the upcoming Dezeen Awards.
The designer’s aim was to create a recognisable chair silhouette, while also responding to the specificities of the 3D printing process.
The chair is essentially a monobloc, with a single component forming the T-shaped seat, two legs, the shelf and a curved backrest.
Its entire form is printed from PLA, the most common bioplastic, although the material is reinforced with cellulose plant fibres. This increases its strength, enabling the cantilevered seat.
Decibal also offers an outdoor version printed from recycled PETG, a thermoplastic polyester.
“I wanted the substantial thickness of the plastic and the way it builds a product layer by layer to translate into features that give the chair its character,” Castillo told Dezeen.
“Following this line of thought allowed me to move beyond mere dimensions and general ergonomic considerations,” the designer said.
“The cantilevered seat, the under-seat storage, and specific details such as the T-junctions naturally emerged.”
The seat’s T-shape was created by cantilevers both forwards and backwards. This makes the chair less rigid than a typical 3D-printed chair, improving comfort.

“By reinforcing the lower part of the seat with a corrugated structure integrated directly into the 3D print, we achieved a chair that offers a slightly broader range of motion than a traditional design,” Castillo said.
“It seamlessly accommodates highly reclined, relaxed postures, as well as more active positions when the user leans forward.”
Kino joins Decibel’s Editions collection, which also includes chairs by designers including Charles Birshaw, Karim Rashid and Deniz Aktay.
The New Jersey-based brand launched this collection with an exhibition at the Alcova show in Milan in 2025, when it was live-printing chairs in the former SNIA factory in Varedo.
The chairs are produced using a Caracol robotic 3D printer, which allows geometries that wouldn’t be possible with injection moulding.

items.title: Teen prodigy, Netflix star, prisoner: the story of Hong Kong dissident Joshua Wong – podcast
paragraphs: Pro-democracy activist Nathan Law and journalist Danny Vincent on the sentencing of the iconic Hong Kong campaigner Joshua Wong to another 10 years in prison. Send your comments and questions to tif.questions@theguardian.com He has been leading protests since he was 14. Joshua Wong has been on the cover of Time magazine, the focus of a Netflix documentary and an icon for Hong Kong’s pro-democracy movement. Wong has been leading the fight against a Chinese squeeze on freedoms in Hong Kong for the last 15 years. He will now spend more than 16 years in prison. Continue reading...

items.title: A negative Outlook: Microsoft scrambles to fix email outage
paragraphs: A Microsoft logo and sign outside the Microsoft Visitor Center are seen at the company's headquarters Monday, Nov. 9, 2026, in Redmond, Wash. Lindsey Wasson/AP hide caption
Millions of individuals, organizations, and businesses – including the NPR newsroom - were left without access to Microsoft's Outlook email on Thursday.
Early Friday, after Outlook had been down for more than 12 hours, Microsoft reported "marginal success."

Very little is known so far about what is behind the outage, but Microsoft has attributed it to an "elevated load," or servers becoming overstretched. The tech giant assured users it was doing everything it could to fix the problem.
"As of now, we are not aware of any malicious activity that is causing this incident. We will continue to treat this incident with urgency and priority until full resolution," the company said.
While Microsoft did not say how many users were affected, Microsoft 365 apps have around 430 million users globally. Its communications platform Teams and AI chatbot Copilot were also affected.
The problem has affected users in more than 70 countries, according to Downdetector, which tracks cyber outages. Countries from the U.S. to South Africa to India and New Zealand were affected.

The U.S. House of Representatives said it was also affected, as were the Australian police and the Japanese government. In Hong Kong, bankers told CNN their work was disrupted. Companies including OpenAI and Anthropic were also affected.
While some people were fuming, others online said they were relishing the opportunity to wind down work early ahead of the weekend.

Social media was full of memes of people slacking off at work or enjoying tranquil scenes without the pinging of a constant barrage of emails, with some telling the Microsoft technicians not to hurry with fixing it.

items.title: Timothée Chalamet among Hollywood stars and charity heroes stepping up for BBC Children In Need
paragraphs: Rylan is confused when an interview with Timothée Chalamet goes awry

This year's BBC Children In Need show is taking place on Friday, with highlights including Timothee Chalamet pranking Rylan Clark, and a "challenge squad" of young people completing feats in the name of charity.

Oscar-nominated actor Chalamet and co-stars Zendaya, Jason Momoa and Anya Taylor-Joy will be seen making Rylan sweat during an interview for their new film Dune: Part Three, with the help of three children, hidden behind the scenes.
The show will also feature Radio 2 presenter Owain Wyn Evans, on a 400-mile cycle challenge through Scotland, Northern Ireland, England and Wales.
Last year's appeal raised more than £45m to help children and young people across the UK, and this year's TV event will be broadcast from 19:00 GMT.
Alex Jones, Rylan Clark, Mel Giedroyc, Tyler West and Sara Cox are the hosts for the live show
The three-hour show will be hosted live from Salford by Alex Jones, Mel Giedroyc, Rylan, Sara Cox and Tyler West.

They will welcome Wyn Evans, who has been the latest Radio 2 DJ to put himself through a gruelling challenge for Children In Need, following in the footsteps of the likes of Sara Cox and Paddy McGuinness.
Owain Wyn Evans has been on the 4 Nations Cycle Challenge
Wyn Evans is being joined on his final leg in Wales on Friday by 22-year-old Harri, who is living with hidden lasting effects of a brain tumour.
He is part of The One Show's "challenge squad" - four young people who have signed up for a series of personal missions for the charity.
Zoe has prepared for her dancing challenge with the help of Strictly pro Amy Dowden

The others are 16-year old Zoe, who has Down's syndrome, who will be seen dancing with the cast of High School Musical; Ana, also 16, who has a rare physical condition and is doing a three-day kayaking challenge; and 22-year-old Serena, who will perform live in memory of her late brother and a childhood friend.

The theme of this year's Children In Need is Challenge Yourself 2026, which has also seen Morning Live presenters Michelle Ackerley and Gethin Jones learn instruments to perform with a band live on the night.
Joe Wicks and Emma Bunton are among the other stars who have been involved, while landmarks including the Blackpool Tower, London Eye and Titanic Belfast will be lit in yellow for the occasion.
Children in Need supports more than 1,600 local charities and projects across the UK.
Children In Need is on BBC One and iPlayer from 19:00-22:00 GMT on Friday.

items.title: Skye Newman gets 'goosebumps' over record-breaking Brixton Academy run
paragraphs: Fast rising pop star Skye Newman began her November five-gig run at Brixton Academy on Thursday - a record for a British female solo artist
The BBC Sound of 2026 winner is set to overtake rapper Little Simz, who headlined three nights at the legendary south London venue in 2021.
It will cap an incredible few years for Brit Award nominee Newman, 23, who performed at Radio 1's Big Weekend in Sunderland, external last month.

Speaking to BBC News's Mark Savage ahead of her record-breaking run, Newman said it had given her "goosebumps and chills". She added: "It's crazy. My jaw drops all the time. I feel honoured to be the first woman, and I don't take it lightly."

Born in south-east London, the "loud, raw and strikingly honest" Newman - according to our music correspondent - exploded onto the scene last year when her debut single, Hairdresser, went straight into the top 20.
The follow-up, Family Matters, reached number five in June. It was the first time a female artist had made the top 20 with their first two singles since Ella Henderson in 2014.
The husky-voiced soul and R&B singer has previously supported Ed Sheeran and Lewis Capaldi on tour, and been called "incredibly talented" and "something else" by Sir Elton John.
Now she stands on the shoulders of pop giants.
Watch: The BBC's Mark Savage sat down with Skye Newman after she won BBC Radio 1's Sound of 2026
Historically, US pop-punk icon Debby Harry and Romy Croft, frontwoman of the band The XX have also enjoyed big Brixton residencies, as well as Phoebe Bridgers, Chappell Roan and Tash Sultana.
But after three more gigs this weekend and one added one next, Newman will newly lead the way for UK female solo stars at one of the country's most prestigious venues.
She also insists on having an all-female band on stage with her.
"Women are the centre of my world," she said. "They're the people that built me. They allowed me space to grow and find myself. So, I definitely had to take that out on stage with me.
"I had to stand by what I stand by. It's quite scary at the minute how much social media is [affecting how women are being treated] so I'm just really big on trying to keep women everywhere."
She continued: "If I can have a woman in place, I will. I'll give a job out. I'll give my helping hand always."

Newman recently paid tribute to another soulful London singer to have graced the same space back in 2007, the late Amy Winehouse, with a rendition of her song Addicted during a special Back to Black anniversary gig for the BBC.
"The thing with Amy's music is it's so incredible that you don't want to touch it," she admitted.

"No-one would ever do it like Amy, and I think it was definitely scary for all of us... that feeling of, you've got to live up to that expectation. You've got to fill her shoes, and they're big shoes to fill.
"But I think we all smashed it, and I think it was honestly the most beautiful, inspirational day I've had in a very long time."

Next month she will head off to Australia with Harry Styles for a series of support slots, which the childhood One Direction fan says is "surreal", and something she agreed to with "no questions asked".
"'Whatever I've got, cancel it'," she joked she had told her team on hearing about the request.
"It felt like a dream because I was the age of One Direction [fans], so that was around when I was a child and obviously I loved them and Harry and Zane were my favourites.
"So then now to go and support Harry Styles is just mental."

items.title: Brand will face 'hell on earth' in Wandsworth prison, says former inmate
paragraphs: Russell Brand has been in HMP Wandsworth for a week
Russell Brand will face "hell on earth" inside HMP Wandsworth, a former inmate at the London prison has said.
Brand, 51, was convicted a week ago of one count of rape and three counts of sexual assault and was sentenced on Monday to 10 years and six months in prison.
He is currently being held at the South London jail, which is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons.
Chris Atkins, who served eight months at HMP Wandsworth for tax fraud, described the prison as "hell on earth".

He continued: "The first month is hands-down the worst. The mental shock is absolutely colossal. It was colossal for me and it's going to be 10 times worse for him because of the nature of his offences and the height from which he's fallen.
"He has to come to terms with it and the pure physical shock of suddenly being trapped in a dungeon for weeks on end with nobody to talk to most of the time is ghastly."
A source close to the disgraced comedian said he was doing "remarkably well considering the circumstances" and that he had been moved from isolation to a main wing in the prison.
A member of staff at Wandsworth said there was "much excitement" among the inmates about Brand's arrival.

"Prisons are boring and Russell Brand being in their space has given them some fun - they've been slamming on cell doors and shouting out his name. He is a rapist, so there's also been some anger about what he's done.
"We're very aware of that feeling," they said.
Brand will have had his possessions confiscated when he arrived at HMP Wandsworth
Brand is likely to still be in a cell on his own. It would usually have a bed, a basin and a toilet. He may have a television and kettle depending on where in the prison he is housed.

On arrival, Brand's possessions will have been confiscated. That will include his mobile phone, clothing, and any other valuables. He will have been issued with a grey prison tracksuit - a uniform that has been described by some of those who've been inside as "itchy" and "often the wrong size".

The former media personality and comedian will have been given a night pack. It contains items such as biscuits, teabags, a small bag of cereal, some sugar and a carton of milk. According to the charity, Prison Reform Trust, this is to help inmates until they can buy goods from the prison shop.
Brand, who has positioned himself as a Christian influencer, would be able to register for the weekly Sunday service in the prison chapel, inmates said.
"Many sign up just to get out of their cell," one added. They said Brand could probably get regular time with the prison chaplain, if he wanted.

Inmates receive money through prison work or from their family. But several former prisoners have told the BBC there are a limited number of jobs in places like workshops, laundry rooms and libraries.
They say it is much harder for sex offenders to get work because their conviction means they are more at risk of assault from mixing with other inmates.
Staff at other prisons say Brand's fame and the offences he has been convicted of could make him a target among other inmates.
Sex offenders are often among those most at risk of being attacked. One prison governor said: "When a trial gets plenty of publicity it highlights the crimes the offender has committed.
"This in turn makes him vulnerable to the inmates own 'justice' system of arbitrary beatings and assaults, especially where sex crimes are involved."
The South London jail is one of England's largest Victorian-era prisons

The prison paperwork is also said to be a huge challenge for newcomers. Getting permission to make phone calls and filling out visitor requests can take a long time and have to go through the system to be signed off.

Atkins said: "He won't have anyone set up on his visitor account - visitors need a series of checks. Phone numbers need to be approved. These checks are not quick and you need to know how to make these applications.
"There is often nobody there to tell you how this all works so you have to work it out." He said it took five weeks to see his young son.
It's just days since Brand was sentenced to more than a decade in prison.
At this stage nobody knows what the future holds for him. In time he may be transferred to a different jail with a less harsh regime and more modern facilities.
The guidelines state offenders jailed for four years or more for some serious violent or sexual offences will be released at the two-thirds point. In Brand's case that would be seven years.

items.title: ‘Hurry, hurry, get your tickets now!’ The last of the great Australian showmen – photo essay
paragraphs: My uncle Teddy Trevor remembers Casey Nelson, a fellow showman, spruiking his double-jointed horse to sideshow punters in the 1960s. The horse, Nelson warned, was “showing here for the last time”. “Too late, too late will be the cry, when Happy Harry has passed you by,” he called. The act continued for another two decades.
The Casey Nelson tent show, featuring Happy Harry the double-jointed horse, circa the late 1940s

I’ve been hearing stories like this my whole life. Ted laughs at Casey’s line as he pours another cup of tea and passes the biscuits at the kitchen table of the family home in Brisbane. At 91, after a lifetime in Australia’s travelling shows, he has no desire to quit the showgrounds yet. While their mid-century heyday may have passed, these grounds are still the lifeblood of his friendships and family.

Ted feels blessed, he says, to belong to two great show families: the Trevors, circus people on his father’s side, and the Fosters, sideshow people on his mother’s. Born on the showgrounds in 1935, he comes from more than eight generations of show folk.
Ted in his kitchen with his cockatiel, Sweetie Pie

Ted’s grandmother Cora Trevor performed an iron-jaw act, hanging upside-down and spinning grown men by her teeth, including her 14-stone (88kg) acrobat father. My great-grandmother Alice Foster, known as LuLu, arrived in Australia in 1913. She was a widow with six sons and a daughter. Lulu kept her whole family fed while running a dancing duck as a sideshow act.

Clockwise from top left: Ted Trevor aged five; Cora Trevor Williams, Ted’s grandmother, performing an ‘iron-jaw’ act; Billy and Vera (left), who performed trapeze and iron-jaw acts, and Ted’s grandmother, Cora (right); Ted’s mother, Frances ‘Girly’ Foster, on stilts on Pitt Street, Sydney

Uncle Teddy’s own entry into work coincided with the second world war, which brought the showgrounds to a halt. He started his career selling fabric door to door from my grandmother’s vardo caravan. As a young man in the 1950s, he worked with my uncle Frank Foster, promoting Slim Dusty’s tent show on the sideshow alley. Those days were hectic. “You start at nine in the morning, you don’t finish till after 11 at night, and you do a show every 20 minutes,” Ted tells me.

“The show was a big event for the town,” Ted says – the biggest day of the year for some places. The men wore suits, hats and ties, the women their best dresses. “Now they go in a pair of shorts and thongs,” he says.
‘The reason they call it the old-time showman is because that’s exactly what it was. You had to be a showman to work with whatever you got’

Teddy says the atmosphere of the sideshow was what everyone came to the show for. He can still recite the lines they used to entice the crowds: “The Slim Dusty show is just about to start! Australia’s top country-and-western recording star, the only Australian to top the hit parade in England, our only gold record-holder, is on this next big program. Hurry boys, hurry girls, get your tickets now! The cowboys, the cowgirls, the knife-throwers, the jugglers, you’ll see and meet them all on the inside.”

Uncle Teddy says that between the advent of TV, RSL clubs offering sideshow talent a new touring strategy, and state-based showground permits hindering showpeople from pivoting beyond the scope of their trade (for example, a clown joint can only do clown business), the landscape of the showgrounds drastically changed in the early 1970s.
Frances Foster with Slim Dusty at the Brisbane Exhibition in the early 1960s
Performers could sing half a dozen songs at an RSL, Ted tells me, “for what three or four days and hundreds of songs paid them on a sideshow”.

Participator numbers also declined, while costs climbed, he says. The big rides came in, worth millions. “The showgrounds are saturated with equipment now,” he says. “There’s no more ground available, so there’s no permits for the young showman.”

The cost escalated, too. “They’re charging $12 for a game on the clown joint. It’s all ridiculous,” he says. In Ted’s day, it used to be “only four bob [40 cents] to go and see the show”. Some shows were three shillings, and a shilling for a child. As he puts it: “The money was sort of nothing.”
Ted in his pool room, where all his favourite photographs are on display
In the last couple of years, I had seen Uncle Teddy posting diary-like entries on Facebook, sharing his memories along with photographs It led me to ask him some more questions.

Uncle Teddy often says: “I’m sorry you were born a bit late to see the action.” It’s clear he thinks I’d have loved it. He describes the camaraderie of the sideshow community, with everyone pitching in when they were needed. “Everyone’s got to do their own thing,” he says. “The stars have got to get out in the middle of the night and knock pegs in if a storm’s coming up.”

From left: Shayne Brophy, who was born and bred on the showgrounds, performing a trapeze act. She also did contortions, whip-cracking, wire-walking, and worked in the snake pit; Jan Foster in a knife act in the Foster’s big tent show in the late 1960s. Johnny Foster’s son Pikey was the one throwing the knives, and no one dared to be the target except Jan, his wife. Over many years and thousands of knives thrown, the worst she suffered was one small nick to the ear; Ted’s twin daughters, Sonia and Tracy Trevor, working on their Knock ’Em Can joint in the early 1980s
“I always loved the showgrounds because of the people,” Ted says.
My cousins still travel the showground runs, working joints, food trucks and rides. The skills of a modern showman are totally different from the past.

“Today you buy a $2m ride and you don’t have to be a showman,” he says. “People either like the ride or they don’t. It’s just got to be a spectacular ride, a thrill ride, and they’ll queue up and go on it … it’s a different ballgame.[Showpeople] don’t have to get up and tell a tale. They just say, ‘Next ride, hurry now, get your tickets for the next big ride,’ and that’s it.”

These days, Uncle Teddy visits his friends and family at the Beenleigh or Brisbane shows, and chats on the phone to his friends across Australia. “You get friends in different towns. You meet their kids, and when you get old, you meet their grandchildren, and they all become like family.”

I take my own child to the Royal Easter Show when it’s on in Sydney, and the moment I spot a laughing-clown joint, I half expect to see Uncle Teddy come around the corner, his eyes sparkling, a joke on his lips and coins jingling in his waist pouch. I tell them the stories Ted told me, alive with dancing ducks and my iron-jawed great-grandmother. Their eyes widen the way mine did at Ted’s kitchen table, and the show rolls on to another generation.

items.title: Flood victim, 95, lived in Wetherspoons after her home was destroyed and died before she could return
paragraphs: Jean Powell was temporarily staying in one of Monmouth Wetherspoons' guest rooms while her flat was being refurbished after it was flooded a year ago
ByPeter ShuttleworthReporting fromMonmouth and Lucy VladevBBC Wales
When neighbours hammered on Jean Powell's door and evacuated her to safety because the nearby river had burst its banks and swamped her town, little did she know she would never return home.

Jean sought a 10-month refuge at her local Wetherspoons but kept asking when she could go back to her flat, which was flooded when the River Monnow hit 18-times its normal level in south Wales last November.
But the 95-year-old never got to go back home and died in September - one of those who suffered a personal toll from the effects of being flooded.
"Jean used to say, when am I going home?" said friend and neighbour Wyn Smith. "All she wanted to do was come back home and we couldn't fulfil that."
The BBC report from November 2025 when Monmouth town centre was hit by severe flooding after Storm Claudia
Jean was forced out of her home when the river hit record levels in the early hours of November 15 last year as a major incident was declared after almost a month's worth of rain fell in 24 hours.

It has been officially described as a one-in-75-year event when the river flooded more than 400 properties in Monmouth during Storm Claudia - and overwhelmed the defences that were built 35 years ago to protect the centre of town.

Jean, like many in the small town near the Wales and England border, was rescued and after sleeping the night on her neighbour's chair sought temporary sanctuary in Monmouth's Wetherspoons as she had no close family to look after her.
"She was happy in the beginning because she was in town where she wanted to be," recalled Wyn, who visited her friend staying in one of The Kings Head's hotel rooms most days.
"The Wetherspoons staff were brilliant with Jean, they'd take her food and really looked after her."
Wyn Smith helped her neighbours to safety when floodwaters swamped their block of flats in Monmouth and now she's awaiting their return as renovations near the end
"We never thought she'd be there that long," said Wyn. "It's nobody's fault, it took a long time to dry her home out. It had to be done properly."
Residents have been with family, some are in rented accommodation, some have been in an Airbnb while another is in a care home.
Their story is typical of many in Monmouth who have been out of their home since Claudia struck - and that trauma and anxiety from the devastation of 12 months ago is never far from the surface.
"Some had been through the war and they said it upset them more than that. It was just awful," said Wyn.
This was how ground floor residents in Jean's Chippenham Court retirement complex found their flats after Storm Claudia
"But unfortunately it could happen again. There's that fear. If they see water coming, it'll freak them out. They need to feel at home and not worry about the weather."
The Met Office estimates that with current levels of global warming, record-breaking wet winters have gone from once in 80-year events to once in 20-year events.

Wales' environmental body has warned long-range forecasts indicate an increased likelihood of wetter, windier weather than usual this winter with Natural Resources Wales (NRW) saying people should prepare for "the unthinkable".
Monmouth's main shopping street was submerged after the nearby River Monnow burst its banks as it reached record levels during Storm Claudia

Apart from three nights at the local Premier Inn over Christmas when Wetherspoons was shut - where Jean had sandwiches from the nearby petrol station for Christmas dinner because she wanted to "remain independent" - she stayed above the pub in the town's main square for almost 10 months.
"As time went on, living in one room was awful for her," recalled Wyn, 70.
"When Jean got ill, it wasn't a place for her to live. Her health deteriorated and she didn't come back home, which is sad."
Jean's death will be acutely felt when the first displaced residents return to the Chippenham Court retirement complex she called home following its £1m refurbishment in the next few weeks.
Emily Frost recalls how she had to wake her two boys in the middle of the night and evacuate their family home before it was flooded during Storm Claudia last year

One in seven properties in Wales are at risk of flooding, including the Frost household on the other side of Monmouth where Emily says she and her young family will never recover from being evacuated on a lifeboat last year.
The mum-of-two breaks down as she recalls being woken by the coastguard telling her she's got five minutes to evacuate her family as the floodwaters surge towards her end-of-terrace cottage.
"Opening the door, I completely freaked out to the lifeguard," Emily told the BBC.

"They were waist deep in water and said our house was at risk. I just needed to get our boys, who were then aged three and five, and they'd be back with a raft. We didn't have time to think about it."
What was supposed to be a night of celebration for her and husband Jake's 10th wedding anniversary, turned into a nightmare.
This was what Emily Frost saw of her house on the left of this picture as she looked back while their family were evacuated on a life raft during Monmouth's flooding in November 2025
Emily and Jake didn't take their boys when they returned home the following day where more than a foot of water had penetrated their home.
"There was sludge and mud everywhere," she recalled.
"We didn't bring the boys home for a good while because we didn't want them seeing everything that they'd treasured had been destroyed.
"It was the toll it would take on them that worried us the most."
The Frosts lived in rental accommodation nearby for six months as they ripped out the downstairs of their home and started again.
Emily and Jake, who had also been flooded in 2020, have seen their boys "playing floods" so know their children have been "trying to process" their ordeal.
This was Emily Frost's kitchen the day after her family home was flooded for the second time in five years
"They couldn't really understand why we weren't able to go home or have their things" said Emily.

"Because it's the time of year, even now when it rains they'll ask "are we staying home, is it okay? Luckily they're resilient as kids, but you still worry. People don't recover, it's something you'll just live with."

Environmental bodies estimate about 275,000 properties in Wales are at risk of flooding with another 400,000 in Scotland, while in England about 6.3 million properties - around 11.3m people - live in flood risk areas.

An official report said the River Monnow swelled to more than six-and-a-half metres after significant rainfall locally and upstream over the Black Mountains during a week where more than half-a-dozen Met Office rain warnings were issued.
Jennifer and Alan Morgan's 18th Century cottage near the banks of the Monnow had two more doors to hang after a five-year renovation when Claudia struck and they had to start it all again.
Alan and Jennifer Morgan said they spent their life savings renovating the house Alan grew up in and has been in his family for three generations so "it means a lot to us"
"I've not slept well for a year as it's been an absolutely living nightmare," said Jennifer, 70.
"The flooding was awful and the renovation has been so stressful, it's had a huge impact on us. We're not anywhere near to going back home, we probably won't be in until next summer.
"People might think because some of the shops and businesses are open that Monmouth is back to as it was before, but that's not the case - and we're proof."
The River Monnow burst its banks and the official report into the flood said floodwater reached depths 1.5m high, almost 2.5m in some extreme cases

The official Section 19 report, external into the flooding said flood warnings - where action is required as properties are in danger of flooding - were issued for all of Monmouth hours before the floods hit.
Wales' highest state of flood alert - the "risk to life and significant disruption" severe flood warning - was issued by NRW for the northern part of Monmouth on the Friday evening.

The severe flood warning for the rest of Monmouth was issued at 03:31 on the Saturday morning - but that was more than two hours after its flood defences were breached and after shops and homes had been flooded.

Emily had signed up to NRW's free flood alert service, external but went to bed because at midnight the rain had stopped and there was no water visible - half an hour before her young family were evacuated.

Prince William was in the Monmouth area last month visiting communities affected by the 2025 flooding caused by extreme weather conditions and met with Natural Resources Wales, the Welsh Government and Monmouthshire County Council
"When it stopped raining everyone probably thought 'oh well this has passed and we don't need to worry'," she said.
"Then the deluge of water just appeared from nowhere. It just shows how quickly it can change."
The official report recommended a review of the timing of severe flood warnings throughout the Monnow catchment "to ensure adequate advance notice is provided for people to respond effectively."
It also called for a review on the "uptake and understanding" of the flood warning service for those who live and work near the River Monnow.
NRW has said it reviews their "response, recovery and flood warning thresholds" after every serious incident to "identify lessons".
Of the one in seven properties in Wales classed as being at risk of flooding, NRW said less than a third of those eligible to receive flood warnings to their phone or email were currently signed up.
This is how the River Monnow usually looks at Monmouth but it swelled to 18-times its normal depth in November 2025 after torrential downpours during Storm Claudia

NRW argues Wales' geography makes it particularly vulnerable - with a vast coastline and "fast-responding" rivers which can fill at speed as rain runs off steep terrain in places like the south Wales valleys.
The official report also recommended a review into whether Monmouth town centre defences are fit for purpose.
"We're looking at our flood modelling and if there's anything else that can be done," said Sara Pearson of NRW.
"We're seeing flooding that we've never experienced before and with climate change that's set to increase. We can't prevent flooding, but we can help minimise the impact."
The Welsh Government has said it is spending almost £1.4m in flood risk management in Monmouthshire, including £700,000 of NRW funding for works at nearby Skenfrith.
"We have made £85m available this year to Natural Resources Wales and local authorities for flood and coastal erosion schemes across Wales," the government said in a statement.
NRW have said they've done work to clear rivers while the local council insist they've got more workers out clearing ditches, gullies and drains.
Storm Claudia devastated the residents of Monmouth in November 2025 when the historic market town was hit by the worst floods in living memory
"We know how serious this is and how worrying it is for people," said Catrin Maby of Monmouthshire council.

"If it was only down to drain clearance we wouldn't need to worry. We need to look at the engineered defences again, we need to look at how we manage the land, we need to allocate sufficient resources into drainage and clearing those drains."

Insurance companies in the UK paid out £565 million to help homeowners recover from storms and floods in 2025 - and Emily's home is one of them with flood defence measures in place like flood gates and flood doors after advice from Flood Mary, external.
"I feel safer," added Emily. "I'll still be very apprehensive when you get the flood alert, it's whether you're gonna go back to that time or not.
"But you don't feel safe, which you should do in your own house."

items.title: How many sewage spills have happened in your part of Scotland?
paragraphs: It is difficult to assess how the numbers compare to the previous year's figures, when 24,000 spills were recorded because of lower coverage.

The sites are all licensed to release untreated or partially-treated waste but just under 12% of overflows are legally required to report their data to the regulator, the Scottish Environment Protection Agency (Sepa).
Sepa said it has a "risk-based approach" which prioritises areas for monitoring based on population and environmental need.
However, none of the new monitors were required to be reported to Sepa.
Scottish Water figures, external show that Glasgow's River Clyde was one of the most impacted waterways in Scotland last year, receiving almost 6,150 spills - or the equivalent of 17 a day.
When adding in the Clyde Estuary, Firth of Clyde and other unnamed tributaries that run into the Clyde's waterways, this almost doubles to nearly 14,200, or 39 a day.
The Clyde Estuary also recorded the longest duration of spills - more than 25,000 hours - followed by the River Clyde with more than 15,000 hours.
Barcloy Mill Burn in Dumfries and Galloway, which is one of the newly-monitored sites, received the most spills last year, with a total of almost 3,500.
The data suggests that 225 sites recorded no spills and 525 recorded fewer than 10. There may also be errors which suggest a monitor is active when it is not.

items.title: What we know so far about Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress
paragraphs: Nvidia interim CEO Colette Kress has served as the company's chief financial officers. Kevin Roose, host of NPR's Machine Gods podcast, talks with Scott Detrow about what to expect from her.

items.title: China rules out hosting Cop33 climate summit in 2028
paragraphs: China has ruled out hosting the Cop33 UN climate summit in 2028 after months of deliberations, leaving the field open for other Asian countries to hold it, the Guardian understands.

The decision will disappoint many countries and climate experts, who had hoped the world’s biggest emitter would take the lead on the global stage, as the US under Donald Trump has vacated all forms of international cooperation on the climate.

Al Gore, the former US vice-president, was among those left disheartened by the decision. “I would be very much in favour of that idea [of China hosting the summit],” he told the Guardian. “It’s too bad.”

China is in the midst of an economic transformation, from being heavily dependent on coal to becoming an “electro state”. John Kerry, the former US secretary of state, told the Guardian that China was leaving the rest of the world behind in forging and using the low-carbon technologies of the future.
Renewable energy generation capacity has now outstripped coal in China, and its greenhouse gas emissions appear to have declined slightly this year.

Sales of electric vehicles in the country have also taken off, making up nearly two-thirds of the market last month, and China’s clean energy industries drove more than 90% of the country’s investment growth last year.
The rules of the UN Framework Convention on Climate Change (UNFCCC) mean an Asian country should host in 2028.

Gareth Redmond-King, the international lead at the Energy and Climate Intelligence Unit thinktank, said China’s position as an industrial powerhouse would have made it a formidable contender to hold the summit.
“It would undoubtedly be significant for the world’s biggest emitter and second-biggest economy to host a climate Cop,” he said.

“They’re leading the world on investment, manufacture and deployment of clean energy tech, and their emissions have started to tick down. As a leadership story, China hosting Cop33 would be a big deal.”

It is not clear why China has decided against hosting the conference, but several experts that spoke to the Guardian suggested that the US electoral cycle was likely to have been a factor. The next US presidential election will take place on 7 November 2028, and Cop33 is scheduled for 6 to 17 November that year.

After the strong showing by Democrats in the recent midterm elections, in which voter concern over the climate crisis was thought to be a factor, the Democrats will be hoping to elect a climate-friendly president in 2028. But even if they succeed, Trump will still be in office until the following January.
The US president rejects climate science and withdrew the US from the Paris agreement, and is also withdrawing from its parent treaty, the 1992 UNFCCC.

China seeks to be seen as a leader among developing countries, but has been wary of stepping into the gap left by the US. Under the Democratic presidents Joe Biden and Barack Obama, the US and China enjoyed a close partnership on climate issues, setting joint targets on reducing methane and developing clean technology.

Cop33 will be an important meeting because it will include the “global stocktake” – a mechanism under the 2015 Paris climate agreement that examines countries’ progress on cutting emissions in line with the goal of limiting global temperature rises to 1.5C.
That limit is now certain to be surpassed, but experts say countries should now try to minimise the temperature “overshoot”, to avoid worse ravages from extreme weather.

India’s government considered offering to host Cop33 for several months earlier this year, but also decided against it. India’s coal use has been increasing, even as the country exceeds its own renewable energy targets.
The Guardian understands that other countries mulling a bid to host Cop33 include Uzbekistan, South Korea, Indonesia and Thailand.
No decision on a host is likely to be made at this year’s Cop31 meeting, which is ongoing in Turkey, with the Turkish and Australian governments jointly presiding over the summit.

items.title: Ukraine looks to international partners to cover growing financing needs
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Ukrainian article.

More than 40 leaders of European countries gathered in Ireland for a summit Thursday, with discussions centering around European security and the need to support Ukraine amid increased attacks by Russia on its infrastructure and businesses.

Funding for Ukraine was a top issue in Europe in the run up to the two-day European Pollical Community and the informal European Council summit. German Chancellor Friedrich Merz urged the European Union to find the money to meet request from President Volodymyr Zelenskyy of Ukraine for an additional $77 billion for the next year.

In his letter to European Council President António Costa, earlier this week, Merz called the new aid an "essential prerequisite" for approving the next EU budget. The content of the letter was first reported by the Financial Times.

The leaders of Slovakia, the Czech Republic, Hungary and Bulgaria have already voiced their opposition to linking approval of the EU’s budget to any new funding for Ukraine, which may delay the approval of the money.

Following the meeting with Zelenskyy on Thursday, European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen assured the Ukrainian leader of the EU's support, covering immediate survival this winter and funds needed through 2027. She announced the European Council will review the Commission's proposal for Ukraine's financing needs by the end of the month.

To alleviate immediate financial pressure, Ukraine hopes to obtain $1.67 billion in fresh funding from the International Monetary Fund by the end of the year. IMF's Director of the Communications Department, Julie Kozack told reporters on October 29 that the money will be released once the IMF completes assessment of its program in Ukraine. The IMF has started the review of the program for Ukraine on Monday.

The U.S., as the most powerful member of the IMF, supports the current Fund's program for Ukraine, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent announced earlier this year (in April) when met he with Ukrainian Prime Minister Yulia Svyrydenko.

"Secretary Bessent underscored President Trump’s efforts for a lasting peace for Ukraine, and highlighted the United States’ support for Ukraine’s new IMF program and for the progress that Ukraine has made on its reforms," a Treasury Department statement said.
An analyst told VOA staying on track with the IMF program is an important anchor for Ukraine to secure support from other international partners.

“There are other partners who support us much more,” Yuliya Markuts, head of the Center for Public Finance and Governance at the Kyiv School of Economics, said. “But the IMF is an anchor that demonstrates to our partners that Ukraine is indeed a country they can work with, they can trust and treat as a reliable partner. Therefore, Ukraine is very much dependent on having an IMF program.”

Over the past several months, Ukraine's parliament has approved several laws envisaged by the program. Markuts says she is “cautiously optimistic” that Ukraine will obtain the favorable review from the IMF.
If Ukraine does not get the fresh funding, the situation could be dire, said Markuts, as Ukraine has virtually no room to cut spending.

“This is actually a very difficult situation. Because shelling is taking place constantly. There are ongoing problems with critical infrastructure, particularly energy infrastructure,” Markuts said. “We have to provide the people living in this country with heating, water, electricity, and so on.”
Markuts stated that Ukraine's current investment is geared towards endurance and providing basic services to its people through the war.
Timothy Ash, chief strategist of BlueBay Asset Management, believes that the IMF supports maintaining the program.

“But the IMF operates in a certain way - the program has to be sustainable," he told VOA. He highlighted that this would require financing assurances from Ukraine’s allies “that those gaps will be met."
Ash says he is confident that Ukraine will be able to secure funding from European partners, despite the opposition from some EU members.

“The big economies in Europe totally get it. Europe has figured out that Ukraine is central to its security in its long-term defense," he said. "Europe needs time to build autonomous defense capability, and the longer Ukraine survives in this war, the longer Europe has to build that autonomous defense capability. So, Europe has an interest now in helping Ukraine defend itself and Europe,” he adds.

items.title: Microsoft begins restoring services amid global outage affecting Outlook and Teams
paragraphs: Microsoft says a portion of servers are returning to service, and a streamlined recovery process is under way to end a global outage that has resulted in nearly 130,000 users worldwide reporting issues accessing its 365 suite of software, including Outlook and Teams.

Outage website Down Detector showed a spike in Microsoft 365 problems, with nearly 130,000 reports of issues affecting access to Word, Excel, PowerPoint, Outlook and Teams as well as enterprise services such as SharePoint and OneDrive. AI assistant Copilot was also affected.
New reports have since fallen from that peak, but many said they couldn’t send and receive emails, or had trouble loading their inboxes altogether.
Posting on X, Microsoft said it was “investigating reports of users experiencing issues accessing Exchange Online mailboxes through multiple connection methods”.

Microsoft later explained that a portion of its infrastructure was “experiencing elevated load” – which it said was “likely contributing to the connectivity errors”. The company determined a number of servers were “unexpectedly unavailable” due to a problem that caused them to fail during automated checks.

At 9pm UTC Thursday, the tech company said it had validated an alternative health check method on a subset of the affected servers, which allowed them to successfully return to service, and that fix was now being applied more broadly.

Microsoft was also preparing an automated process to detect and restart unresponsive servers. It said the review of recent changes has identified configuration updates as a potential cause for the issue, but said it was still being investigated.
At 9.41pm UTC, Microsoft said it was working through restarting and validating the affected servers, and looking to expedite the process.
“In parallel, we’re assessing whether reverting the small number of recent configuration updates we identified could help accelerate recovery.”
But by 10.11pm UTC, Microsoft said it was “continuing to pursue all available pathways to restore service” as the actions taken so far “have not provided the anticipated relief”.
The company said a core process on the affected servers was becoming overwhelmed, causing the servers to stop responding.
At 11.06pm UTC, Microsoft said a “portion of the affected servers” had begun being returned to service and were remaining stable.
“We’ve also shifted traffic and connections to alternative pathways wherever possible and have observed limited recovery in some regions.”

The company said it had streamlined its recovery process to expedite returning the remaining affected servers to service, and Microsoft had implemented protective traffic management to reduce the load to the affected servers.
Customers may experience a gradual recovery as users reconnect to 365 services, Microsoft said.
An earlier service degradation alert on Microsoft’s site said it was “aggressively pursuing all pathways to reduce impact” and said it was “restarting affected servers to return them to service”.
“As a precaution, we’ve paused all deployments and configuration changes while we review recent changes for any correlation to this event.

“We’ve determined that the elevated load isn’t driven by an overall increase in traffic, but by a large number of servers being unexpectedly unavailable, which is shifting load onto the remaining infrastructure.
“We’re investigating what’s causing these servers to become unavailable while we work to safely return them to service.”

Mark Gregory, associate professor in the School of Engineering at RMIT University, said the outage appears to be affecting the network layer in Microsoft’s systems, and was potentially similar to the configuration issue which brought down Optus’s network in 2023.
He said when some of the servers have configuration issues, it means customers are forced to share a smaller pool of servers to access the cloud services.
“If you lose part of that pool, then all of the users are trying to access the remaining servers, and that overloads them. And then they go down.
“And so you end up with a cascading problem. Then it takes time to find the underlying problem, in this case, a misconfiguration in the network layer.”

Gregory said it showed companies should invest more in testing environments for configuration changes before deployment in the live network, and said businesses reliant on cloud services such as Microsoft 365 should have backup options.
“From a global perspective, there is someone somewhere that’s that’s been badly affected by this and you end up with lost productivity,” he said.
“They’re being left high and trying now … it then becomes important to have an alternative.”
“Many people would keep a Gmail account, if their Microsoft goes down, they use Gmail. If Gmail goes down, they use Microsoft.”
Both OpenAI and Anthropic reported the issue was affecting the Microsoft 365 connector that links ChatGPT and Claude AI to Microsoft services.
Earlier, the company said it had “successfully restored” problems related to Microsoft Teams in North America, although some users continued to report connectivity issues.

items.title: US-based Russian activist sentenced to 6 years in absentia for "military fakes"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Russian article.

A court in Ulan-Ude, Russia, has sentenced U.S.-based activist and researcher Maria Vyushkova in absentia to six years in prison on a charge of allegedly “spreading knowingly false information” about the Russian armed forces.
"The kind of persecution in absentia and then attempts to put pressure on relatives who remained in Russia" are now becoming more widespread, Vyushkova VOA's Russian service.

The case stemmed from her research on the killings of hundreds of civilians in Bucha, Ukraine, in March of 2022. Russia has consistently denied any involvement in the killings and has called the evidence staged.
Some media accounts at the time singled out Buryat soldiers in the Russian army as being responsible. Buryats are an Indigenous people who live mainly in southern Siberia near the Mongolian border.

Vyushkova, herself a Buryat, argued that Russian paratroopers from Pskov were in Bucha at the time of the killings. The court said it found her statements were motivated by political hatred, according to the independent outlet Glasnaya.

Vyushkova, a citizen of the Russian Federation and the United States, is one of the co-founders of the Free Buryatia Foundation, which has been recognized in Russia as an "undesirable", "terrorist" and "extremist" organization.
In April 2026, the Russian authorities put Vyushkova on the register of foreign agents, and in July, the Ministry of Internal Affairs put her on the wanted list.
Vyushkova, who lives in the United States and has not traveled to Russia for many years, says she is surprised by the attention of the Russian authorities to her activities.

She says she believes that "this is part of a large, coordinated campaign against activists from regional ethnic groups, because this case was opened against me in the summer of 2026 for an interview that I gave in the summer of 2023."
Vyushkova says she plans to completely ignore the sentencing. "I do not recognize any right of the Russian authorities to put me on trial, to accuse me of something and to judge me," she told VOA.

items.title: Finnegan Shannon installs conveyor belt for displaying art accessibly in Brooklyn
paragraphs: New York City-based artist Finnegan Shannon has installed a conveyor belt to display art at cultural centre Pioneer Works in Brooklyn, USA, as a commentary on accessibility in art.
According to Pioneer Works, the There’s No Me Without You installation fulfils Shannon’s “longtime fantasy of an exhibition space that would meet their access needs”.

Chairs were placed around the closed-loop 12-foot-long mechanism, letting visitors sit when viewing and engaging with exhibited objects, archival materials and portable DVD players placed on a series of moving trays.

It was created from a restaurant-style system similar to those used in sushi restaurants where the food is delivered via a conveyor belt. The rest of the room on the upper floor of the arts centre was covered in rich fabrics and built-in benches along the perimeter.

“My conveyor belt, technically a retail and restaurant-style display system, is a tool for me to be in less pain when I’m experiencing art,” said Shannon, who was diagnosed with cerebral palsy at birth. “I notice I am a much more patient and curious visitor when I’m sitting down.”
The title of the installation reflects the artist’s relationship to the concept of interdependence.
“If disabled people were in charge, we would have a bunch of varied and deluxe options for sitting and lying down in exhibition spaces,” they said.
“Instead we live in a world where this type of infrastructure is quite basic and sparse.”

The installation is being used to present new commissions by artists with disabilities Joselia Rebekah Hughes, Ariana Martinez and Alex Dolores Salerno. For the three consecutive exhibitions, visitors are invited to interact with the work through touch, sight, and sound.
Air filters with bright colours were included in the middle of the conveyor belt to assist with air quality and masks were encouraged for visitors.
Shannon emphasised the collaborative nature of artistic endeavour through the exhibition.
“We know that on some fundamental level, no solo exhibition is truly a solo endeavor,” Shannon said.
“Putting together an exhibition takes immense collaboration and support – art handlers, facilities staff, curators, registrars, accountants, assistants – and that is all within the institution.”
“You can trace that entanglement further: I’m dependent on workers, paid and unpaid care labor, and friendships, family, and more, both locally and across the globe.”

“I never want someone to come away from an exhibition with my work feeling like they’ve experienced something that is mine,” they said. “Instead I hope they have threads to follow to learn more about the vast world of knowledge that is disability culture.”

Shannon’s other projects have focused on access. Alt Text as Poetry, a collaboration with Bojana Coklyat exploring image description and Do You Want Us Here or Not is a series of museum benches and cushions designed to encourage rest.
