Other designs that prioritise accessibility were showcased at The Fashion Institute of Technology’s Adapt/Evolve exhibition in New York last year.
There’s No Me Without You is on show at Pioneer Works in Brooklyn from 12 September to 20 December. For more exhibitions, installations and talks worldwide, visit Dezeen Events Guide.

items.title: Explainer: From undercover employment to corporate data breaches: the "Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act"
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Korean article.

A bipartisan bill that could help U.S. small businesses recognize threats from foreign adversaries, including the risk posed by North Korean workers posing as job candidates, was debated and passed in the House of Representatives on Wednesday. It now moves on to the Senate.

The core provision requires the Small Business Administration to develop and distribute educational materials so that businesses can recognize the risks identified by the U.S. government and learn how to respond.

Its official title is the “Combating Foreign Threats to Main Street Act of 2026." It requires the Small Business Administration to guide businesses on how to identify, prevent, and respond to threats. The bill requires the SBA to develop materials in collaboration with relevant agencies and distribute them through regional offices and existing support programs. The SBA would be expected to use its existing budget to produce new materials.

Rep. Roger Williams, a Republican from Texas’s 25th Congressional District and chairman of the House Small Business Committee, is leading the effort. Williams has specifically identified China, Russia and North Korea as foreign threats the legislation seeks to address. Explaining the need for the bill, he said that “while many small businesses are exposed to foreign threats, they lack the resources and expertise to respond.”
Rep. Derek Tran, a Democrat representing California’s 45th Congressional District, is also involved in the effort. He serves on the House Small Business and Armed Services committees.
Why Is This Important for Small and Medium-Sized Enterprises?
“Even small companies have technology and information that needs to be protected”, according to the proposed bill.

For example, even a small software company may have programs it developed in-house. “If a manufacturer’s blueprints or customer and business partner information are leaked, it could harm the business”.
Chairman Williams’ office explained that “many small businesses lack the resources or expertise to identify and respond to increasingly sophisticated threats”.
The bill goes beyond simply alerting businesses to risk; it also provides guidance on prevention methods and where to seek assistance.
It includes guidelines to ensure that while risks are assessed when conducting business or receiving investments overseas, legitimate commercial activities are not unnecessarily restricted.

The bill relies on the Commerce Department’s definition of “foreign adversary,” which includes North Korea. While it does not specifically address North Korea’s use of covert IT workers in U.S. companies, its coverage of cyber intrusions and its catch-all provision for emerging threats could allow the SBA to include such schemes.
During hiring: North Korean IT workers misrepresent their identities and actual work locations to secure remote work positions.
Once hired: They gain access to the company’s computer networks and the data necessary to perform their duties.
If that access is abused: It can lead to the theft of corporate information or extortion.

Last January, the FBI warned of a case in which North Korean IT personnel stole sensitive corporate data and program source code from a company and, after being discovered, used this as leverage to demand money.
In July of the same year, the FBI stated that companies that outsource IT work to third-party vendors may face additional vulnerabilities because they cannot directly manage the hiring process.
This alert is directed at U.S. companies in general. It does not mean that all affected companies are small and medium-sized enterprises.
What kind of assistance will companies receive?
The bill requires the SBA to guide companies on how to protect intellectual property, trade secrets, sensitive corporate information, and supply chains.
The proposed bill covers not only cybersecurity but also the import of goods produced through forced labor, counterfeit goods and illicit trade, and predatory investment practices.
The bill now moves to the Senate. There is currently no Senate version of the bill, and this session of Congress ends in early January.
- September 10: The bill was introduced by Rep. Roger Williams (R-Texas), with Rep. Derek Tran (D-Calif.) as the Democratic co-sponsor.
- September 16: The House Small Business Committee voted 22–0 to recommend the bill to the full House.
- October 9: The committee’s official report was submitted.
- November 11: Passed by a voice vote. The Senate must approve it with the same wording, and the President must sign it.

items.title: Duran Duran drummer quits band due to tinnitus
paragraphs: Duran Duran drummer Roger Taylor said he will leave the band due to his worsening tinnitus.

Taylor has been the chart-topping group's drummer since they formed in Birmingham in 1978, which he described as "the joy of my life", but said he had "reached the point where I must now listen to my body and my doctors".
The 66-year-old said his condition has been getting steadily worse, leading to him making one of his hardest decisions to quit the band.

The group, made up of Simon Le Bon, keyboardist Nick Rhodes and guitarist John Taylor, said his decision came after "careful consideration and medical advice", which said that "protecting his hearing and long-term health must now come first".

Taylor, who left the band in 1985 before returning in 2001, said: "Playing drums in this band has been the joy of my life, and I'll never be able to properly thank the fans for the love they've shown us over the years.
"But the truth is that my tinnitus has been getting steadily worse," he said.
He said deciding on the timing had been difficult but he was pleased to be "going out on a real high".

"We've just returned from a hugely successful UK and European tour, which followed our second headline show at BST Hyde Park, our induction into the Rock & Roll Hall Of Fame, and a return to the studio with Nile Rodgers.
"I couldn't have asked for a better final chapter, with so many special moments that I'll treasure forever.
"I move on with enormous pride, and with nothing but love for Simon, Nick and John," he said.

Taylor's band members added that he had helped define the sound of the group, performing on 10 hit albums, their two number one singles - Is There Something I Should Know? and The Reflex - and the band's 1985 James Bond theme A View To A Kill.
"His drumming helped define the sound of Duran Duran from the very beginning and having him back with us since 2001 has been incredibly important to us all.
"We completely support his decision and wish him health and happiness.
"He will always be part of this family, while we continue exploring new and exciting projects with the band."

items.title: Jensen Huang was a busted flush at Nvidia – he had to go | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Half the tech world made up its mind before the facts could be assessed properly. Jensen Huang was “irreplaceable”, said the chorus at the start of this week. Nvidia would melt without the co-founder’s brilliance, apparently. The chipmaker’s board had to find a way to save its genius for the sake of corporate America and the entire AI universe.
It was always nonsense because, after the passage of only a few days since his confession of infidelity, Huang looked less like a towering corporate titan and more like a political liability.

An extramarital affair is not usually a resigning matter in itself – saintliness is not an absolute requirement of the job. But the circumstances here were different. A relationship with the Chinese boss of a Singapore-based firm suspected of smuggling Nvidia chips into China? That displayed recklessness on top of mere unfaithfulness.

Did he know the Megaspeed executive, Alice Huang (no relation), was regarded as a Chinese spy by US officials? It hardly matters. In the ultra-political world of in-demand AI computer chips, there were enough reasons for him to be careful in the extreme. The conflict of interest, and the risk of landing Nvidia in a quagmire of national security inquiries in Washington, would have been obvious.

Reports of a second affair with a senior Nvidia employee compounded matters – US companies tend to be sensitive about such relationships. But the company’s directors might also have wondered what else could be revealed in coming weeks. Rule number one in these situations is to get all the bad news out on day one.

The kneejerk reaction to Jensen Huang’s resignation was 13% off the share price. That was understandable – some investors truly believed the “irreplaceable” thesis. However, sitting in Nvidia’s boardroom, the job was not to worry about the initial stock market response but about what was best for the business. For multiple reasons, it was time to “rip off the Band-Aid and take Nvidia into its next chapter”, as Dan Ives, a senior tech analyst, put it.

First, the congressional investigations will happen anyway. Democratic senators have asked administration officials to preserve all documents and communications related to the sale of Nvidia’s advanced AI chips to China. At heart, that issue is wider than Nvidia – it’s about whether US officials have themselves jeopardised the country’s lead over China in AI. But, one way or another, the company’s activities, and ties to the Trump administration, will come under scrutiny like never before. Nvidia is better placed to defend itself without Huang in the top job.

Second, his personal lobbying clout on export policy had evaporated. After this week’s revelations, he had no credibility as an advocate of looser restrictions. The political demand will be entirely in the other direction – for loopholes to be closed.

Third, there is the issue Nvidia’s underpowered board has dodged for too long: over-reliance on one individual. Never mind the risk of scandal, there is always a danger in concentrating too much day-to-day power in the hands of one individual. Nobody doubts Huang’s commercial talents, but even “godfathers of AI” in leather jackets don’t go on forever. Better to have a setup that can cope with change at the top.

Colette Kress, the chief financial officer who will stand in as chief executive, is well regarded on Wall Street. Nvidia will not be short of outside applicants on a permanent basis. And the board has heard the governance criticism that a multitrillion-dollar company ought to have an independent chair: Harvey Jones, a former chief executive at semiconductor company Synopsys and a member of the current crew of directors, has got the gig. Then comes the task of creating some proper governance checks and balances, which may require fresh faces among the independent directors.

Within a couple of hours, the fall in the share price had narrowed to 5% as investors remembered that Nvidia still has the best, and most in-demand, graphics processing units in the world and that many pioneering companies have prospered after the exit of an “irreplaceable” chief executive.

Nobody pretends the management job will be easy. Nvidia will be different, not least because the political winds in the US have shifted. But there was no point trying to cling to a chief executive, however successful, who had made himself a busted flush. Huang had to go.

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigns as US lawmakers push tougher chip export controls
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Mandarin article.

Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang resigned Thursday following controversy surrounding an extramarital affair and concerns about potential national security risks, as members of Congress urge tighter restrictions on exports of advanced SI (commonly referred to as AI) chips.
Nvidia has named Chief Financial Officer Colette Kress as interim CEO.

The resignation comes amid growing concerns about possible national security risks linked to Huang's relationship with Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, a former executive at Singapore-based technology company Megaspeed. U.S. intelligence officials suspect Alice Huang of gathering information for Beijing.
The developments have intensified scrutiny of Nvidia's business ties to China and renewed calls in Congress for tighter restrictions on exports of advanced super intelligence chips.
U.S. lawmakers from both parties are pushing to include new restrictions in the annual National Defense Authorization Act, or NDAA, which Congress hopes to pass before the end of the year.
The House Select Committee on China, led by Republican Representative John Moolenaar, called for stronger export controls following Huang’s resignation.

“Jensen Huang’s firing from the company he founded is an unfortunate end that could have been avoided,” Moolenaar said in a statement, “Nvidia must now change its corporate practices and appoint leadership that makes national security its top priority. In Congress we must act quickly to pass bipartisan export control legislation in the year-end national defense bill.”
House Speaker Mike Johnson, a Republican, told Politico that he supports adding stronger chip export restrictions to the NDAA.
Democrats have also urged Congress to act.
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries said Monday that he would work to ensure chip export restrictions remain in the final version of the NDAA.
Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer has also urged lawmakers to pass legislation limiting China's access to advanced U.S. technology, warning that Congress must act before it is too late.

Congress is considering several legislative proposals designed to strengthen U.S. oversight of semiconductor exports and prevent sensitive technology from reaching countries considered national security threats.

The AI Overwatch Act, introduced by Republican Representative Brian Mast, would restrict exports of advanced artificial intelligence chips to China and other countries considered national security concerns.

The Chip Security Act, introduced by Republican Representative Bill Huizenga, would require advanced AI chips to have location-verification technology and require companies to report suspicious transfers of sensitive technology.

The Remote Access Security Act, introduced by Republican Representative Mike Lawler, would expand U.S. export controls to cover remote access to certain technologies when it poses a serious national security threat.

The Multilateral Alignment of Technology Controls on Hardware Act, or MATCH Act, would tighten restrictions on exports of advanced semiconductor manufacturing equipment and improve coordination with U.S. allies.

The Senate version of the 2027 NDAA already includes provisions from several of these bills. The House and Senate must agree on identical versions before the legislation can go to the president for signature.
The current Congress ends January 3, 2027. If lawmakers fail to pass the legislation before then, they will have to restart the process in the new Congress.

items.title: Crosslam completes Brazil's tallest mass-timber tower
paragraphs: Engineering company Crosslam has designed and built Aurora 275, a hybrid building with mass-timber elements that the company claims is the tallest of its type in Brazil.

Standing 22 metres tall, Aurora 275 is considered a hybrid-timber building, with a structural system consisting of a reinforced concrete core, metal, and mass-timber elements including glued-laminated timber (glulam) beams and columns.
Located in the Suzano area of São Paulo, according to Crosslam, it is the tallest building of its type in Brazil.
Crosslam, which usually acts as an engineer for other firms, designed the building itself to demonstrate the potential of mass timber in Brazil.
“We believed that, to sell the first timber building, we first had to build our own,” said Crosslam founder José Alberto Corrêa. “Otherwise, the Brazilian market wouldn’t trust that it was possible.”

To further demonstrate the method’s viability, the building was constructed in four weeks by a five-person team, according to Crosslam. The timber was produced in the company’s factory using wood sourced from Brazil.
Aurora 275 sits next to smaller residential buildings. It features a metal-clad facade, with yellow detailing running up its face.
It extends in two directions from a concrete core, with balconies for each of the 10 apartments.
On the outside, the timber elements are only visible on the undersides of the balconies.
However, on the inside, the timber elements are more visible, with the cross-laminated timber floorplates and glulam beams exposed, giving the interiors a warm feel.
Crosslam said that the structure shows the potential for timber buildings for industrial-style housing production in the country.
“Using engineered timber offers benefits related to the industrialisation of construction, the efficiency of the assembly process, and building performance,” said the project teaam.
“The main advantages include: faster assembly, dimensional precision, reduced waste on the construction site, a lighter structure, and lower carbon emissions.”
The company claimed that the building is carbon neutral.

Timber construction for tall buildings is gaining popularity across the world, with inroads into construction in North America and Europe. The current tallest timber structure in the world recently topped out in Australia.

items.title: Participating in art and culture has measurable benefits on our wellbeing | Letter
paragraphs: Reading Emma Brockes’ response to a recent Art Fund study, I felt the significance of the research may have been lost in its packaging (Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll, 5 November).

The language of “prescribing” art has its roots in social prescribing. I understand why this might make people uncomfortable, particularly if it suggests that culture is being instrumentalised rather than enjoyed for its own sake.

Yet these findings matter for two reasons. First, they provide evidence for what many of us know intuitively: that participating in and experiencing art and culture are not only enriching, but also have measurable benefits for our health and wellbeing.

Second, with budgets for culture under pressure, this evidence strengthens our case for public investment. Surely that’s another argument for keeping our national museums free and ensuring everyone can access their wellbeing benefits.

Rather than viewing this study cynically, we should recognise the opportunities it presents. As Daisy Fancourt, who is quoted in Brockes’ article, explores in her excellent and insightful book Art Cure, the evidence extends far beyond visiting galleries and museums.

In the London borough of Ealing, we’re piloting a free creative health programme bringing residents and council staff together through activities ranging from clay workshops to Islamic geometric drawing. Almost all participants have reported improved wellbeing following these sessions. But beyond the evaluation, conversations have shown me how even an hour spent being creative can positively change the course of someone’s day, while regular participation can have a lasting impact on their lives.

Art shouldn’t have to justify its existence through its health benefits. But understanding those benefits strengthens the case for everyone to experience, participate in and benefit from art and culture.

And if the thought of visiting a museum makes Brockes’ eyes roll, I’d happily invite her to one of our workshops. She might leave having learned a new skill, but I suspect she’d take away rather more than that. William Rees Culture officer, Ealing council

items.title: Jensen Huang built an AI kingdom. Now he’s gone, will Nvidia’s ramparts be breached?
paragraphs: Can the AI economy survive without its “central bank”? What does Jensen Huang’s fall mean for the world’s second-most valuable company, and what might a tremor in its fortunes mean for the world?

Nvidia’s sky-high valuation is based on the fact that it designs and sells the advanced AI chips, called graphics processing units (GPUs), that underpin the AI economy. Without these, AI models such as ChatGPT and Claude could not be trained and would not run.
This has made the chipmaker arguably the most important player in AI and, at times, the most valuable company in the world. Huang’s departure sent shares in Nvidia plunging 13% in early trading.

Nvidia is not the only company that designs these chips. Most leading tech companies, including Microsoft, Meta and Google, are trying to make their own lines of AI chips. Some of these, such as Google’s tensor processing units, appear to be at least as good as Nvidia’s, and even better for certain purposes.
What makes Nvidia irreplaceable – and far more integral to the AI economy – is its web of relationships, most of these led by Huang himself.

One aspect of this is Nvidia’s complex web of ties with the companies actually building AI infrastructure, a mess of circular finance that implicates US tech giants and many of the world’s governments.

In recent years, Huang has been the kingmaker when it comes to AI. In 2025, he met numerous world leaders – including Mohammed bin Salman, Keir Starmer and Emmanuel Macron – persuading them of the urgency of developing “sovereign AI” with his product. His presence served as a guarantee of those nations’ AI plans. These meetings were followed by deals in which Nvidia announced it had arrangements to supply those governments with precious, hard-to-get chips.

None of these agreements were particularly transparent. While Nvidia appears to have promised 260,000 advanced chips to South Korea, for example, it was never immediately apparent when those chips would be delivered, who would pay for them, and on what terms.

Meanwhile, Nvidia financed a web of companies called “neoclouds” to buy its chips and put them in datacentres, there to be rented to the world’s biggest AI companies. These neoclouds have done wonders for Nvidia, propping up demand and keeping the risk associated with building datacentres and finding customers for them off its balance sheets.

Neoclouds are not the only thing financed by Nvidia. It has become known as the “central bank of AI” because it is enmeshed in almost every layer of the AI economy. Nvidia has invested in a spate of AI startups that could become future customers. It has offered massive sums of cash to companies such as OpenAI, to be used to buy its chips. This investment runs to hundreds of billions of dollars of Nvidia’s money, circling again and again through a limited set of accounts.

Then there is Nvidia’s relationship with a Taiwanese company called TSMC, or the Taiwan Semiconductor Manufacturing Company. TSMC makes the world’s AI chips, churning them out across several fabrication plants on the north-west of the island.

As far as geopolitics goes, TSMC is arguably more important than Nvidia or any other chip designer. Other companies can design AI chips, but TSMC manufactures the overwhelming majority of them and has no real competitor. This is because manufacturing AI chips is one of the most expensive and challenging industrial processes to date.

Each chip is etched with nanometre lines by lasers working in the extreme ultraviolet spectrum, which cost billions of dollars and two decades of research to develop. While TSMC has refined its process to make these chips for more than two decades, it still has only a 60% yield rate for its most advanced chips, which means that 40% of them have defects. It’s a staggeringly high rate for one of the world’s most expensive technologies.

Nvidia has worked closely with TSMC to help it develop its processes and products. Lore has it that Huang wrote the chief executive of TSMC a letter introducing himself in 1997. These are high-trust relationships built over decades.

Will it all be the same without Huang? This is almost impossible to answer because Nvidia’s relationships are so opaque. Investigators following the supply chain of its chips run up against secretive corporate contracts and tangled export records. There is known to be a years-long queue of customers waiting to obtain its chips, but questions regarding who is in that queue, in what order, and how many chips have been shipped remain open.

This murkiness was brought into sharp focus by Megaspeed, a small Singaporean company that was getting access to lots of GPUs, even as other companies struggled. One of Megaspeed’s executives, Alice Huang, was later revealed to be having an affair with Nvidia’s chief executive, and to be an alleged Chinese spy. This relationship appears to have allowed Megaspeed to secure roughly $7.5bn (£5.67bn) worth of Nvidia chips, which were allegedly smuggled into China.

Was Huang and his glad-handing a source of this opacity? Perhaps a new chief executive could bring some transparency and predictability to the business, at least in terms of chips contracts and supply chains.

But what else could be laid bare if the “central bank of AI” became more transparent, or came under external scrutiny? Many questions surround its contracts and relationships; lots of elaborate debt structures and handshake agreements may yet be uncovered.

Huang dazzled the world in his leather jacket; he convinced heads of government that his technology held the keys to transformation and to power. When the patina wears off, will this still seem the case?

items.title: Fuel shortages in Iraqi Kurdistan spark dispute over separate queues for women
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.

Fuel shortages in Iraq's Kurdistan Region have sparked a dispute over how subsidized gasoline is distributed, with women drivers in Halabja complaining of discrimination after authorities introduced restrictions on their access to filling stations.
Long queues have become a common sight outside government-run fuel stations across the region since U.S. and Israeli military operations against Iran began in late February, disrupting fuel imports.
Despite being OPEC's second-largest oil producer, Iraq relies heavily on imported petroleum products because domestic refineries cannot produce enough gasoline to meet demand.
In Halabja, in Northeast Iraq near the Iranian border, motorists spend hours waiting for fuel, while others queue overnight to secure gasoline at government-subsidized prices.

According to the most recent information from August, a liter of gasoline costs 750 Iraqi dinars at government stations, compared with around 1,150 dinars at privately operated stations, a price gap that has encouraged drivers to endure lengthy waits.
To ease the burden on women, who generally face greater social constraints on waiting overnight, Halabja's fuel committee initially introduced separate queues for male and female drivers.

But the arrangement prompted complaints from some men, who argued that women were receiving preferential treatment. Some also accused female drivers of bringing their husbands' vehicles to obtain cheaper fuel.

Authorities subsequently changed the system, allowing one female driver to enter a station after every 10 male drivers. Women are also required to present driving licenses; a requirement not imposed on men.
The changes have angered women who say they face longer waits, additional scrutiny and harassment from male motorists.
"Many men go through, eight or 10 of them, before one woman is allowed in," said Kurda Jamal, a local driver.

"They then ask women for their driving licenses and accuse them of driving cars belonging to their husbands," she said, adding that such accusations were embarrassing and made the experience increasingly difficult.
Another female driver, Kizhan Osman, called for equal treatment.

"If a man gets gasoline, the next person should be a woman," she said. "It should not be 10 men followed by one woman. We want this discrimination to end at all fuel stations in Kurdistan Region, particularly in Halabja."
Male drivers have also expressed frustration, saying the shortages have disrupted their work and daily lives.
Aram Abdullah, a local motorist, said teachers, government employees and other workers were losing valuable time waiting for fuel.
"You might spend half your day just getting a few liters of gasoline," he said. "What time is left for the rest of your life?"
Residents also complained that the allocation of just one gasoline tanker a day to Halabja was insufficient to meet demand.
Halabja district administrator Simko Salar attributed the congestion to reduced fuel allocations and defended the revised distribution system as fair.

"Equality does not mean allowing one woman and then one man through," Salar said, arguing that the much shorter queues for women under the previous arrangement meant men could wait seven hours while women received fuel in half an hour.
"Both are human beings," he said, adding that authorities respected women and would investigate their complaints.
For many motorists, however, the financial incentive remains difficult to ignore.

The lower price of subsidized gasoline has prompted some residents to begin queuing a day before deliveries arrive, spending the night outside filling stations in hopes of securing fuel the following morning.

items.title: UN representative urges Taliban to end child recruitment and recognize 18 as age of adulthood
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Pashto article.

The United Nations has urged the Taliban to align their definition of a child with the Convention on the Rights of the Child, amid growing concerns over the recruitment and use of children by the group in Afghanistan.

The U.N. Special Representative for Children and Armed Conflict, Vanessa Frazier, told VOA that the age of adulthood must be set at 18, warning that physical signs of puberty cannot replace the internationally recognized legal definition of a child.
The Taliban leader issued a decree banning the recruitment of children “who do not show physical signs of puberty” into their ranks.
Frazier, however, said that the main problem is how these directives define a child.

“The problem that we have is that the distinguishing element that is used in the edicts of the Taliban is signs of puberty, and not the age of 18, which comes out of the Convention on the Rights of the Child,” said Frazier.
The U.N. special representative called on the Taliban to align their definition of a child with the Convention on the Rights of the Child to which Afghanistan is a party.
A new U.N. report released in September said that the task force verified the recruitment of 557 boys, some as young as 12 years old, by the Taliban from 2023 to 2025.

The U.S. State Department’s 2026 Trafficking in Persons Report, released in October, said that there was a pattern of recruiting and using children both in combat and support roles, as well as a pattern of sexual slavery through bacha bazi, a practice in which men exploit boys for social and sexual entertainment.

The report accused the Taliban of not taking measures to prevent the recruitment and use of children for combat and support roles, and that the Taliban did not make efforts to protect the victims of bacha bazi.

However, the report acknowledged that the Taliban established a commission to identify and demobilize children among its forces and that an international organization was able to secure the release of 58 children from their ranks.
Frazier said poverty and economic hardship could also leave Afghan children vulnerable to recruitment.
“Families struggling to feed their children may see joining an armed force as a source of food, security and income,” she told VOA.
Frazier said that boys are reportedly used in a range of roles, including cooking, carrying weapons, fighting and serving as border guards.
She also said that the militarization of schools and ideological indoctrination of children under the Taliban is concerning.
"And so, when they are recruited, there's already been some indoctrination that has happened in madrasas,” Frazier added.

The Annual Report of the U.N. Secretary-General on Children and Armed Conflict for 2025 reported 1,070 verified grave violations against children, including recruiting and using 204 boys by the Taliban in combat, 62 in support roles and 142 verified.
The U.N. also reported the killing of 100 and maiming of 290 children, including the killing of 103 children in the air strikes by Pakistani forces.
The report called on the Taliban to “immediately take all actions to better protect and uphold the rights of children and ensure accountability.”

items.title: These are 13 of the best earphones on the market – and they’re all discounted for early Black Friday
paragraphs: As the 11/11 sale swings into early Black Friday discounts, I've found 13 (mainly) in-ear monitor (IEM) deals that I'd personally buy today – in fact I already own 10 of them, so I don't think you can get a stronger recommendation!

All of the below wired earphones are distributed by the IEM retailer, curator, and distributor Linsoul, and with that comes a certain guarantee of quality. Everyone I've tested from them has hit a high level of quality control, so really all you as the potential buyer have to worry about, is if the sound profile is to your taste.

As I've tried most of them, I'm going to give you my tuning impressions, plus any design and comfort highlights for each of them. Many of them feature in my list of the best IEMs under $500, and my favourite budget IEMs under $100 – so these aren't just random IEM deals, but rather a curated list of genuinely excellent options.

I were to pick only one? Considering price, sound and build quality, I would get the Kiwi Ears KE4 down from $199 to $169. It's a fantastic, modern IEM that has a best-seller since its 2024 release for very good reason.

The Kiwi Ears KE4 is the one I'd recommend to most people out of all of these IEMs. That's because it has such a deliciously detailed midrange, and loads of bass (though admittedly too much for me sometimes). For $200, it's great value, and real audiophile quality. Read my full Kiwi Ears KE4 review.

The Horizon is for those that want more detail, and can handle more treble than most IEMs. Some will find it too bright, but it's just on the right side for me. With a detailed bass and decent midrange, things may be touch lean, but they are also separated and detailed. Read my Ziigaat Horizon review.

I really like these, and especially because they're only $50 – well, $42 now! For a fun, V-shape sound signature, that's a really great price, and though things get a little fatiguing after a while with the Cadenza II's full upper mids, it's still a very good IEM for under $50. Read my Kiwi Ears Cadenza II review in full.

Now you're talking... $315 may seem like too much for many people to be spending on a pair of earphones. All I can say is, if you want the best balanced tuned IEM on the market, then this is it, and that's the price for entry. Honestly, Crin could have put the price up considerable, and I believe it's great value at the discounted price.

Like bass?! Yeah, so does HBB, and although he's made several IEMs with different brands, the Deuce is one of the most beloved. I certainly think the wads of bass bring detail as well as head-throbbing amounts. But the rest of the frequencies are well-tuned too. Definitely not for everyone, this, but it's the best basshead set I've heard yet.

This is one of my favourite IEMs to date. It's bassy and warm without losing impact in the lower end, or detail in the lower mids. There's plenty (too much?) upper treble, but I find it all very nicely balanced. It's lush, warm and musical, and I love it. Read my Xenns Tea Pro review.

This IEM is fun, fun, fun. There's plenty of bass and treble, and it is a straight down the road V-shape tuning, but there's just enough detail and richness in the midrange to bring this out of the low-brow, commercial-style fare... I think its discounted price of $250 is good for this IEM.

I haven't heard this IEM, but like I say, Linsoul promises a level of quality that makes me confident in telling you about this deal. For $65 its promised reduced treble sound like an interesting approach – it's often the opposite for cheaper IEMs. Worth a punt!

I'm really interested in the Avant, as it's the first IEM that's made from Linsoul with the Linsoul brand in the name. Remember, Linsoul makes THeiaudio, Ziigaat and Kiwi Ears – that is, a lot of the best IEMs on the market today. Can't wait to hear these.

Want a pair of warm/neutral over-ear, open-back headphones? Well the Cypher is a good option, especially if you value great quality build. I found the sound to be a little soft in my Cypher review, but I can still see it being someone's ideal all-rounder.

The Halcyon IEM is a good option for those wanting that elevated treble that brings more detail to music, and who values a very small shell size. These things are tiny! I found them comfortable enough, but at the retail price I thought the Binary EP 321 were a better option. At the new sale price of $220, I think they're worth considering. Read my Kiwi Ears Halcyon review.

paragraphs: Technology has made it easier for creative professionals to work from anywhere at anytime, but travel can still bring some challenges. items.title: Switch 2 gets a rare discount to $469, just in time to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time
paragraphs: The Nintendo Switch 2 is finally seeing some proper discounts, just in time to play The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, although you'll need to look beyond the US for the best deal. Woot, the Amazon-owned discount retailer, has dropped the price of Nintendo's latest console to $469, saving $30 off its $499.99 US retail price. The catch? You'll need an Amazon Prime subscription to get the discount.

It's not a massive saving, especially since Nintendo's 'next gen' console used to be cheaper than Switch 2's new US price, but discounts on Nintendo hardware are still relatively rare. For comparison, the console and Ocarina of Time bundle is $568, so it's cheaper to buy the Woot deal and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time separately, since it's $49.99 as a digital download. (That's $10 less than the physical edition.)

There's also a growing selection of UK deals to consider, and as with the US, it's rare to see Switch 2 drop in price outside of big sales events like Black Friday – it feels like Nintendo really wants you to play Ocarina of Time.

Amazon UK lists the standard Switch 2 through third-party sellers, with prices starting at £399.99 on its current listing, although the cheapest visible offer is a Like New console for £369.99 rather than a new console from Amazon itself.

Elsewhere, Sports Direct (yes, they sell Switch 2 and Nikes) has been listing the standalone console for £395.99, while EE has it for £405. Even better, EE has a Switch 2 and Mario Kart World bundle for £409, making the extra £4 a no-brainer if you don't already own the game.

Very is also worth a look, with its standalone console listed at £389.99, alongside bundles including Ocarina of Time, Donkey Kong Bananza and Mario Kart World. My pick? The Switch 2 Console bundle with Nintendo Switch Sports Resort and The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, as you get the console's biggest game and the latest party game. The same bundle is £489 at Currys.

Speaking of which, one of my picks at Currys is a Switch 2 and Splatoon Raiders Bundle, spotted for £424 – it's one of my favourite Nintendo games released this year (read our Splatoon Raiders review to discover why). That's a particularly tempting option if you're after a game as well as the hardware.

The Woot deal is excellent if you're already an Amazon Prime member or want to join before Black Friday. But it does suggest there could be deals around the end of November for the year's big sales event.
If you just want The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, buying it digitally 'saves' you $10 off the physical edition price.
In the UK, I'd be looking at the £390–£410 mark for a Switch 2 console, especially bundles that include a full-price game for very little extra. There are more offers around right now, too.

items.title: US public workers are fighting to protect their jobs from AI – and some are winning
paragraphs: In the shadow of Silicon Valley, workers for the city of Oakland, California, worry the region will deploy AI systems that could increase surveillance and inaccurately evaluate their performance. Pushing for protections to ensure workers won’t be laid off or disciplined by AI, their union overwhelmingly voted on 22 October to authorize a strike, with 94.1% in favor.

“We just want the city administration to really be intentional about how it’s engaging with AI products,” said Julian Ware, an Oakland spatial data administrator and member of International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers Local 21. “Sometimes with a fancy new toy, it actually costs more, it’s more difficult to implement and the results are not as good.”

The nearly unanimous vote had an impact. The city government of Oakland and the union reached a tentative, three-year agreement that includes AI-related protections, such as requiring the city to retrain or reassign workers displaced by AI rather than firing them. As a result, the 5 November strike has been put on hold.

The Bay Area union is one of many public-sector labor groups nationwide seeking explicit protections against AI and automation, which union representatives say could worsen working conditions and threaten jobs. Following decades of automation efforts by companies and growing concern about AI since ChatGPT’s debut in 2022, ongoing labor disputes reveal hardening battle lines between public-sector bosses and their increasingly vocal workers.

“The bosses have such zeal for use of this technology,” said John Samuelsen, the Transport Workers Union president and a New York City subway track inspector. “Our members know that automation is the ultimate threat to their jobs … In transport, it’s here, it’s in our faces, we’re fighting it every day.”

Over the past few years, AI and automation technologies have infiltrated multiple sectors and are gradually making their way into public-sector workplaces across the country. Already, nearly 70% of state and local government agencies say they have adopted or are implementing generative AI, according to a survey by Ernst and Young conducted from July to August 2026. At the same time, workers are organizing and starting to win protections.

Policy makers have been moving too slowly to address AI’s potential effects on workers, so workers have to fight for themselves, argues Liz Shuler, AFL-CIO president and founder of its Technology Institute. “We’re using our contract negotiations to institute guardrails that policymakers won’t.”

Some unions have been prepared for this moment, having watched private-sector unions fight similar battles, said Kung Feng, a researcher with the University of California at Berkeley’s Labor Center and former director of San Francisco Jobs With Justice. For example, in 2023, Communications Workers of America recommended AI protections, and won some of them for California workers in October 2026.
“Workers versus billionaires has been the theme of this whole election … and bargain cycle,” Feng said. “This is the contest that we have over the future of technology in the workplace.”

Researchers call it bossware: AI tools that public- and private-sector employers are increasingly rolling out across industries to monitor and supervise employees, according to an October report Feng co-authored. Some tools rank and evaluate workers for hiring, firing and promotions. Others track location and activity, monitor productivity, scan biometrics for timekeeping, use cameras, wearable devices and sensors, or leverage analytics to predict emotions.

Amazon has used algorithms to push workers to operate at dangerous speeds in its warehouses, and now that strategy is being deployed in the public sector, said Lorena Gonzalez, the California Federation of Labor Unions president.
“We think AI doesn’t belong on big-rig trucks, and it doesn’t belong in hospitals and schools,” Gonzalez said.

Some automation technologies could aid public-sector workers, like vehicle safety systems in public transit, but humans should always be in charge, providing oversight, Gonzalez said. Computers have been able to fly a plane for years, but every aircraft carries two pilots who can use human judgment and skill to override the system when necessary, she said.
“If we’re using a computer or AI, it has to be controlled by a human being, not the other way around,” she said.

Employers in the public sector often deploy automation technologies during claimed attempts to improve efficiency and cut costs when budgets are slim, Feng said. But unions have been pushing for AI protections since the late 2010s, and those battles are only intensifying as automation advances and generative AI becomes more common, he said. Workers’ requests include receiving advance notice before a new technology is rolled out, getting information about that technology and ensuring the right to negotiate over its use, he added.

Examples abound of worker pushback. Last year, Pennsylvania became the first state to run a pilot program with OpenAI. The state encouraged employees, like unemployment claim workers and social workers, to use ChatGPT Enterprise to test for time savings.

“But there were no guarantees or agreements for the workers,” said Steve Catanese, president of Service Employees International Union Local 668, which represents more than 10,000 statewide public-sector workers. “With generative AI, workers are building their own gallows sometimes.”

Then the union spoke up, inspired by the California screenwriters’ victory in 2023, one of the longest strikes in Hollywood history that secured protections against AI replacing writers. The Pennsylvania SEIU Local 668 pushed the governor, Josh Shapiro, to agree to a policy guaranteeing that the state’s use of AI will include employee input and supervision, and that the tech won’t be used to discipline workers.

“It’s powerful for elected leaders to say, there will always be human public servants under my watch,” Catanese said, referring to commitments that AI won’t displace workers. He expects these issues to resurface when the union negotiates for a new contract in 2027.

In transportation, public workers in states including Florida and New York are proactively trying to block Waymo and city governments from deploying autonomous vehicles, calling them unsafe and a threat to their jobs. They’re hoping to replicate a 2024 victory in Columbus, Ohio, where the Transport Workers Union secured contracts giving it veto power over any plan by the Central Ohio Transit Authority to deploy autonomous vehicles.
But the TWU doesn’t oppose new technologies, said Samuelsen, the union president. It supports systems that can aid with collision avoidance and improving bus and train timing, he said.

But he worries that many industries are pushing for AI and automation without regard for safety. For example, some airlines have begun experimenting with using drones to inspect aircraft from afar rather than relying on human jet mechanics, who can do a more thorough, up-close inspection.

AI and automation are “in every single element of passenger transport, and even freight transport, that you can imagine. It has completely infiltrated us,” Samuelsen said. “Where there’s no … union that’s willing to fight, workers are doomed.”
This isn’t the first time emerging technologies have negatively affected labor markets and working conditions across industries, union representatives said.
“We’ve seen this movie before,” Schuler said. Unions have faced mass job loss before, such as when automation in assembly-line factories in the midwest reduced manufacturing jobs, she said.

Some legislators, especially at the state level, have been making strides toward new policies. For example, the IFPTE and other unions supported the No Robo Bosses bill in California, which bars employers from relying solely on automated systems to discipline or fire workers. Unions also supported another California bill that prohibited employers from using workplace AI surveillance tools, such as those that could monitor employees’ emotional states. Gavin Newsom signed both into law on 30 September.

Public-sector workers have also backed AI-related legislation in other states. Public-sector unions in New York supported a law, effective December 2025, that protects workers at state agencies from being displaced by AI.

Though tech CEOs have warned of AI’s hypothetical risks to humanity, the more pressing issue is how employees are being negatively affected by the technology today, said Keith Brown, executive secretary-treasurer of the Alameda Labor Council, which serves public and private-sector workers in California’s Alameda county.
“We’ve seen in the news a lot of headlines about the threat of AI destroying civilization,” Brown said. “But for workers, we’ve been facing these harms from AI tech companies for a long time.”

items.title: Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang steps down amid alleged spy scandal
paragraphs: Jensen Huang gives a keynote address at the Nvidia Berlin GPU Technology Conference on Oct. 21, 2026. Sean Gallup/Getty Images hide caption
Jensen Huang, CEO of the chipmaking juggernaut Nvidia, is stepping down, the company's board announced Thursday.

The decision comes days after the company took the extraordinary step of launching an investigation following news reports alleging that Huang had had an extramarital affair with one of the company's clients, who U.S. intelligence officials concluded had been recruited by China's top spy agency, according to the New York Times. NPR has not independently confirmed those reports.
In an email to Nvidia staff on Sunday, Huang admitted to cheating on his wife, and said he would cooperate with the investigation.
The company's share price dropped sharply on Wednesday, after the New York Times reported that Huang had had a second affair, this one with an Nvidia executive who reported to him.
Nvidia did not immediately respond to an NPR request for comment.

Huang was widely seen as one of the most important business leaders in the United States. Nvidia dominates the market for the chips used to train and run artificial intelligence. Huang also had President Trump's ear on AI policy, with Trump even calling Huang's phone in September while Huang was onstage during a conference.

The scandal that brought down Huang snowballed quickly over the past two weeks. The New York Times reported in late October that Huang had a close relationship with a Chinese woman at a Singapore-based company that was buying Nvidia chips. Citing unidentified sources, it said U.S. intelligence officials believed she had been recruited by the Chinese government to spy on him and possibly try to influence policy. NPR has not independently confirmed this reporting.

A drip-drip of scoops followed — from the Times and other outlets — suggesting that the relationship was romantic, that senior Trump administration officials knew about the allegations some time ago, and that Huang had had a second affair.
China's foreign ministry has said the allegations of spying are baseless and part of a smear campaign against China.
Huang's departure launches Nvidia into uncharted territory.
Huang's relationship with the alleged Chinese agent and what the Trump administration knew about it will likely be the subject of an investigation when Democrats take control of Congress in January.

"We should all be extremely concerned about this, and the fact that the White House knew about this for weeks, maybe months now, is is is very disturbing as well," said Rep. Yvette Clarke, D-NY, a senior member of the House Energy and Commerce Committee in an interview with NPR.

The company's Chief Financial Officer, Colette Kress, has been appointed interim CEO. The board said in their statement they would conduct a full search for a new CEO and consider both internal and external candidates.

"There's no obvious replacement," said Stephen Witt, author of a book about Nvidia called The Thinking Machine. "It's not even clear Nvidia can be the same kind of company without Jensen. I have a hard time imagining what Nvidia looks like without Jensen."
Nvidia still plans to report its quarterly earnings on Tuesday.

Huang was one of the longest-serving CEOs in U.S. corporate history, stepping into the role after launching the company with partners over bottomless cups of coffee at a Denny's restaurant in San Jose, Calif., 33 years ago. Nvidia got its start making specialized chips to create 3D graphics for computers that would come to be known as graphics processing units, or GPUs.
He was the face of Nvidia and an unlikely celebrity, giving countless keynote speeches and interviews in his trademark leather jacket, or posing for selfies with adoring fans.

Huang was also the company's driving force. Under his leadership, Nvidia made a big and early bet on artificial intelligence, investing heavily to transform its niche graphics chips into general-purpose processing units that were ideal for the volume of computations required to create AI.

That bet would pay off in spades as GPUs became the go-to chip for AI creators. When AI burst into the public consciousness in late 2022 with the launch of OpenAI's ChatGPT — a chatbot trained and run on Nvidia chips — the firm was worth about $400 billion. Today, it's valued at more than $4 trillion, among the most valuable in the world, and it dominates the market for GPUs.
But analysts say despite Huang's visionary management of the business, he had a blind spot for succession and hadn't articulated a clear plan, at least publicly.

In a Bloomberg interview from mid-October, Huang was vague about succession plans. "I'm really hoping that the next CEO of the company is already at the company, but 20 years from now, I hope I stay healthy and I hope I continue to earn my keep."

Huang's adult children, Spencer and Madison Huang, both work at Nvidia. Asked about talk that Madison might be in line to succeed him, he paused, and told Bloomberg: "if that's their aspiration, Spencer or Madison's, they have to go earn it. And it's really, really hard work. It takes a lot of sacrifice."
Daniel Newman, CEO of the Futurum Group, a tech research firm, said the company will inevitably be different without Huang, and its future success is unclear.
"They've always had Jensen as this sort of visionary at the front," he said. "I don't think that's replaceable."

items.title: ‘To them, we’re just NPCs’: the artists and activists challenging Trump’s video game propaganda
paragraphs: In early September, the Trump White House announced a surprising new addition to its official website. Named simply Arcade, it is a collection of browser games based on classic titles such as Flappy Bird, Snake, and Tetris, but re-tuned as flagrant works of political propaganda. Designed to court reactionary gamers, they push the administration’s policies on immigration and other hot-button issues, while dehumanising their targets. There have recently been some new additions: a Temple Run clone named Red Scare about crossing the “ration market” and escaping the Democratic Socialists of America, and another simple item-matching game about the threat of socialism. In the midst of increasing fuel, utility and grocery prices thanks to the Iran war, these were naked attempts to distract voters by appealing to their video game nostalgia.

After an explosion of news coverage, Arcade caught the attention of the games industry. The Tetris Company warned on social media that it “took copyright infringement very seriously.” Days later, the game was removed from the White House site. However, aside from a March 2026 statement from the Pokémon Company condemning the White House for using its characters in Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) propaganda, major video game companies have been relatively silent in the face of the administration’s widespread usage of their IP.

But now, video game creators and artists are pushing back, looking to regain ground the industry has ceded to reactionary ideologies over the last decade by turning the gamification of politics back on Trump. Anonymous art collective The Secret Handshake has been known for its political activism since installing a sculpture of Donald Trump and sex offender Jeffrey Epstein at the National Mall in downtown Washington, DC. This spring, the group developed a game entitled Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell and made it available online, as well as installing three free arcade cabinets on the National Mall.

A satire on the Trump administration, the game allows players to control the president in a Pokémon-style challenge that starts with an important choice: order a Diet Coke, or invade Iran. As the game progresses, Trump heads to Iran to collect barrels of oil (called “lube” in the game) and encounters administration members such as vice-president JD Vance, secretary of state Marco Rubio, and “secretary of war”, Pete Hegseth. It’s unwinnable, which is the point, though you can get a “Game Over” screen by trying to hold Melania Trump’s hand.

The Secret Handshake had never made a video game until Operation Epic Furious: Strait to Hell. “The ‘form’ was really dictated by the Trump Administration,” a member of Secret Handshake says via email. “It’s not that we wanted to make a video game; it’s that the Pentagon began using video games to promote their war in Iran and make it seem ‘cool’. They actually introduced the idea of a video game, not us. We felt like, well, if they’re going to use video games to promote their war, let’s make a video game satirising that war.”

The collective followed similar logic when creating their second free game, Operation Epic Furious: Nuuk ’Em All which tasks players with speaking to Trump’s advisers, including a UFC fighter as “secretary of combat” and a no-bid contractor helping renovate The White House. The aim is to piece together enough “Big Brainpower” to figure out how to distract voters from the oil crisis. After Trump accidentally hits on his own daughter, Ivanka, and speaks to enough advisers to collect enough partial ideas to make one “big beautiful idea”, he decides to invade Greenland.

For The Secret Handshake, the video game as a medium helps people take in “the insanity” of what’s happening, which the collective believes may be hard to ascertain from just headlines. “When you are using a medium that’s very familiar, like a video game, and you’re going through these actions, it allows you to experience the headlines in a different way,” a spokesperson says. “This game is meant to be a caricature and satire, but it’s full of things in there that aren’t. Trump calling a woman a maggot felt very intense to experience in the form of a game.”

The Secret Handshake had to learn how to build a game on the fly for Operation Epic Furious. “We had no idea what we were doing,” a spokesperson explains. “It was a lot of trial and error, and figuring it out as we went along. We did have someone helping that understood this world and could actually make it happen, but no one was a game designer.” They describe the games as, “held together with duct tape”.

Still, there are avid gamers in the group, and they pulled inspiration from Japanese role-playing adventures, particularly the early Final Fantasy titles, while the invidious, scatalogical tone is similar to South Park games such as The Stick of Truth and The Fractured But Whole. The aim was for the games to be funny and to properly satirise the absurdity of the current administration. So far, more than 350,000 people have played them online.

Two further anti-Trump games mimic the iconic arcade shooter Space Invaders, and they couldn’t have been made in more different ways. This summer, game developer Richie Branson partnered with nonprofit All for America to create Tax Evaders, in which you choose one of four playable pilots (President Trump, vice-president JD Vance, House speaker Mike Johnson, or Senate leader John Thune) before jumping into the first level, destroying healthcare and lining billionaire pockets.

“There’s something a bit unsettling about playing as the ‘villain’,” says Branson, who created Tax Evaders using the free and open-source game development engine, Godot. “The intent here is to drive home the point that these officials are destroying beneficial programmes with the same combination of enthusiasm and indifference as someone blowing up enemy space ships in an arcade game.”

The Trump administration’s aggressive push into online culture is working, according to Branson, who said the White House team is, “on a rampage” with its memelord and gaming culture posts. “It’s a very cunning way of spreading whatever message they’re trying to spread,” he says, before referring to the White House Arcade as “gamified propaganda”, and “garbage, [with] no love for the art”. Tax Evaders has had over 50,000 players and over 2m page impressions since July.

Alfie Souter and Carlota Real work in advertising together. They often chat about breaking news and trending topics, so when they saw the White House release its propaganda arcade, they decided to do something about it. “The craziest thing is the oversimplification of such a complex issue, like immigration,” says Real. “What they’re trying to do is boil this down to the minimum that people understand. A Tetris game; everyone on the planet has probably played it once, and they apply it to the shitshow that they’re doing.”

Angered by the administration’s trivialision of the issues and its demonisation of immigrants, the duo started brainstorming their own version of a simplified game with a political message. With no background in game design, they decided to build it in ChatGPT, which itself is perhaps a satirical message: many believe the Trump Arcade games are “vibe-coded”, or built using plain language to describe a game to a generative AI program, which then codes it.

The result is Corrupt Invaders. Essentially a homage to Space Invaders with an anti-Trump filter, the game tasks you with moving Trump’s “$400m Qatari gift” (his aeroplane) to “collect another $1.4bn in crypto.” Your final score is subtracted from Trump’s reported cryptocurrency earnings. According to Souter the duo wanted the game to be focused on something that felt inarguable about the Trump regime and settled on corruption, using the $400m Boeing 747-8 luxury jet gifted by Qatar. Federal law says US officials can only accept gifts under $480, but the Trump White House insisted Trump accepting the aircraft was legal. “We thought about that jet, and also the $1.4bn earnings in crypto last year – those numbers are so ridiculous,” says Souter. “That’s why when you play the game, you subtract it from the score, because it’s such an unfathomable number”.

The two wanted to focus on the money that President Trump and his close allies have earned since his second presidency and juxtapose that against Americans’ consistent concerns with the cost of living crisis. The games are designed to makes the dichotomy crystal clear. Recently, the duo launched Diesel Kong, a parody of the classic Nintendo platformer Donkey Kong in the context of rising oil prices due to the continued war in Iran. “Prices are going up. Putin’s throwing useless barrels, can Trump be saved?” asks the starting screen. Trump stands in place of Princess Peach, while a nondescript Maga supporter wearing an American flag shirt and red hat tries to make his way up the ramps and ladders.

The developers and activists behind these games are pushing back against the Trump administration’s gamified propaganda while looking to subvert the gaming subcultures the president has co-opted. “Our current administration runs the country as if were a video game, with no real sense of sympathy for the people affected by the losses incurred by their policies,” said Branson. “Gas prices are crazy right now, people’s lives are being affected, but to our nation’s leadership, we’re just NPCs.”

items.title: Love for pumpkin spice – level 1
paragraphs: People love pumpkin spice. The spice is a mixture of several spices. For example, they are cinnamon, nutmeg, or ginger. It smells very good. It brings happy feelings.
No pumpkin is in the mixture. Some people think that Starbucks makes pumpkin spice. The recipe is much older.
American settlers use the spices to keep food fresh during the winter. The foods are meat, fruit, and vegetables.

In 1976, Amelia Simmons writes a pumpkin spice recipe. She puts pumpkin spice in the first American cookbook. In the 1990s, Starbucks creates the pumpkin spice latte. Many people love it. The drink helps them welcome the fall after a hot summer.
Difficult words: mixture (several things put together), nutmeg (a hard seed of a tropical tree), settler (a person who lives in a new country).
You can watch the original video in the Level 3 section.
News in Levels is designed to teach you 3000 words in English. Please follow the instructions below.

items.title: Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza cleared of using AI to write prize-winning story
paragraphs: The Zimbabwean author Simbarashe Kundizeza has been cleared of using AI to write a prize-winning short story, after the prestigious Caine prize for African writers concluded that his entry was “human-written” after a month-long investigation.
Kundizeza’s story The Blue Fighter, which charts the declining fortunes of a family after the father invests in fish tanks, was announced as the winner of the £10,000 prize on 6 October.

Five days later, the Atlantic published an article titled “Yet another literary prize winner seems to be AI”, in which the author and journalist Vauhini Vara said the AI-detection software Pangram, which itself uses AI, had deemed the story to be almost completely artificially generated.

The Caine prize chair, Ellah Wakatama, said in a statement: “From our detailed investigation, we feel the evidence is clear: The Blue Fighter was human-written. We now look forward to awarding and celebrating Simbarashe Steyn Kundizeza … before the end of the year.”
She said: “When concerns were raised, we have a duty as an organisation to look at them carefully and fairly,” adding that the prize had taken a “human-centred” approach to its investigation.

“Our review included interviews with the author, the 2026 judging panel and The Shallow Tales Review, where the story was first published,” Wakatama said. “It also included independent and expert-led metadata analysis of drafts written by the author.”

Kundizeza, who had strongly denied using generative AI to write the story, said he was “relieved” that the allegations had been dismissed after the investigation. “It was not necessary in the first place, I am happy to put all this behind me and continue with my writing journey,” he said.
Vara’s article prompted outrage online, with many claiming that Black writers, and Africans in particular, were being unfairly singled out by allegations of the use of AI.
Associated Press contributed to this report

items.title: Four video tracks and a doughnut shop – how Dispatch got its start
paragraphs: A year ago, Dispatch released a game that surprised many people, including me. It's a superhero game about managing reformed villains from behind a desk, launched on PC and PlayStation 5. It has since sold five million copies, and a mobile version arrives on iOS and Android on 9 December, following October's Dispatch anniversary Deluxe Edition.

Dispatch was made in Unreal Engine and stars Breaking Bad's Aaron Paul as former hero Robert Robertson, alongside Jeffrey Wright, Laura Bailey, and members of the Critical Role cast. It's an animated, episodic workplace comedy that plays like a TV series, but it wasn't always a game, and that's perhaps why it feels so unique. AdHoc was founded in Los Angeles in 2018 by Telltale Games alumni who planned to make interactive experiences with real actors on screen, and Dispatch began that way.
I asked co-founders Nick Herman and Dennis Lenart, the studio's COO and CTO and both co-creative directors, what survived the jump from live-action series to animated game, and what had to change.

One piece of the original script made it through every draft: the doughnut shop scene in episode two. Lenart says it was "one of the pieces from the early script that just kind of kept hanging around through every draft all the way from live action into the animated game".

The set-up was different back then. You watched a camera feed as the hero Invisigal dealt with a thief, and your job was to feed her the information she needed to succeed. In the live-action version, that meant switching cameras and pulling information from what each camera showed. Herman says the scene was "purely built around the technology" AdHoc was using to create its interactive live action. It ran in a browser and had hard limits, including, as Herman recalls, “I think it was like four simultaneous tracks of video”.

The team turned that restriction into a mechanic. Watch the alley behind the shop, and you couldn't see what was happening inside the front. "By choosing where you were going to give your attention, the game would adjust, and you'd learn different things based on where you were looking," says Herman, calling it the perfect place to test the idea.

Because they'd spent so long on it, they carried it forward. In the game, Lenart says, they wove in mechanics from the final design, such as hacking, "to make it feel a little bit more like Robert was helping out Invisigal".

The original story was a mentorship, centred on the one-on-one relationship between Robert and Invisigal. Pivoting it into a game changed that. AdHoc wanted a dispatch mechanic, with the player sending heroes out on calls, and that needs a roster. "So the Z-Team was created to support the gameplay," Lenart says, "which then informed the story, and then changed the overall arc of the season, which brought a whole team into it as opposed to just a one-on-one mentorship with Invisigal."

It's a neat illustration of how the studio works. "Everything at AdHoc starts with story," says Herman, contrasting that with studios that pick a genre first, polish the mechanics and the game-feel, and only later ask what the story is. AdHoc begins with the world, the characters and who the player is, then asks what that means for gameplay. "Oh, well, you're a superhero dispatcher, so maybe we should have some sort of dispatching mechanic, right?"

Once there's a script, it moves on to storyboards, animatics and animation. That storyboard stage is now part of the product: the anniversary Deluxe Edition update adds Storyboard Mode, which plays the whole game through its original animatics. It's a new mode that offers genuine insight into how a scene was planned, scripted and animated.

The move to animation was driven by budget constraints, to an extent, because they could do more with a little extra, and it also changed the game's scale, given Dispatch's live-action origins; Lenart says the team knew they were "severely limited from a budget standpoint compared to big-budget superhero tentpole movies". For budgetary reasons, the story was largely set in an office with a small cast.

Animation flipped that constraint and aligned with trends like Mixtape's hand-made animation, giving the team room to grow and aim higher within the new art form. "We're able to have a giant action scene because it doesn't cost that much more than having a bunch of characters walking around talking," Lenart explains. That let AdHoc expand the moments that deserved spectacle: "Let's really go all out and try to compete with some of the other best-in-class versions of these scenes in animation."

Ask whether players have done anything that made AdHoc rethink how interactive stories should work, and Herman is refreshingly honest. “I don’t know that there have been any major epiphanies,” he says, before steering to a different answer: launching Dispatch “was a labour of love”, the culmination of a lot of work distilled into one experience the team felt was exciting and high quality.

He adds: "The success of the game has just really injected a lot of confidence into us and other developers making similar types of games. For a long time, there hadn't been a really clear or recent example of something like this reaching a level of success that a developer could go out and raise funding for."

He's proud of who found it, too. Dispatch "was able to pierce a new audience who perhaps thought gaming wasn't for them". Lenart agrees, saying the success feels like "motivation to keep making these types of games and expand our possibilities even more".
The Dispatch Deluxe Edition is out now on PlayStation 5, Xbox Series X, and Nintendo Switch / Switch 2, and $10.99 digital upgrade path for existing owners
Dispatch - Deluxe Edition - PlayStation 5
Dispatch - Deluxe Edition - Nintendo Switch 2
Dispatch - Deluxe Edition - XBOX Series X

Ian Dean is Editor, Digital Arts & 3D at Creative Bloq, and the former editor of many leading magazines. These titles included ImagineFX, 3D World and video game titles Play and Official PlayStation Magazine. Ian launched Xbox magazine X360 and edited PlayStation World. For Creative Bloq, Ian combines his experiences to bring the latest news on digital art, VFX and video games and tech, and in his spare time he doodles in Procreate, ArtRage, and Rebelle while finding time to play Xbox and PS5.

items.title: Schools, libraries and parents face 'difficult decision' over David Walliams books
paragraphs: Speaking to BBC Breakfast, Mr Di'Iasio urged the government to give schools national guidance, so they are "not leaving this open to one or two head teachers making one decision and others making a different one".
Darren Morgan, head of Kings Road Primary School in Manchester, told the programme that he has taken the decision to remove Walliams' publications.
The stories have been useful to promote reading, but "when there are these allegations it's really difficult to keep these books on the shelves", he said.
Steve Chalke, head of Oasis Academies, which runs more than 50 schools, said it was impossible to stop children seeing the current stories about Walliams.
"So when a child wanders into a school and into the library and sees his name or perhaps sees his photograph on a book, it can be very traumatising for some children," he said.

Author Chloe Combi, who has written about "how it feels to be young in modern Britain" and Generation Z, said banning Walliams' books is not appropriate, and could mean that important conversations about him "get swept under the carpet".
"I think by talking about it and what has happened - and the responsibility of parents to have that conversation with their kids - that actually makes more sense," she told BBC Radio 5 Live.
"I'm totally sympathetic with schools for withdrawing him and bookshops withdrawing him as an individual decision. But the point is, none of that is going to erase what's happened."
The Department for Education has been asked for comment.
Retailers including Waterstones, TG Jones, and The Works, say they will no longer sell Walliams' books, and his publisher HarperCollins cut ties with him in September.
Public libraries have also faced calls to remove his books.
Librarians' body CILIP said it "recognises that dealing with challenges made to books or other resources can be an extremely complex and stressful situation for library staff".
Decisions about stocking books are made by local councils.
Among them, Kent County Council said it had no plans to remove Walliams' titles from its libraries.
"The starting point is that books should be available to readers unless their content is unlawful," a spokesperson said.

"Decisions about library stock are not made through blanket bans on individual authors. Collections are regularly reviewed and refreshed to reflect factors such as reader demand, condition and relevance of stock."

A Telford and Wrekin council spokesperson added that after the "recent media coverage and allegations published in the press" they had taken the decision to "remove all Walliams' books and audio books from their library catalogues".
Surrey County Council said that demand for Walliams' books had "fallen significantly in recent years", but his titles are "not illegal" and "remain available for readers to borrow".
Camden Council in north London said it was putting Walliams' books in storage.
A spokesperson told the Camden New Journal: "We are committed to making Camden a safer place for women and girls, to challenging harmful attitudes, and promoting healthy relationships.
"Following these allegations, we believe the most appropriate action is to remove these books from display."

On Tuesday, ITV News and the Guardian published reports alleging that Walliams has been accused of sexual misconduct by several women, including some who accused him of "grooming" them when they were teenagers.
In a letter to journalists published by the paper, Walliams said he was "not a sexual predator" and had not "broken the law".

items.title: Intelligence officer's rare Aston Martin to be sold
paragraphs: An Aston Martin car owned by a British intelligence officer, and of the same model made famous by the James Bond films, is expected to fetch up to £400,000 when it goes to auction.
The red Aston Martin DB5 Sports Saloon car will go on sale at Sandown Park in Esher, Surrey.
It was owned by PH Manners Wood, who interpreted decoded enigma messages at Bletchley Park during World War Two, and who bought the car in the same year Bond first hit the big screen.

Paul Cheetham, of auctioneers H&H Classics, said: "James Bond was not the only British intelligence officer to take delivery of an Aston Martin DB5 during 1964, as seen with this wonderful example first owned by Manners Wood."
He added that the car had "links to a real British hero who, along with his colleagues, made such a difference to help end the hostilities in the Second World War".
The Aston Martin DB5 has also become synonymous with the Bond films thanks to its use in movies such as Goldfinger alongside Sean Connery, and Skyfall with Daniel Craig's 007.
The next James Bond film is currently reported to be casting its new lead, with speculation as to which actor will take up the mantle.
Manners Wood's rare DB5 is among just under 900 of the cars to be produced and has had two owners since, including its current owner who has looked after it for 56 years, according to H&H Classics.
The intelligence officer worked at Bletchley Park and was credited with saving thousands of lives by General Dwight D Eisenhower, later to become US president.
H&H Classics says the DB5 will go on display at Sandown Park on 9 December, ahead of the auction the following day.
