Petra Heights is their biggest proof of concept yet. It rises above the station platform like an elemental cliff, with chunks of stone bulging out at points in bouldery lumps. The three towers, which taper as they climb, are connected to a central lift and stairs, and joined by a precipitous bridge at the upper levels. Wrapped with steel mesh, the stairway is open to the elements and spills on to a lush communal roof garden, all adding to the feeling of hiking up a rocky mountain path.

The foliage will soon grow its way up the facade, as at Clerkenwell, lending it the air of an ancient ruin. In a world first, even the lift shaft is made of stone. The slabs, three metres high and 10cm thick, were shipped from Norway and assembled on site, reaching the shaft’s full height in a single day. You half expect the lift itself to be a hollowed-out boulder winched up on a rope, but even Taha’s clients have their limits.

Originally designed in 2015, the project had a bumpy ride. As is not uncommon for developments in London, the site went through three different owners before the towers were built, each time seeing the original ambition somewhat diluted as successive developers cashed in on the increased land values. The proposed mass timber frame was deemed too expensive, although Taha says the switch to concrete ended up costing much more. That change also had knock-on effects, with stone elements getting chunkier to hold up the additional weight, and braced in places by steel diagonals.

The pandemic added further setbacks. The lower floors of Sicilian basalt were already up when Covid interrupted supply, leading the remaining floors to be built with igneous grey larvikite from Norway. Both were stained with a reddish wash to match. The colour variation gives an appropriately antique feel, heightened at the base by fragments of Celtic patterns carved into the pillars, as if these venerable columns might date back much further. This archaic quality is emphasised by the names of the architects, engineers, masons and contractors being carved in a runic typeface and picked out in gold. Perhaps more architects should sign their buildings, so passersby know where to direct their praise – or ire.

“The common reaction from developers is that structural stone is too shocking,” says Taha. “They think the British population aren’t ready for it, and that people prefer brick. But if you look at the lists of the most popular towns and villages in the UK, it’s often Bath, Edinburgh, the Cotswolds. Guess what? They’re all made of stone.”

Webb is fiercely critical of the scourge of carbon-hungry bricks as the default. “Bricks are the heaviest form of decoration you can imagine,” he says. “They require a huge amount of energy to fire – often using coal – and they’re weak as shit. They put a lot of weight on the building’s frame, so the frame and the foundations have to get bigger, and they’re really inconvenient because they expand and contract, so you have to put movement joints everywhere. And they’re not holding anything up – it’s just really heavy and expensive wallpaper.”

In the last 10,000 years of building history, he argues, walls have held the floors up. But now we’ve got it back to front. “In the last 50 years or so, we’ve moved to floors holding the walls up,” he says, “which is utterly stupid.” He gestures out of the window of his office to a host of new high-rise blocks, where precast brick cladding panels are being craned on to concrete frames, each hefty piece of wall connected with steel brackets to the floor below. A stone-framed facade, however, can play the role of superstructure and cladding in one. It has a fraction of the embodied carbon, doesn’t move as much, and it’s cheaper. The slabs of Norwegian larvikite, for example, were rejects, of the kind usually used for motorway embankments.

British quarries are slowly catching up. Taha and Webb see the most potential in smaller-sized offcuts, which could be used in the same way as bricks and laid by regular bricklayers, without the need for stonemasonry expertise. They have put their ideas to the test in a remarkable “stone demonstrator house”, a temporary structure in Earl’s Court that showcases pre-tensioned stone beams and columns, stone floor slabs and a self-supporting stone brick facade.

Commissioned by the Design Museum’s Future Observatory research hub, it represents up to a 90% carbon saving compared to conventional construction. And for anyone wondering if there is enough stone to go around, Webb has a sobering fact. If all eight billion people on the planet decided to rebuild their homes in stone, the total volume required would be about the same as Ben Nevis.

Taha is busy on his next lithophilic project, a mixed-use development on the canal in Hackney using stone bricks and blocks, with dowel-laminated timber walls and floors, making it “carbon negative”. Incorporating photovoltaic brise-soleil shading panels and a canal water source heat pump, he says the building will generate 135% of its energy needs. It will sell power back to the grid in the warmer months, offering a bill-free life across the year.

Webb, meanwhile, is working on a load-bearing stone option for a 200-metre tower near Liverpool Street, which he says would do away with the usual colossal concrete core and columns. Heavy, dark granite elements at the base could transition to lighter, thinner limestone pieces towards the top, expressing the structural loads on the facade, and using each kind of stone for what it does best.

“It’s a massive opportunity for architects to change it up – a reason to make a new style,” says Webb. “The first iron bridge in Telford was designed with timber-like connections, because that’s all we knew. Similarly, the first concrete buildings copied stone techniques. At the moment, we’re basically just reinterpreting concrete buildings, but using stone. We’ve shown that you can make stone trusses, stone grid-shells, really high-tech stone structures.” His eyes widen. “Imagine a future of stone electricity pylons everywhere!”

items.title: A flaccid roam through Bloomsbury’s desperately mediocre modernists: Vanessa Bell & Duncan Grant review
paragraphs: The Bloomsbury Group once induced yawns as the smug epitome of a snobbish high culture but they’re now admired for their feminism and queer abandon. There’s a West End play about the loves of the Bloomsbury economist John Maynard Keynes and if you visit the National Trust’s Sissinghurst, its flowerbeds are set alight by Vita Sackville-West’s affair with Virginia Woolf.

But biography can’t set art alight, as Tate Britain’s epic yet flaccid roam through the complicated lives and desperately mediocre paintings of the co-habiting Vanessa Bell and Duncan Grant proves. While Keynes was quite the economist and Woolf a literary genius, I honestly can’t see enough interest in the visual art of Bloomsbury to detain anyone for long. That was true when their sex lives were spoken of in a more muted way (I read a biography of Keynes as a student and don’t remember any hanky-panky at all) and it’s true now, even as we trawl their paintings for gay and feminist meanings.

One caption for a male nude by Duncan Grant is so preoccupied with the erotic undertones, it says nothing about what is surely most interesting about the naked young man sitting on a table – that he is the same George Mallory who would vanish trying to climb Everest in 1924 and whose frozen body would be rediscovered there in 1999.

Perhaps the Himalaya is too wild to be encompassed in the sophisticated yet genteel world of Bloomsbury. Then again, so is Paris, in this exhibition. There is no French art here even though both Bell and Grant emulated French modernism, sometimes very belatedly. Grant’s portrait of Mallory, for instance, which dates from 1913, assiduously apes the style of Georges Seurat, who died in 1891.

In the early 1900s, almost every country in continental Europe was throwing up revolutionary modernist geniuses from Munch to Malevich, Schiele to Boccioni, but Britain was so visually repressed that the Bloomsbury Group seemed frightfully clever to have heard of modern art at all. It would have been more honest and interesting to show how this happened. Bell and Grant didn’t just see “post-impressionist” art, as their friend Roger Fry dubbed it, in exhibitions or magazines: they lived with it intimately. In 1918, Keynes famously hid a Cézanne still life of seven apples in a hedge near Bell and Grant’s place in the country, Charleston, because he couldn’t drive it up a muddy lane. When he got it to the house, the group all loved it.

Cézanne’s painting is a compacted philosophical masterpiece, which the Bloomsbury Group were right to admire, but it’s not here. Nor is the early cubist still life by Picasso, Pots and Lemon, that Vanessa’s art critic husband Clive Bell bought in 1911. Their inclusion would have given more context, and certainly more artistic excitement, to this show.

Instead in a section on “modernisms” (what modernisms? There was only one modernism in the early 20th century) it feels as if the wool is being pulled over our eyes. We are supposed to believe that when Grant painted Head of Eve in 1913, a simplified totemic nude like a wooden carving, he was doing something utterly original rather than catching up with Picasso’s African-inspired fetishes, or that when Bell painted her wanly cubistic Portrait of Molly MacCarthy, she was in no way influenced by having a Picasso in the house.

The problem isn’t that Bell and Grant are playing catchup with Paris. It’s that both artists appear so detached and passionless. They try on avant garde ideas but always come back to tradition. Grant’s 1920s views of the South of France have a veneer of modern style but are the kind of holiday art a Victorian painter such as Lord Leighton might have done.

Sophistication and knowledge don’t guarantee greatness, nor does having an interesting life. Tate Britain probably wouldn’t put on a show by artists who were wife and husband but Vanessa and Duncan had a unique lifelong relationship even though he was gay and she married Clive Bell with whom she had children. But the pair don’t seem to influence or rival each other in a way to make a joint show come alive: indeed they cancel each other out. The pull of queer desire that’s a recurring impulse in Grant distracts you from the quiet still observations of Bell. Here is a openly sexed portrait by Grant of his lover David Garnett, over there a painting by Bell of her sister Woolf looking melancholically introspective.

In the Britain of their day, art was barely considered a serious pursuit and, for all their knowledge of French modernism, Bell and Grant are timid about how much any of this playing with brushes matters. But then you go into a little room near the end and find something with real belief: Grant’s erotic drawings. They are totally uninhibited, explicit and beautiful. His classical yet raw depictions of men having sex are like a queer version of Picasso’s Vollard Suite and for once the influence is digested in a creative, powerful way.
It’s the only time in this show that either artist seems truly driven. The rest is the stuff of Bloomsbury costume dramas.

items.title: Apple MacBook Pro review: lighter, thinner and a stunning OLED touchscreen
paragraphs: Apple’s MacBook Pro has been redesigned for the first time in five years, getting slightly slimmer, significantly lighter and adding a fantastic new OLED display with the first touchscreen on a Mac.

The new MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display comes in two sizes, 14in and 16in, but rather than replacing the standard MacBook Pro they sit alongside them as an even more expensive option. The OLED machines start at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) – a £400 or equivalent upgrade on the matching spec LCD models – serious prices for serious work machines, not helped by significant cost increases driven by RAMageddon.

Shut, the new OLED MacBook Pro looks almost identical to its predecessors: a little smaller in every direction but with the same aluminium body, combination of ports and overall profile. But pick it up and the weight loss is immediately noticeable. The 14in version is 14% lighter than its predecessor at 1.38kg, which makes it only 150g heavier than the 13in MacBook Air, and the 16in version is 15% lighter at 1.82kg.

The new touchscreen is the biggest change, complete with the dynamic island around the web cam like a modern iPhone. The screen on the LCD MacBook Pro was already fantastic, but the switch to OLED has several benefits. The screen is even brighter, hitting an incredible peak of 2,000 nits for outdoor or HDR content viewing, making it one of the brightest laptop screens available.

OLED displays have individually lit pixels, which gives them dramatically better contrast with the deepest blacks and eliminates any blooming effects. That makes the new screen one of the very best on any product and a genuine joy to use to create or watch content. It is super crisp, vibrant and smooth, and makes the most of dark mode.
14in screen: 14.2in tandem OLED (3024x1986; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)
16in screen: 16.3in tandem OLED (3472x2266; 254 ppi) ProMotion (10-120Hz)
Connectivity: wifi 7, Bluetooth 6, Thread, 3x Thunderbolt 5/USB 4, HDMI 2.1, SDXC card, headphones

The OLED MacBook Pro isn’t the first laptop with a touchscreen – they’ve been common on Windows laptops since 2012 – but it is the first Mac with one. For the most part the touchscreen mirrors mouse clicks, so you can single tap on just about anything or tap and hold for right click on most things.

It also supports most of the gestures available on a trackpad, including swipes, pinch to zoom and rotate. Three-finger swipes trigger mission control so you can switch between windows, while flicking them left or right snaps them to the screen’s edge – though unsnapping them requires a mouse for some reason. Swipe in from the right side of the screen for notification centre, down from the top right for control centre and from the dynamic island for Spotlight or Siri.

The Mac is not touch-first like an iPad and there is no touchscreen keyboard. But Apple has built new touch systems that third-party app developers can use to do unique things, such as tools that fan out around your finger or scrubbing dials. Those are few and far between at the moment.

That leaves touching the screen an optional extra. Like Windows machines, it is handy to have direct interaction with something using your finger sometimes. Pinch to zoom or rotating a photo is a lot easier directly on the screen than the touchpad, as is tapping the screen to pause video. The touchscreen is also useful for performing various gestures if you use a mouse rather than a trackpad.

The OLED MacBook Pros come with the same M5 Pro or Max chips and memory choices as the regular MacBook Pros with essentially the same performance in benchmarks and during general use. They also have similar battery life, lasting for about two days of office work while mainly using the browser, writing, messaging and note-taking tools.

For more intensive workloads, such as developing and editing photos or other mid-level creative apps, the 16in version with M5 Max still managed to end the day with 40% left in the tank. If pushed to the limit, the battery lasts about two hours, which is still long enough to get a solid task or two done when away from the charger.

The MacBook Pro OLED is made of 55% recycled materials, which Apple breaks down in its environmental impact report. The battery should last in excess of 1,000 full charge cycles and can be replaced for £225 by Apple. Apple makes repair manuals available, offers trade-in and free recycling schemes.
The MacBook Pro with PROLED starts at £2,899 (€3,299/$2,899/A$4,599) for the 14in version or £3,399 (€3,899/$3,399/A$5,499) for the 16in version.

For comparison, the 14in M6 MacBook Pro costs £1,999, the 14in M5 Pro MacBook Pro costs £2,499, the 13in MacBook Air costs £1,299, the Dell XPS 14 costs from £2,038.45 and the Microsoft Surface Laptop Ultra costs £2,599.
The OLED MacBook Pro might be the first touchscreen Mac, but touch is the least interesting part about it.

The reduced weight, slimmer body and absolutely stunning new screen are meaningful upgrades that will no doubt see the MacBook Pro through another five years as one of the very best pro laptops you can get.
The light-up Apple logo on the lid is a welcome blast from the past, while the dynamic island at the top of the screen takes up less space and is more useful than the notch it replaces.

The touchscreen is best thought of a value-added extra that is useful on occasion or for certain types of tasks. This isn’t a touch-first laptop, it’s more like one that just happens to have a touchscreen similar to many of the best Windows rivals, which is just fine.

I still wish the dynamic island contained Face ID like it does on an iPhone. The Touch ID fingerprint scanner is fine, but face recognition on a laptop is better. And no matter how you slice it, any of the new MacBook Pros cost a lot of money, part of which can be blamed on RAMageddon.

As crazy as it might sound, if you’re currently hoping to replace an older machine with a new high-end M5 Pro or Max Apple laptop, the extra £400 or equivalent for the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR is worth it over the regular LCD MacBook Pro.

Pros: stunning OLED touchscreen, dynamic island with great Centre Stage camera, thinner and lighter, choice of extremely potent M5 Pro or Max chips, long battery life, plenty of ports and an SD card slot, brilliant speakers, Touch ID, first-class keyboard and trackpad, wifi 7, Bluetooth 6 and Thread support.
Cons: extremely expensive, no Face ID, no USB-A, RAM or SSD cannot be upgraded after purchase, touchscreen only occasionally useful.

items.title: I took Vinted to court to get my money back
paragraphs: Mali Osmelak never imagined that selling clothes on Vinted would end with a court claim to recover almost £6,000.
She started trading on the platform to earn an income while managing Crohn's disease and caring for her four-year-old daughter.

But when she became a professional seller in March, she was unable to complete Vinted's verification process, leaving thousands of pounds inaccessible in her Vinted wallet. After several weeks of trying to resolve the issue, Mali took legal action.

Vinted says sellers may be asked to complete verification checks to comply with legal and regulatory requirements and 98% of transactions are completed smoothly without needing help from its support team.
Vinted is hugely popular in the UK with 17 million users. The online marketplace does not charge a fee to sellers for listing on there.
After the BBC reported on users whose accounts had been suspended or banned, dozens of people got in touch describing difficulties accessing money held in their Vinted wallets.
Mali joined Vinted in 2024 as a side-hustle. Demand for her second-hand gymwear grew rapidly and, within months, she had set up a limited company to expand the business.
This year she signed up for a Vinted Pro seller account - designed for people who want to sell a high volume of items and who are registered as a business.

Within weeks she had generated almost £6,000 in sales. But when she tried to withdraw the money, she discovered her account had been restricted and was told she needed to complete a verification process.
"I thought, 'That's OK. It's not rocket science,'" she says. "I'd set up the business with the help of an accountant and had all the information they needed."

Mali says she spotted an error Vinted had made with her name and she flagged it with Vinted, but "again nothing was done and the verification kept failing". She found herself stuck in a cycle of automated responses.

In an effort to break the deadlock, she also contacted Mangopay, the payments company that at the time operated Vinted sellers' wallets and processed transactions on the platform. She was directed back to Vinted.
After eight weeks without access to the money, Mali decided to take both companies to the small claims court, spending £455 in court fees.
Three days after the court claim was filed, Mali says the account was "magically verified" and she could withdraw the funds.
She still pressed ahead with the case though to try to recover her court fees, costs and interest.
In June, she obtained a default judgement after neither Vinted nor Mangopay responded to her claim, with the court ordering the companies to pay £1,207.50.
But she has yet to receive the money. She has since been informed that Vinted and Mangopay have applied to have the judgement set aside, with a hearing scheduled for December.
"It's been ridiculous and incredibly stressful," she says.
"I need that cash. I will fight it. I'm going to tell the court their system is completely broken. I needed help and nobody helped me."
Vinted said: "Ms Osmelak's check was not successful because her documents did not match the name on her Vinted account. We have since helped her update it, and her account is now verified."
The company did not respond to the BBC's questions about the legal action Mali has taken and continues to pursue.

Mangopay said it was "bound to professional secrecy and data protection obligations. We are, therefore, not allowed to comment on individual cases involving our clients or their users, nor can we share details about specific accounts, transactions or legal matters."

items.title: Iraq say it has made progress in talks with armed groups
paragraphs: Editor's note: this story was translated from the original VOA Kurdish article.
The Iraqi government has made significant progress in talks with armed militia groups and that five of them had agreed to place their weapons under state control, a government spokesman told VOA.
“The government has completed the requirements and the details of negotiations” with five, armed groups, spokesman Haydar al-Aboudi told VOA Kurdish reporter Diyar Jamal in an interview in Baghdad.
Aboudi also said talks continue with two other groups, and that the hope is that those negotiations will be concluded successfully by June 2027.

Aboudi did not name the groups or explain and questions about the negotiations have yet to be announced, and it’s unclear if the militias have agreed to surrender their weapons or join Iraq’s official security forces.
The issue of armed groups operating outside government control has been a longstanding concern. Some of the country’s most powerful armed factions have close ties to Iran.
Washington has repeatedly called on Baghdad to bring all weapons under government control and prevent armed groups from acting independently.
Aboudi said the government had taken steps to address the issue since Prime Minister Ali Falih al-Zaidi took office in May 2026.
He said June 2027 was the deadline set by the government to complete the process.

U.S. envoy Tom Barrack on Sunday praised Iraqi Prime Minister Ali al-Zaidi for taking action against Iran-backed militias. He singled out the government's decision to cancel some contracts at Mosul International Airport over alleged links to armed groups. The contracts cover airport counters, parking facilities and taxi services, and Zaidi suggested they be awarded to international companies. Barrack said al-Zaidi was sending a clear message that “militia influence has no place in Iraq’s institutions,” calling the move “sovereignty in action.”
Aboudi described Iraq’s relations with Washington as moving toward greater economic cooperation based on shared interests and mutual respect.
The United States and Iraq agreed on a phased transition of the coalition’s military mission, with Iraqi forces taking greater responsibility for the country’s security.
Asked about the possibility of regional conflicts spreading into Iraq, Aboudi said the government was taking political, economic and security measures to keep the country out of regional disputes.
He said decisions concerning Iraq’s security and foreign policy were made by the Iraqi government and that no outside country had the authority to make those decisions.
Aboudi also rejected claims that Iranian forces had entered Iraqi territory in parts of Diyala province and the Kurdistan Region.
“These are just rumors,” he said, adding that government reports did not support the claims.

When asked about Sunday's drone attacks on the Khor Mor gas field in the Kurdistan Region, Aboudi said a security committee headed by Iraq’s national security adviser was working with relevant government agencies to address the issue and discover who was behind the attacks.
Aboudi also addressed differing reports that Baghdad and Tehran had reached an agreement concerning Iranian Kurdish opposition groups based in the Kurdistan Region.

Iran’s ambassador to Iraq said Baghdad had agreed to expel Iranian Kurdish opposition members from the Kurdistan Region. Aboudi would only say that discussions were underway through a security committee but did not provide details about the measures being considered.
He emphasized that Iraq would not allow its territory to be used to launch attacks against neighboring countries.
Aboudi expressed confidence in Iraq’s ability to maintain security following the withdrawal of U.S.-led coalition forces on September 30th.
He said Iraqi security forces, including the army, Interior Ministry forces and Kurdish Peshmerga, were prepared to respond to potential threats.
“ISIS is no longer an effective force on the ground,” he said.
Islamic State lost control of the territory it held in Iraq in 2017, although remnants of the group have continued to carry out attacks.
Aboudi said Iraq’s security forces were ready to deal with any new threats.

items.title: Jensen Huang’s image has been shattered. Could he be pushed out at Nvidia?
paragraphs: For more than 30 years, Jensen Huang has been the seemingly unshakable public face of Nvidia. He co-founded the company as a young engineer in 1993 and oversaw its growth into a multitrillion dollar chipmaker and bellwether of the AI industry at large.

He’s also made it a family business. His children, Madison and Spencer, have taken leadership roles at the firm. While not a company executive, his wife, Lori Mills Huang, leads the family foundation which, as of 2024, controls over 60m Nvidia shares.

But Huang’s image as a family man has been shattered as of Sunday. After the New York Times revealed at the end of October that Huang may have been targeted by a Chinese intelligence asset who he had developed a close relationship with, he admitted in a letter to employees on Sunday that he had been having an affair.

Initially, Nvidia spokesperson John Rizzo said there was nothing out of the ordinary about Huang’s interactions with Alice Huang, an executive at a Singaporean datacenter firm, Megaspeed. US government officials had suspected Huang of smuggling American chips into China, prompting those officials to surveil and monitor her, the Times first reported. In the course of that surveillance, officials allegedly determined that Alice Huang was a Chinese spy and had gotten close with the Nvidia leader.
Nvidia’s board of directors have now launched an independent investigation about the national security concerns surrounding Huang’s relationship.

“I support the investigation and will cooperate fully,” Huang wrote in his letter. “I love our country and our company. I am committed to protecting Nvidia and supporting America’s national security. I am proud and grateful to be an American.”
Megaspeed did not respond to a Guardian request for comment before publication.

In his letter, Huang apologized to his family, acknowledging how much they’ve supported him. His wife, Mills, kept a relatively low profile and didn’t play a formal role at Nvidia. However, in a 2023 interview with the New Yorker, Huang shared that Mills had also worked in Silicon Valley as a microchips engineer before stepping away to raise their children.

“Throughout my life, my family has given me love and support,” Huang wrote in his letter to employees. “They deserve my honesty and loyalty. Instead, I let them down and damaged the life we built together. I take full responsibility for what I did and the hurt I caused, and I accept the criticism that comes with it.”

Both his children now hold high ranking roles at the company, despite not initially pursuing careers in tech. His daughter, Madison, serves as the senior director of product and technical marketing for physical AI platforms, but got her start as a chef. She attended the Culinary Institute of America and Le Cordon Bleu before going to business school and transitioning to luxury marketing. She previously worked at LVMH – the parent company of Lous Vuitton.

Spencer, for his part, now serves as the director of product for Robotics at Nvidia but spent much of his career as a consultant before joining his father’s company as a product manager. Before consulting, he owned and co-founded a craft cocktail bar in Taiwan.

In his letter, Huang reiterated his commitment to Nvidia, saying he hoped to earn back his colleagues’ and employees’ trust. However, analysts and investors say there’s a chance he may be removed as CEO after the board’s investigation.

“This is a black eye moment for Jensen and will spark multiple congressional inquiries at a minimum and will create an overhang on the stock for a myriad of reasons,” said Dan Ives, a partner and analyst at investment bank Yorkville Ives. “There is clearly risk as discussed that Jensen could be removed as CEO depending on the board investigation and this will add risk to the stock as he is so important to the Nvidia story and strategy globally.”
Ives said the family’s role at Nvidia adds some complexities for the board.

“The board has to make its decision independent of the family spider web of Jensen and his family at Nvidia,” Ives told the Guardian. “It makes this a very complex situation for the board to navigate with the world watching.”

Huang is to Nvidia what Steve Jobs was to Apple, said Ken Mahoney, the CEO and president of Mahoney Asset Management. “If you asked any Nvidia investor or anyone involved in tech and markets, would they like to see Jensen gone? Definitely not, but [Nvidia] would survive,” Mahoney said.

“Losing Huang would introduce a lot of uncertainty, particularly given his influence over Nvidia’s strategy, culture, and relationships with major technology companies,” he continued. “The bigger question is whether a successor could maintain Huang’s strategic vision and ability to anticipate where the industry is heading, and how that new leader could be tested along the way if things become difficult.”

Executive affairs or inappropriate relationships have recently unseated CEOs, according to executive recruiting and coaching firm Challenger Gray and Christmas. In 2024, the CEO of Astronomer was caught on a kiss cam with the company’s chief people officer, leading him to resign shortly after. Nestlé fired CEO Laurent Freixe for a relationship with a subordinate.

Nvidia offers a more complex picture. On one hand, Huang’s affair is not just a matter morals or ethics, there are potential national security concerns. On the other, Huang is core to the DNA of Nvidia which in turn is the bedrock of the entire AI industry – an industry upon which the economy relies greatly.
Nvidia shares fell 7.5% as soon as the stock market opened, wiping over $330bn off the company’s value.

“When the CEO of the most valuable company in the world is tied to a counterintelligence investigation because of a personal relationship, every board in America should be paying attention,” said Andy Challenger, chief revenue officer at Challenger, Gray & Christmas. “It’s not just a question of romance or morality any more. It’s a question of judgment, national security exposure, shareholder trust, and whether the person at the top can be relied on to protect the enterprise.”
In a statement, Nvidia’s board said they do not believe either national security or company secrets were compromised but they will “examine all available information.”
“The Board has confidence in Jensen and his leadership team and will provide further updates as appropriate,” the board said in a statement.

items.title: The French fridge hacks were relatively unsophisticated. An AI-enabled attack would raise the stakes
paragraphs: In 2023 a state-backed group interrupted TV streaming services in the United Arab Emirates to broadcast a deepfake report on the war in Gaza. In the same year, hackers affiliated with Iran displayed the slogan “down with Israel” on the screens of water-control equipment made by an Israeli firm.
Now France has attributed an attack on supermarket fridges to hackers operating under the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, a key branch of Iran’s military establishment.

There was no message this time, but the disruption made headlines around the world. Some refrigerators had their temperature turned up so high they caught fire. ‌In the hours after the hack, supermarket employees dumped piles of perished meat and melted ice-cream into rubbish containers.
France’s foreign minister described it as an act of “unprecedented scale and unprecedented aggression” and promised “Europe-wide sanctions” would be imposed against those responsible.

It follows attacks on industrial freezers at an Israeli food production plant in May and a wave of freezer malfunctions that spoiled food at US military bases in August that are now reportedly being treated as a suspected hack. Those attacks have not been officially attributed to Iran, but the French announcement is the first to implicate the state in this type of hack.

Rafe Pilling, a senior director at Sophos, a cybersecurity firm, said the relatively unsophisticated nature of the attack – hackers used default passwords to access fridge controls – was in line with Iranian capabilities. “The attacks themselves were not particularly complex,” he said.
Pilling said there was now a presumption the French attacks and a wave of rogue defrosting hacks across Europe last week were linked.

Hostile cyber operations against the west tend to come from a vexatious quartet of China, Russia, Iran and North Korea. All have different aims and characteristics: China has focused on industrial espionage and mass data gathering, Russia on disrupting enemy infrastructure and spreading disinformation, and North Korea on hacking crypto exchanges because it needs money. Iran, according to Pilling, wants to put a shot across the bow of its enemies.
“In general Iran uses cyber-attacks to project power internationally and to signal their political displeasure with regional and international adversaries,” Pilling said.

The fridge hacks came as the UK’s national cybersecurity centre warned the country is in the “foothills” of a new level of cyber threat – and should expect a “huge rise” in the volume of incidents. The main concern is AI, a technology now capable of highlighting previously unforeseen flaws in IT systems and helping attackers plan and carry out attacks.

However, the underlying context of the fridge attacks is not AI but geopolitics. After all, the refrigeration system vulnerabilities were relatively easy to find and exploit. But a combination of groundbreaking technology and tense global relations makes for an alarming landscape.

items.title: Nvidia’s board needs to do some succession planning – sharpish | Nils Pratley
paragraphs: Too big – and too well-connected – to sack? One doesn’t have to be overly cynical to think Jensen Huang, the Nvidia boss, starts with one huge advantage as the chipmaker’s board starts its independent investigation into the alleged honeytrap spy scandal. The world of US big tech is not, to put it mildly, strong on checks and balances on a founder’s power.

Huang does not enjoy the supercharged voting rights that are par for the course elsewhere – his shareholding is a plain vanilla 3.6%. On the other hand, Nvidia’s board does not appear to have spent much time worrying about succession planning and “key person risk” or other standard concerns of corporate governance wonks outside the US.

There isn’t even a Nvidia board member with the title of chair. Instead, a “lead director” is “designated annually by a majority of the independent directors”, which sounds like a formula for ensuring the attention remains wholly focused on Huang, the sole executive member.

It’s the American way, of course: the cult of the superstar founder or chief executive runs deep and there is a fair argument that such set-ups encourage adventurous risk-taking in pursuit of grand corporate visions. But such governance arrangements look unsuited to situations where the behaviour of the boss is under scrutiny and the role of the board itself is being examined.

The investigation will examine whether Huang “has been the target of a foreign intelligence effort” but the independent directors stressed there is now “no reason to believe that either national security or Nvidia secrets were compromised.”

OK, but legitimate questions don’t end there. Did Huang break Nvidia’s internal code of conduct? Did he mislead the board about his relationship with Alice Huang (no relation), the alleged Chinese spy? Was the board aware of US intelligence reports that Ms Huang had been hired by China’s ministry of state security to spy on the Nvidia boss, as reported by the New York Times? What security precautions were in place? Other boards in other countries might have insisted on suspending the boss until all the facts are in.

In the meantime, the defence of Huang from elsewhere has begun. “An honourable guy. I think he probably has an excuse for it,” said Donald Trump. “Jensen is irreplaceable for America’s AI leadership,” opined Shaun Maguire, a partner at Sequoia Capital, the powerful Silicon Valley investor. Yes, there is little doubt the US tech and political establishment would like this saga to end up in a series of bland conclusions about an everyday infidelity.

Nvidia’s board, however, would be wise not to rely on the “irreplaceable” consensus holding, or the political heat going away. This affair will be trawled over by newly empowered Democrats in Congress because it touches on how forcefully – or not – the administration has been enforcing its own national security restrictions on chip sales to China. This process will go on for months. Huang’s personal relationship with Trump will come under the spotlight like never before.

Will the Nvidia boss, even if he is cleared by the board’s investigation, still look so all-conquering by the end? His lobbying clout in Washington will be diminished. And Nvidia’s shareholders, if they’re doing the job properly, will surely insist on far greater visibility on where the company’s chips end up.

There may come a point where it is in Nvidia’s own interests to move on from the Jensen Huang era. The 63-year-old deserves all his accolades for spotting the enormous AI opportunity for the GPU chips that originated in the world of video games. The rise of Nvidia has been extraordinary. But over-reliance on one individual is also a business risk. Time for some overdue succession planning – it may be needed.

items.title: 'I've got a band now' - Club anthem star Shygirl on why she's switching up her sound
paragraphs: Shygirl is known for big dance bangers, but her latest album has a more stripped-back sound
Hard-hitting beats, club anthems and unapologetically sexy lyrics are what Shygirl is known for.
But the singer and DJ - real name Blane Muise - has introduced a different sound for her second album, Swallow!, which dropped on Friday.
Shygirl hasn't totally left her electronic roots behind though.
You can still hear the sweat-soaked energy of Charli XCX's 365 remix and relentless pulse of 2024 hit mr useless on her latest record.
But there's also guitar strums, heartfelt songwriting and a dreamy haze, giving it an indie edge.
"I've learned over the 10 years I've been making music to have this confidence and to not be afraid of failure," she tells BBC Newsbeat.
"The big part of starting this record was wanting to have natural instrumentation and not feel like that was barred from me."
Shygirl puts the change down to a desire for a more "authentic" sound - a growing trend among British electronic artists who've been bringing a rockier influence to their music.
Asked why she took this musical direction, the 33-year-old says it was down to "the nostalgia of the indie sound".
"I felt the familiarity of that feeling, embracing the teenager within and the angst that I had and all the sounds that coloured that environment," she says.
Long-time producers Karma Kid and Casey MQ were "surprised" when Shygirl told them about her desire to work in more indie sounds, but she says the pair trusted her with the new direction.
Fans have been patiently waiting for something other than singles since her debut album Nymph was released in 2022.
The question now is whether they'll relate to this more rose-tinted version of Shygirl.
"It's not like I changed overnight," she insists. "In fact, it was because I was the girl I was in all the other songs that I became who I am now."
The album's artwork shows a chick hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth
There are clear signs that Shygirl is entering a new chapter.
She cleared her Instagram feed before beginning the album rollout, and the artwork shows a bird hatching from an egg, symbolising rebirth.
But she points out the journey is an "evolution" rather than reinvention.
"I think it's less about moving away from me, but I would hate to repeat myself," she says.
"I would only wish to pick up the same tool if I felt like I had grown somewhat or had a renewed expertise for it."
That growth can be heard in tracks like Live the Life You Like - one of Shygirl's favourites on the album.
It features a gritty bassline and a manipulated riff that echoes a klaxon, which she describes as giving off "punk energy".
Leaning into that side of her sound has only made her more excited to take the record on a tour, starting with Europe in March.
"I've got a band now," she reveals with a grin. "I work with a drummer and a multi-instrumentalist and sometimes a bassist.
"It's just so fun to share the stage and be so inspired. We've rehearsed, but there's still so many moments for spontaneity and for us to look at each other and vibe."
Shygirl's the latest artist known for electronic music who's embraced a more organic sound.
Her close friend Charli XCX featured a rockier, guitar-driven style on her latest album Music, Fashion, Film.
One of the standout tracks on that album for Shygirl is SS26, because "her voice is so natural and exposed".
"You forget other people don't know that voice and they need to get to know that starting point to be able to appreciate everything else."
Shygirl believes that same stripped-back approach is shaping much of the current wave of British dance music, including her latest album.
"There's so many of us now, especially coming from the Brit pack, that are doing the same thing," she says.
Shygirl's friend Charli XCX introduced drums and guitars for her latest album
Artists like PinkPantheress and Fred Again have also spoken about bringing indie influences into electronic music, something Shygirl says is "a reflection of what is going on in the world".
"I think there is a natural desire to have a sense of truth or something grounding," she says.
"And what is more grounding or more truthful than knowing exactly where a sound comes from."
So with artists borrowing more and more from across the musical spectrum, does genre still matter?
For Shygirl, it's less about what box listeners put her music in and more about whether it connects with them.
"Regardless if they like it or they hate it, I want someone to feel something. To be apathetic to my music would be the biggest insult to me."
Listen to Newsbeat live at 12:45 and 17:45 weekdays - or listen back here.

items.title: Print commissioned by Nasa uncovered for exhibition
paragraphs: A print by a Yorkshire artist commissioned by Nasa in the early days of space travel will go on show as part of a pop art exhibition.
Komtek I by Michael Fossick, who studied at Bradford School of Art, was created in 1962 to celebrate a Hong Kong company that produced microcomputers in the early days of space travel.
The print was part of a Nasa project to document the effort of sending the first humans to the moon and is on display as part of the Pop Art at Cartwright Hall exhibition.
The display tells the story of the British International Print Biennale, which took place at the Bradford gallery on 11 occasions between 1968 and 1990, and runs until March 2027.
While the exhibition also includes work by Andy Warhol and David Hockney, there is "definitely stuff that people won't have seen before", said curator Jill Iredale.
"It's a completely bizarre sort of connection somehow that an artist born in Sheffield that went to Bradford School of Art was somehow commissioned by Nasa," said Iredale.
"It was actually a screen print, but it was made from a very early computerised image," she said.
In March 1962, Nasa administrator James Webb awarded commissions to 38 artists, including Fossick, to document the space agency's achievements.

John H. Glenn became the first American to orbit the earth on 20 February 1962 and in the following decade Nasa's Mercury programme led to the Apollo missions, and eventually to Neil Armstrong setting foot on the moon in 1969.
Fossick chose to honour Komtek I, a microcomputer produced by Komtek Technologies Ltd in Hong Kong that was significant in the early years of the space programme.
He submitted the print to the First British International Print Biennale held at Cartwright Hall in 1968 where it won a prize.
Created by a group of local print makers and artists, at its height the British International Print Biennale included more than 500 works selected from more than 3,000 entries.
It received work by artists such as Andy Warhol, Roy Licthenstein and David Hockney, which remain in the gallery today.
Hockney was invited to be a judge on the first biennial in 1968 and created the poster for the show, which is on display in the exhibition.
Iredale said the pop art explosion in Bradford was a reaction to the seriousness of the World War Two and the boost in commercial print culture.
"Bradford had quite a strong, experimental kind of light, pretty kind of DIY aesthetic with artists and with the college as well," she explained.
"There was simply loads more young people around, post-baby boom, and an increase in opportunities for working-class youth."

items.title: Collision of two trains in Egypt kills at least four
paragraphs: At least four people were killed and almost 90 others were injured when two trains collided on Sunday south of Cairo, authorities have said.

The crash occurred in al-Ayyat district in Giza province, about 30 miles (5okm) south of the capital, when a train travelling to the south-western Fayoum province crashed into the rear of a train heading to the southern province of Aswan, according to the transport ministry. It said one of the trains had derailed.
The health ministry said at least four people had been killed and 88 injured. The injured were taken to nearby hospitals for treatment, it said.
The president, Abdel Fatah al-Sisi, said in a social media post that he had ordered a prompt investigation into the crash to hold those responsible accountable.
Emergency teams and cranes were dispatched to the scene to clear the wreckage and restore services to their normal schedule as soon as possible, the Egyptian railway authority said.
A train driver and his assistant were injured in September last year when two freight trains collided in the same district.

items.title: How African philosophies inspired a new approach to staging film festivals in Manchester
paragraphs: African philosophies including exploring how lessons from the past can shape the present and near future have inspired a film festival coming to Manchester.
See My World, a day dedicated to independent creators from across the African diaspora in the north of England, will take place at the Contact theatre on 21 November.
The festival is part of See My World’s year-round programme showcasing pan-African arts, culture and events.

It reflects the determination among creatives and activists in Manchester to build on the legacy of the 1945 Pan-African Congress in Manchester – which connected luminaries of postwar independence movements with a shared vision of liberation – after last year’s 80th anniversary commemorations.

See My World’s CEO and artistic director, Tunde Adekoya, said this month’s film festival was taking inspiration from across the spectrum of pan-African thought, including the works of Kenyan writers John Mbiti, an Anglican theologian who died in 2019, and Ngũgĩ wa Thiong’o, the author of the groundbreaking 1986 book Decolonising the Mind who died last year.

Both writers rejected the colonial conceit that African thought was inferior, stressed the importance of community and saw reclaiming African ways of knowing as essential to a people’s self-understanding.

While Mbiti sought common ground between African religions and Christianity, Ngũgĩ was a Marxist. He argued colonialism was motivated by cultural and economic conquest, and that European powers used language as their sharpest instrument. Ngũgĩ famously abandoned English to write in Gikuyu, a Bantu language mainly spoken in Kenya and criticised the role missionary Christianity played in colonial rule.

Adekoya said: “It’s a day dedicated to pan-African and global majority films from the north of England with exclusive premieres of documentaries we’ve been working on, which weave together expressions of liberation through art forms like poetry and dance.
“The whole idea is that it’s like a playground in search of strategies of liberation, using the festival as a way to explore different philosophies.

“John Mbiti explores the philosophy and spiritual understandings of time through the concept of Sasa na Zamani – in which the past informs everything that happens moving forward. That reflects how we constantly go back to pan-African histories to inform how we progress.”
Film-makers have been invited to submit films lasting up to 30 minutes from across genres, with no screening fees charged.

As well as submissions, the festival will feature documentaries produced by See My World. They include Homage, a “cinematic love letter to dance” that traces a culture through present-day portraits illustrating dance artists and archival material from Manchester, telling a story of joy, loss, migration, rhythm and resistance. Meanwhile, Poetic Justice explores how pan-African thought and Manchester’s poetry scene speak across decades.

Adekoya added: “The idea is that we would go against the norm of how film festivals are, because when we think about decolonisation, we think about how structures have been created to alienate and exclude communities.

“So we thought our film festival would look more at how we make film accessible and how stories that deserve to be seen get seen. Throughout the day we will have different activities, from exhibitions to explorations of our performances, discussions, Q&As, insights into directors’ processes, and workshops.

“We’ve been looking for literature and concepts that inform us and give us an understanding of who we truly are. And as works from thinkers like John Mbiti have come into our sphere, they have really emboldened us to think differently about our place in the world and what we do.”
See My World film festival runs from 2pm to 11pm on Saturday 21 November at Contact theatre, Oxford Road, Manchester.

items.title: Kenyan doomsday sect leader jailed for 200 years for murder of 190 children
paragraphs: The leader of a Kenyan doomsday sect has been sentenced to 200 years in prison for the murders of 190 children and one adult in one of the world’s worst cult disasters in recent history.

The sentence, comprising 100 years for murder by starvation and 100 years by direct homicide, came two weeks after the court in Kenya’s coastal city of Mombasa found the cult leader guilty of the crimes.

Prosecutors said Paul Mackenzie and his Good News International church ran ​a Christian doomsday sect whose members were ordered to starve themselves and their children to death to go to heaven before the world ended.
His accomplices threatened and beat victims to ensure they followed his orders. The emaciated bodies were found scattered in shallow graves and dumped in latrines. Some had been buried alive.
Mackenzie was arrested in 2023 after police received a tipoff, and weeks later authorities began uncovering bodies in shallow graves in the Shakahola forest near the coast in south-eastern Kenya.
In total, more than 400 bodies have been recovered. Many were severely decomposed and only 26 could be identified.
Mackenzie denied murder charges, saying he did not force the victims to starve, but the court rejected that argument.
The Shakahola tragedy has gripped Kenya since the discovery of mass graves in the forest more than three years ago.
It raised questions about how Mackenzie was able to continue operating despite being on the radar of the authorities since 2017, when police searched his premises.
In 2019, authorities shut down Mackenzie’s church and he relocated ‌to the Shakahola forest, police said.
The case has also led to calls for tougher oversight of churches and other religious organisations in a country where religious faith plays a prominent role in public life.
Mackenzie, a former taxi driver, forbade cult members from sending their children to school and from going to hospital when they were ill, describing such institutions as satanic.
Cult members lived in makeshift homes of polythene sheeting and thatch that Mackenzie divided into areas with biblical names such as Jerusalem and Judea.
The plight of his followers began ​to emerge in March 2023, when a man told ​police his brother and wife had starved their children ​to death in the forest on Mackenzie’s orders.

Mackenzie was arrested but released on bail, after which relatives said he brought forward the date ​on which he told his followers the ‌world would end. Police rearrested him and ​started combing through the forest more systematically and began exhuming mass graves.
Last month’s judgment covered 191 deaths while investigations into more than 200 other deaths are continuing.
Justice Diana Kavedza-Mochache said in a hearing lasting more than eight hours that in some cases children were isolated and denied food while their parents watched.
Mackenzie faces other charges over the forest deaths, including those of terrorism, which he has denied.
Prosecutors said that while he was in detention he also directed the deaths of 52 people in Kwa Binzaro village, about 18 miles from Shakahola. Mackenzie has pleaded not guilty in that case.

items.title: US rockets firm could take over mothballed Highland spaceport
paragraphs: HIE and Economy Secretary Stephen Flynn have welcomed the agreement.
The site is on Melness Crofters Estate, an area of small-scale farms on the A' Mhoine Peninsula in Sutherland in the north-west Highlands.
Chairwoman Dorothy Pritchard said the estate was delighted to welcome Leap as a potential launch operator.

She said: "We believe their presence here will be an important step towards establishing a thriving and sustainable spaceport that can bring long-term benefits to Sutherland and the UK's growing space industry.

"Alongside other UK launch sites, both developed and emerging, an operational Sutherland Spaceport will become an integral part of a resilient and diverse UK launch ecosystem, securing the UK position within the global space economy, something we welcome and support.
"Melness Crofters Estate looks forward to seeing the spaceport become a driver of economic opportunity."

items.title: Powerhouse Parramatta opens this weekend – and it’s dazzling inside and out
paragraphs: Dubbed the “Opera House of western Sydney”, Powerhouse Parramatta’s white lattice exoskeleton, composed from 1,300 individual pieces and wrapping 30,000 sq metres of interior space, has already become a familiar landmark.

Even better known, perhaps, is the project’s controversial history. Since the Parramatta outpost was announced in 2014, a vocal group of dissenters led by former staff and trustees has lamented what they see as the neglect of the museum’s Ultimo site in favour of a new infrastructure project, and what they say is a shift away from the museum’s core business towards contemporary art and events.

The eye-watering price tag – $915m, in an era of funding precarity for the arts – has also come under scrutiny, culminating in a New South Wales Treasury investigation into allegations over the museum’s governance and procurement practices. In late August, 10 weeks from the scheduled opening, CEO Lisa Havilah was stood down while the investigation unfolded.

When the major new venue opens to the public on Saturday, the big question will be: was it worth it? What will it bring to Parramatta – and will it be enough to bring the rest of Sydney, and the rest of Australia, out west?

Powerhouse is sweetening the pot with a 23-day opening festival of performances, parties, talks, screenings and workshops, with 65% of the program free. When Guardian Australia visited last week, the space was crowded with installation crew in hi-vis, hard hats and steel-capped boots. But even with its exhibitions in various states of readiness, it was hard not to be dazzled.

The steel exoskeleton that has been such a prominent addition to Parramatta’s skyline is more than decorative. Encasing two towers, and built from 12,000 tonnes of steel, it’s what allows the building to boast massive column-free exhibition spaces up to 18m in height, including the largest in Australia.

But at first encounter, perhaps the most striking thing about the Moreau Kusunoki and Genton-designed building is the sense of calm it evokes. This is a building that is constantly calling you to slow down, take a breath and look beyond its architecture to the city, landscape and Parramatta River below.

The glass facade and abundance of natural light is complemented by an airy colour palette, all creams, white and light greys – including interior walls covered in a pale, textured render made from 600,000 crushed oyster shells, locally and sustainably sourced. Wide corridors flanking the exhibition spaces are lined with chairs and lounges that invite you to pause and take in the view.

This peace is particularly necessary given the dizzying spectacles of Powerhouse Parramatta’s five opening exhibitions – including a tribute to space and flight; a celebration of the shopping mall; a kids’ exhibition themed around the dark; and a showcase of British designer Es Devlin – which otherwise risk sensory overload.

Coups de théâtre abound: secret doorways and dramatic reveals; a mirror maze; a copse of Christmas firs; a massive replica meteorite taking up an entire exhibition space. There’s a recreation of the historic Roselands shopping mall fountain; a restored 1920s elevator transporting visitors with access needs between exhibition floors; and a rainbow-hued walk-in installation by American light artist James Turrell at the top of a tower.

Throughout the spaces, museum objects (more than 1,600 from the 500,000-strong collection, supplemented by around as many loans) jostle with specially commissioned artworks, lavishly designed displays and interactive exhibits. The exhibitions are fuelled by wonder, spectacle and nostalgia – and are hard to resist.

Task Eternal is Powerhouse Parramatta’s flagship opening exhibition – and the only one that adults will have to pay an entry fee for ($30/$20 concession; 16 and unders get in free). A celebration of flight and space travel, it takes over the museum’s main hall: 2,000 sq metres with 18-metre-high ceilings, bringing together objects from the Powerhouse collection as well as loans, commissions and literary texts – including excerpts from US science fiction author Ted Chiang, whose short story Tower of Babylon inspired the exhibition’s structure, including a zigzagging tower which visitors ascend and descend.

Hero items include delicate sketches by Leonardo da Vinci; a bumarang (boomerang) – an example of ingenious Indigenous aerodynamic design – collected from Burramatta/Parramatta in the early 19th century; a “boilerplate” (or testing model) Apollo command module from the 1960s; and the spacesuit worn by Leonard Nimoy’s Spock in Star Trek.

Aircraft from different eras, including the ingenious 19th-century flying rigs of Australian aviation pioneer Lawrence Hargrave, take pride of place. There is an entire room full of engines, and lots of rockets too, including a Skylark research rocket deployed at Woomera in the 70s, and a fully functional retro Rocket Playground from the 1960s.

Among the many stunning artworks, the star exhibit – at the top of the tower – is a perception-testing “ganzfeld” installation by US light artist James Turrell, accessible for those who bought a special Turrell-inclusive ticket ($40 for adults, $10 for kids). Eight viewers at a time are invited into a room with curved walls and a shifting cycle of coloured light, which induces the kind of disorientation experienced by pilots in certain altitudes and atmospheres.

Task Eternal is overwhelming in its scope and visual magnificence. It’s also a little discombobulating. Rather than chronology, it is structured around four “acts” exploring not only the history and technology of air and space travel, but our “cultural relationship with the sky” and “the human compulsion to ascend, leave Earth and return”. It zigzags between eras, topics and modes of storytelling; between science, engineering, design and art.

It also works hard to shed the western, patriarchal and colonial narratives around space and flight, and to weave in lesser-known histories and perspectives, including First Nations technologies and cosmologies. This doesn’t make for a smooth, coherent journey; though time, attention to wall texts and repeat visits may yield the kind of rich experience it aims for.

The Mall, a tribute to the social, cultural and design history of shopping centres, was only partially installed a week ahead of opening, but looks to be similarly maximalist. The Dark, the Powerhouse’s exhibition for children aged 4 to 12 set in a massive replica meteorite more than 22m long, will be an absolute hit – and not just because it’s top secret: no photographs are allowed, and visitors will have to bag their smartphones before entering.

We are allowed to describe how it works though: visitors enter via a dark, narrow tunnel followed by a series of glowing chambers, lined and stuffed with more than 800 objects, including sparkling minerals, retro toys, ancient artefacts and modern treasures (including the first item the museum collected, in 1882: a jar of peas). Part playground, part discovery trail, items are arranged from toddler to adult height, and there are enough hidden delights and nostalgic treats to thaw the most frosty heart – including animations drawing on First Nations creation stories, and the museum’s most Googled object: a heart-emblazoned shirt worn by Leonardo DiCaprio in Baz Luhrmann’s Romeo + Juliet. There’s not much narrative here, and some might grumble that it is light on science and learning, but museums desperately need to attract young audiences – and this might do the trick.

The calmest of the opening exhibits, titled Overflow, is an installation on the eastern building’s third floor: a 16-metre high-definition LED display of short films by director Ivan Sen, featuring breathtaking footage, each spotlighting one of seven Indigenous organisations from NSW who care for water, country and community.

In front of the screen is a shallow pool with water that laps with the tides of the river. Visitors are encouraged to take their shoes off and get their feet wet; there’s a sensorial magic about being 30m high, with your feet in the water and the sky on either side of you.

“We’re on a flood plain,” says Beau James, director of First Nations for the Powerhouse, gesturing to the Parramatta River out the window. In fact the location of the building was its own controversy for that very reason. “That river has always ebbed and flowed, that’s its natural way of moving. We wanted to honour water.”

As part of the commission, the museum invested an undisclosed amount of money in the organisations featured in Sen’s films. “We asked them: ‘What’s something you’ve always really wanted to do but have never been able to get funds for?’” says James.

The funded proposals include tagging marine life in Gamay (Botany Bay); clearing rubbish and mitigating pollution in the Parramatta River; and an initiative for clearing invasive European carp from the Barwon River in Brewarrina.

The final exhibition brings together recent works by British designer Es Devlin whose peripatetic career has encompassed theatre, fashion, public art and arena concerts (she has designed tours for Beyoncé, U2 and Lady Gaga, as well as Olympic ceremonies and Super Bowl half-time shows).

But Powerhouse’s exhibition – her Australian debut – sees Devlin in a more poetic and philosophical mode. Made over the last decade (and adjusted here for their Australian debuts), the five works, spread across four main rooms, represent Devlin’s attempts to use participatory art and interactive design to induce shifts of awareness and perspective; and to help rewire our sense of connection to the living world and each other.

The visual highlight is a giant mirror maze, designed to represent the “arterial geometries of lungs and trees”. But the soul of the exhibition is the participatory work Collective Portrait: a room with a 24m table and an equally long, unspooling reel of white paper, with an invitation to sit down on either side of the table for 15 minutes and draw the person opposite you.

The point is not so much the drawing as the silent interpersonal exchange between strangers. “I’ve been practising this around the world, and I’ve found whoever I practise it with, it can be quietly transformational,” says Devlin.

She has also created a sixth, temporary work for the museum’s month-long opening festival: an Australian iteration of her 2022 outdoor work Come Home Again, featuring her own hand-drawn sketches of 244 endangered local species, and choral tributes which will be performed at dusk most nights through November within her illuminated outdoor installation on the Powerhouse’s riverside lawn.
“I’m hoping that if we set up the rhythm of these evensong moments over the opening days and weeks, that people will continue to gather here. That it’s like a beacon.”

Devlin, who has exhibited in the world’s top galleries and museums, describes Powerhouse Parramatta as a “magnificent” building with “astounding” opening exhibitions. “The fact that people are going to not just learn things but feel things and therefore remember what they learned? I think it’s going to make it a destination for people to come from far and wide.”

items.title: Art is good for your health? Allow me a quick eyeroll | Emma Brockes
paragraphs: As the long autumn subsides and we finally head into winter, so we hit that point in the calendar when two rival theories of seasonal survival play out: one, the permission-giving invitation to give up and power down, encapsulated by Scandinavian hygge and Katherine May’s 2020 blockbuster Wintering; and two, the exhortation to push through the discomfort and get out there. If the midterm results in the US give us a huge boost this week, still we have to keep going until spring.

The latest contribution to the get-up-and-out-there branch of motivational badgering comes in the form of a report by an arts charity suggesting that, as with exercise and being in nature, our baseline mood may be improved by exposing ourselves to art on a regular basis. According to Art Fund, a national body that promotes access to the arts, a person’s mental and physical wellbeing may be meaningfully affected by abiding by a handy acronym – RDA for recommended dose of art – and attaching it to what appears to be an entirely arbitrary prescription, namely 60 minutes of art ingestion a month. According to Daisy Fancourt, a professor of psychobiology and epidemiology at University College London who wrote the report’s foreword, do this and, “alongside having a balanced diet, regular exercise and spending time outdoors”, your health will thank you.

I don’t mean to sound sceptical. There are excellent reasons for promoting this theory: the ability of art in any form to take us out of ourselves and put us back in a slightly different place. What is fascinating to me is how Art Fund has found it necessary to sell the idea by appealing to a standard that, if not antithetical to art, exactly, seems at the very least to be highly irrelevant. In other words, the key sell for engaging with art in this case is that there is science – a real expertise! – backing it up, to reassure those on the fence that it’s not all a clanging, nebulous waste of time.

There’s probably a way to blame Malcolm Gladwell for this, or take your pick from any number of other narrow-track, extremely literal thinkers who don’t trust any experience of life that can’t be tabulated. And while Art Fund is just conforming to publishing trends, which require measurable takeaways from every single thing we do, I can’t help finding something dispiriting and babyish about the way they’ve gone about it. Not to get too Walter Pater about it all, but the minute you start trying to measure future benefits in relation to standing in front of a painting or reading a book, not only do you wander into upsetting territory where phrases such as “value proposition” and “what’s the unlock on this?” reside, but it risks interfering with the experience itself.

I know, I’m being a snob. The enthusiasm for boiling life down to a series of self-optimising items on an endless, dreary to-do list, however, does get a bit much at times. In this particular case, it is technically true, I suppose, that art belongs in a very broad category with nutrition. And you can hold two apparently contradictory thoughts in your head at the same time, so that the fleeting experience of being immersed in an artwork can live alongside the understanding that there is some future, unspecified benefit to the exercise.

But when so much weight is put on health and welfare as the ultimate goal, it does risk shifting the experience from pleasure to chore. A more accurate presentation of the value of art might be that going to the National Gallery for the afternoon is less like eating a bowl of grains and doing a quick workout than spooning frosting into your mouth, fixing you greedily and indulgently in the thrill of the moment. Only guess what?! Without the cholesterol!

Is the science of art-as-health-benefit a real science? I’ll never find out because, apparently, I have no desire to improve myself by reading the data – although if curiosity or a whimsical need to do something I’m not interested in ever gets the better of me, I’ll certainly look into it.

All of which misses the point, of course, which is about selling a laudable and true idea about how art enriches your life to a possibly sceptical public. I tip my hat to Art Fund for framing this conviction in a publicity-friendly way, which is surely more sensible than wanging on about hard, gemlike flames and watching it dive to the bottom of the news list. Just allow me a quick eyeroll first.

items.title: Apple iPad mini A20 Pro review: the best small tablet but with a big price
paragraphs: The new iPad mini takes Apple’s fan-favourite tiny tablet and upgrades just about everything about it, including giving it a new OLED screen, serious performance, speakers embedded into the display and even water resistance, all with a big new price tag.

The eighth-generation iPad mini costs from £699 (€749/$699/A$1,099), which is £200 or equivalent more than the original price of its predecessor as RAMageddon continues to bite. That makes it uncomfortably expensive, costing £270 more than the base model iPad (A16) and only £50 cheaper than the bigger 11in iPad Air M4.

The new mini reads like a wishlist from small iPad owners. The tablet is about 1mm thinner, 38g lighter and slightly smaller compared with its predecessor, but still manages to fit in a 0.2in larger screen. The mini is the first iPad to have IP67 water resistance, which means trips to the beach or pool are less fraught with danger. Even the video call camera has been moved to a more sensible position in the landscape edge of the tablet. It lacks Face ID, though, making it reliant on the Touch ID fingerprint scanner in the power button.

The new 8.5in OLED screen is the star of the show: bright, vibrant and with inky blacks to make the absolute most of your content. But it lacks the “ProMotion” display technology Apple uses on many of its other devices to keep scrolling and interactions super smooth. It is particularly jarring when you move from a modern iPhone with its 120Hz screen back to the iPad with its relatively slow 60Hz display.

The new speaker system has a pair of tweeters that fire out of slimline gaps between the screen glass and aluminium body with woofers that play directly through the screen. They sound really very good for something this slim, with direct, powerful audio you can’t block with your hand while holding the sides of the tablet.
Screen: 8.5in Super Retina XDR OLED (326ppi)
Processor: Apple A20 Pro (5- or 6-core CPU)
Connectivity: wifi 7 (5G eSim-only), Bluetooth 6, Thread, USB-C, Touch ID
Water resistance: IP67 (1 metre for 30 mins)

Inside the new iPad is the A20 Pro chip from the iPhone 18 Pro and Duo, which absolutely flies. It comes in two versions depending on storage, with all but the most expensive model having one fewer CPU cores and half the NPU performance. Most will not miss it.

The battery lasts a solid nine to 10 hours of active screen use for lighter tasks such as browsing the web, answering emails, taking notes, watching movies or viewing photos. Playing games dents the battery to more like six to eight hours. The tablet charges to about 50% in under 30 minutes using a 35W or greater USB-C power adaptor (not included) and reaches 100% in about 100 minutes.
The battery will last more than 1,000 full-charge cycles with at least 80% of its original capacity and can be replaced for £115. Other out-of-warranty damage, including screen repairs, costs £519.
It contains 35% recycled material. The company breaks down the tablet’s environmental impact in its report. Apple offers trade-in and free recycling schemes, including for non-Apple products.

The iPad mini A20 Pro costs from £699 (€749/$699/A$1,099). For comparison, the iPad costs £429, the iPad Air 11in costs £749, and the iPad Pro 11in costs £1,199. The iPhone Duo costs £1,999 and the Lenovo Legion Tab 5th gen costs £649.

The iPad mini is the best small tablet available. That was true for previous models and is doubly true for the new one. Almost everything about it has been upgraded – the screen, the body, the camera, speakers and chip – yet it feels and works very similarly to the last few iPad minis.

The mini has a loyal following for whom the bigger screen than a phone and the portability of a compact tablet are the sweet spot. They are typically public transport commuters, people who fly a lot or those that have turned to it for a notepad replacement. They will love this revamp.

But you also see a lot of them in the workplace. Minis are used on building sites, as payment systems in stores, check-in terminals for greeters, by waiting staff in restaurants or in universities used for handwritten notes and marking up scientific papers.

The iPad mini isn’t quite the perfect small tablet. The screen should be faster and it is jarring that it isn’t, particularly at this very high price. It still lacks Face ID. And for most people the cheaper basic iPad or iPad Air is a better buy.

Pros: compact and light design, top performance, 10-hour battery life, great OLED screen, water resistance, landscape camera, USB-C, great speakers, full multitasking and external display support, long software support, recycled aluminium, Apple Pencil Pro support.
Cons: very expensive, screen not 120Hz, no Face ID, small size is cramped for some uses.

items.title: Constantinople to Istanbul review – you won’t want to leave this lavish celebration of double imperial splendour
paragraphs: Two empires compete to bewitch you in this exhibition that offers a double bubble of beauty. It collides the Byzantine empire, whose capital Constantinople was officially inaugurated on 11 May AD330, with the Ottoman Turks who conquered this great city in 1453 and turned it into Istanbul. The combined glories of two lost worlds – the Ottoman empire was dissolved in 1922 – beget an utterly enrapturing blockbuster. I lost all track of time in this dream city of gold and ivory.

Even the human form is magically transfigured here into mineral and metal. The martyred abbess St Eudokia becomes a Byzantine icon of marble inlaid with coloured glass, wearing a crown of precious stones and an exquisite dress patterned with diamonds and decorated with pearls and emeralds. It is a masterpiece of abstract splendour that looks like a Klimt painting, but this icon can’t have influenced him because it wasn’t excavated until 1929.

Beat that for splendour – but the Ottoman empire could. A 16th-century kaftan, probably worn by Sultan Selim II, irradiates you with light-giving yellow and geometric white designs, part flower, part solar disc: it is made of zerbaft, a fabric said to be “woven from gold”, and looks it.

Staggering. But it’s not all precious metals. There are blue and white glazed tiles from a hamam that conjure images of steaming bathhouse comfort, along with a bath wrap of red silk. Wooden foot supports from a women’s hamam are inlaid with mother of pearl. As a wall text points out, if you have a nice bathroom you are living under the influence of Ottoman Istanbul.

The story all begins with Constantine, the emperor who accepted Christianity. He created New Rome, or Constantinople, at a strategic point between Europe and Asia to deal with the unmanageably vast Roman empire. You can see here sublime relics of this eastern capital including a mosaic from Constantine’s palace of a huge moustached face of weird godlike mystery.

That luxury was seen in public places too. Constantine brought the Roman policy of “bread and circuses” here and adorned the chariot racing hub, the Hippodrome, with artistic masterpieces pillaged from ancient Greece and Egypt. Here you can see the bronze head of a snake that was part of the celebrated Serpent Column and a less scary goose. Ivory reliefs portray consuls at the Hippodrome, holding a mappa, the piece of cloth they let fall to start the games. These men are ancient Romans, with names such as Flavius Taurus Clementinus but by their time, the sixth century AD, the Roman empire in western Europe and north Africa was finished.

Yet it lived on in the east. Byzantine schoolchildren studied Homer and monasteries preserved Plato’s writings.
